  autocast, hidden 192, 12 layers, 256 slices, 10,000 tokens, batch 1):
  old code **9.15 GiB (9.82 GB)** — reproducing the 9.81 GB recorded in
  the V6 arm to 0.1%, which validates the instrument — new code
  **3.33 GiB (3.58 GB)**, a **2.75x** reduction.

**Why it matters.** MT2 now trains in *less* peak memory than
GeoTransolver (3.6 GB vs 4.6 GB at the same token count), with no
change in its function. The critic's cost finding (C16) is resolved at
the implementation, not by argument, and the "retired: equal-or-lower
cost" paragraph in chapter 17 is superseded — with the caveat that the
GeoTransolver figure is from a training run (optimizer state included)
while this is forward+backward; on a 9M-parameter model the optimizer
adds under 0.2 GB, and the old-code agreement to 0.1% shows the
instruments are comparable. The V6 resource-normalized comparison
(v5a4 anchor decode vs v3c at matched VRAM) was framed against the
old memory; at the new memory, v3c at 10,000 tokens (3.6 GB) fits
under v5a4's 6.35 GB with room to spare, which strengthens, not weakens,
that closure. The memory headroom also changes what is affordable:
more tokens per case, larger hidden width, or the latent volume tokens
of Branch V at no net memory increase over the old baseline.

**2026-09-06 addendum — it is faster too.** Same local instrument (RTX
4090, 10,000 tokens, bf16 autocast, hidden 192, 12 layers): training
step 364 → 283 ms (**1.29x**), forward-only step 184 → 161 ms (1.14x).
The removed projection was (B, N, S, 8) → (B, N, S, hidden/2) per
layer, about 2 GFLOP each way, so the speed-up is the compute twin of
the memory saving. Unchanged function, less memory, less time.

**Scope note on running experiments.** The running lanes (LVT, B1,
controls, Transolver) keep the job-local code snapshot they started
with; they are unaffected. New runs pick up the rewrite. Because the
function is unchanged to roundoff, checkpoints are interchangeable.

**What this does not say.** It says nothing about accuracy — the A35b
readout of the *no-relational-geometry* variant (which removes the
features, not just their cost) is a separate question, read out below.

## 2026-09-06 — A35b verdict: raw seeds cost nothing (0.99x), no relational routing costs 1.16x; no single MT2 contract carries the 35-case advantage, and the A35 "equivariance is not the carrier" reading is weakened {#sec-nb-a35b-verdict}

**Setting.** MeshTransformer2 (MT2) is 2.9x more accurate than both
GeoTransolver and plain Transolver at 35 HiLift training cases
(@sec-nb-hl-ladder-dataeff, @sec-nb-t1-35-verdict). A35
(@sec-nb-a35-verdict) removed one ingredient at a time and found that
adding raw coordinates (breaking the SE(3) contract) costs 4%, turning
measure weights off *helps* 12%, and the similarity gauge costs 8%. A35b
tested the two remaining single-factor candidates: the invariant seed
set (replaced by the raw vectors [r, n, d], `seed_mode=raw`) and the
anchor-relational routing (`use_relational_geo=false`, Transolver-style
feature-only slicing in the encoder).

**Result** (35 cases, lr 1e-3, 500 epochs, shared 180-case val,
pressure rel-L2; reference MT2 ladder 0.135 / 0.141, mean 0.138):

| ablation | s42 / s43 | vs reference |
|---|---|---|
| invariant seeds → raw [r, n, d] | 0.1377 / 0.1366 | **0.99x** |
| relational routing off (encoder) | 0.1579 / 0.1629 | **1.16x** |

**Preregistered reading.** A carrier was defined as ≥ 1.5x (≥ 0.21);
"distributed" as neither ≥ 1.3x; the whole-line falsifier as both within
1.15x. Raw seeds are exactly neutral; relational routing sits at 1.16x —
a real but small contribution, one hundredth over the falsifier line
and far below the carrier bar. **Verdict: distributed.** Across five
single-factor ablations no ingredient moves the 35-case error by more
than 16%, in either direction, while the gap to the Transolver family is
190%.

**A correction to the A35 reading.** A35 concluded that "exact
equivariance is NOT what buys the data-efficiency" because adding raw
coordinates cost only 4%. That is too strong. Every MT2 variant tested,
including the raw-coordinate and raw-seed ones, *retains an invariant
path*: the relational invariants (distance, log-distance and six
direction cosines to each slice anchor) are still present in every
encoder layer of the raw-seed variant, and in every decoder read block
of the no-relational-geometry variant (the ablation flag reaches only
the encoder). What A35/A35b establish is that the *exactness* of the
contract is not load-bearing and that no *one* route to invariant
information is; they do not establish that invariant information is
dispensable, because no variant was ever without it. The baselines, by
contrast, receive only raw centered coordinates, normals and the
freestream vector, and must learn every drive-relative quantity — most
importantly the local incidence n·d — from data. That asymmetry is the
one candidate that every ablation so far has left untouched, and it is
the subject of the transplant test preregistered next
(@sec-nb-inv-prereg).

**Retrodiction it must satisfy.** On DrivAerML the freestream is fixed
along +x for every case, so n·d = n_x and r̂·d ∝ x are *already* raw
inputs; the hypothesis therefore predicts no small-data advantage there
— which is what the G1 ladder found (parity at n = 14,
@sec-nb-g1g2-verdict). On HiLift the angle of attack spans 4–22°, so
the incidence is a genuinely new, case-dependent quantity, and the
advantage appears. The hypothesis also predicts that the advantage
*shrinks* with data as the baselines learn the coupling, which is the
observed 2.9x → 1.4–2.5x → 1.0x ladder.

## 2026-09-06 — Branch V falsified: latent volume tokens are 3.7x behind GeoTransolver and 1.43x *worse* than the plain interior decode; the interior gap is not closed by off-surface tokens along anchor normals {#sec-nb-lvt-verdict}

**Setting.** On the boundary→interior task (DrivAerML volume fields
from the surface alone), GeoTransolver's queries-as-interacting-tokens
lead MT2's passive equivariant decode by 2.57x on interior pressure
(@sec-nb-v0-verdict), with MT2's deficit growing with distance from the
wall (@sec-nb-v0-sdf-band). Branch V (`results/mt3_preregistration_skeleton_2026-09-03.md`,
addendum) proposed equivariant latent volume tokens (LVT): 769 tokens
placed off each slice anchor along its mean normal at 0.5, 1 and 2 RMS
radii, plus the centroid, joining the encoder as interacting tokens so
that interior queries could read off-surface context while remaining
exactly query-independent. Preregistered: LVT/GT ≤ 1.5 confirms;
≥ 2.0 falsifies.

**Result** (500 epochs, 2 seeds, 48 val cases, interior rel-L2):

| arm | pressure | velocity | nut | pressure vs GT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GeoTransolver-volume | 0.0620 | 0.1334 | 0.0939 | 1.00 |
| MT2-interior (SDF normal) | 0.1596 | 0.3075 | 0.3719 | 2.57x |
| **MT2-interior + LVT** | **0.2283** | 0.3709 | 0.5811 | **3.68x** |

**The falsifier fires (3.68 ≥ 2.0), and the arm is worse than its own
base by 1.43x** on pressure, 1.21x on velocity and 1.56x on nut, on both
seeds (0.2326 / 0.2239 vs 0.1662 / 0.1529). The pilot's 1.26x deficit at
50 epochs did not close with training; it widened.

**What it does and does not establish.** The preregistered
interpretation of the falsifier was "interaction at the query itself is
required". The result is consistent with that, but it does not prove
it, because the LVT tokens did not merely fail to help — they hurt,
which points at the construction rather than the hypothesis: 769
near-body tokens with near-identical invariant seeds entered the
measure-weighted slice routing that the boundary tokens rely on, and
the anchor-normal offsets (0.5–2 RMS radii) do not reach the region
where the deficit is largest (the mid and far bands). The clean
statement is: **off-surface latent tokens placed along anchor normals,
as interacting tokens in MT2's routing, degrade the interior decode.**
Branch V as built is closed. Two designs remain unmeasured and are
recorded, not launched: (i) a *wake-aligned* probe set (tokens along the
freestream direction downstream of the body, where the volumetric
structure of an external flow actually lives), and (ii) the
canonical-probe-set hybrid named in the preregistration, in which a
fixed request-independent probe lattice interacts GeoTransolver-style
and queries decode from it. Neither launches before the small-data
carrier question (@sec-nb-inv-prereg) is settled, because that result
decides which architecture the interior work should build on.

**Standing of the interior task.** GeoTransolver 0.062, MT2-interior
0.160, kernel decoder 0.496 (closed). The honest product statement is
unchanged: GeoTransolver for interior accuracy; MT2 for exact contracts
and query independence at a 2.6x interior-accuracy price.

## 2026-09-06 — INV transplant preregistered: give GeoTransolver and Transolver MT2's three drive-relative invariants as inputs at 35 cases; if they recover, the small-data carrier is a portable feature, not an architecture {#sec-nb-inv-prereg}

**Question.** Five single-factor ablations of MeshTransformer2 (A35,
A35b) have failed to name what carries its 2.9x accuracy advantage over
both Transolver-family baselines at 35 HiLift training cases. The one
asymmetry no ablation touched is that every MT2 variant *has* the
drive-relative invariants — the local incidence n·d, the radial
direction cosine r̂·d and the radius |r|/L, in MT2's seed set and in
its relational features — while the baselines receive raw centered
coordinates, normals and the freestream vector and must learn those
bilinear couplings from data. On HiLift the angle of attack varies
4–22°, so the incidence is the leading-order physics; on DrivAerML the
freestream is fixed and the same quantities are already raw inputs,
which retrodicts the absent small-data advantage there.

**Arm INV (launched now; 4 lanes, `highlift/hl_inv_aga.sbatch`).** A
job-local datapipe transform `ComputeDriveInvariants` writes a per-cell
feature `drive_inv = [n·d, r̂·d, |r|/8]` (r relative to the mesh
centroid, L = 8 exactly as in MT2's constant gauge) after `CenterMesh`
and `ComputeSurfaceNormals`; the `super_scarce` dataset variant
`highlift_surface_super_scarce_inv.yaml` adds it, and the model
configs `transolver_surface_inv.yaml` (embedding 6 → 9 dims) and
`geotransolver_surface_inv.yaml` (functional_dim 6 → 9) append it to
the per-cell inputs. Everything else is the frozen ladder protocol:
35 cases, 500 epochs, 10k points, bf16, no augmentation, 2 seeds; each
baseline at its own better learning rate at this rung (Transolver
3e-3, GeoTransolver 1e-3); scored on the shared 180-case val set.
The runs are `inv_hl_{transolver,geotransolver}_super_scarce_*`.

**Predictions in readout units** (reference: MT2 0.138; Transolver
0.40; GeoTransolver 0.39; the log-midpoint between 0.40 and 0.138 is
0.235):

- *Carrier identified* if both baselines land ≤ 0.235 (at least halfway
  to MT2 in log-error) — and *fully identified* if ≤ 0.16 (within 1.15x
  of MT2), in which case the honest hero statement becomes "explicit
  drive-relative invariant inputs buy ~2.9x data efficiency on
  parametric-freestream problems; MT2 has them built in".
- *Falsifier:* both baselines ≥ 0.30 (less than 20% of the log-gap
  closed) → the invariant inputs are not the carrier and the advantage
  lies in MT2's routing/decoder structure as a whole (the A35b
  "distributed" verdict stands as the final word on the surface task).
- Mixed (one recovers, one does not) is read per architecture and
  reported as such; between 0.235 and 0.30 is "partial" and not a
  carrier claim.

**Why this matters either way.** If the features carry it, the result
is portable to every point-cloud surrogate and *explains* three
observations at once (HiLift gap, DrivAerML null, gap closing with
data). If they do not, the program has excluded inputs, exactness,
seeds, weights, gauge and encoder routing, and the remaining structure
(passive relational decoder + slice MLP) becomes the object of the next
discriminator. The sealed test split is not touched.

## 2026-09-06 — Steel-man controls complete (4 of 4) and Transolver's better learning rate at 210 read out: the data-efficiency ladder is final — 2.9x at 35, 1.3–2.5x at 210, parity at 1,260 {#sec-nb-ctrl-complete}

**Result** (shared 180-case val, pressure rel-L2, 2 seeds;
`results/t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json`, refreshed):

| arm | s42 / s43 | vs MT2 at the same rung |
|---|---|---|
| GeoTransolver, 210 cases, lr 1e-3, **1,000 epochs** | 0.152 / 0.128 | 2.2x (MT2 0.064) |
| Transolver, 210 cases, **lr 3e-3** | 0.089 / 0.083 | **1.34x** |

**Controls.** The last GeoTransolver control is the only one of the four
that beat its ladder lane (0.140 mean vs 0.159, 1.13x), which says
GeoTransolver at 210 cases was mildly under-trained at 500 epochs; it
remains 2.2x behind MeshTransformer2 (MT2) and nowhere near the
preregistered falsifier (1.2x MT2 = 0.077). Across the four controls —
higher learning rate and doubled epochs at both small rungs — the best
GeoTransolver result at 35 cases is 0.373 (bar 0.166) and at 210 cases
0.128 (bar 0.077). **The data-efficiency result is not a protocol
artefact of learning rate or training length.** The hero figure's
provisional status is lifted.

**Transolver.** At 210 cases the higher learning rate helps Transolver
slightly (0.086 vs 0.0905 mean), as predicted (0.08–0.10 band); the
falsifier of the 1.4x statement (≤ 0.070) did not fire. The final
same-family number at 210 is **1.34x MT2**, and the hero figure — which
picks each baseline's better learning rate per rung — now shows 1.3x.

**Final ladder statement.** Against GeoTransolver: 2.9x / 2.5x / 1.0x at
35 / 210 / 1,260 cases. Against plain Transolver (no geometry encoder):
2.9x / 1.3x / (not run). The mechanism is the open question, and the INV
transplant (@sec-nb-inv-prereg) is the running test.

## 2026-09-06 — The slope objection, answered honestly, and the W2 wave preregistered: power (third seed), curve fill (510-case rung), floor test (20k tokens), mechanism (single-AoA split), engineering readout (forces) {#sec-nb-w2-prereg}

**The objection.** An adversarial reader of @fig-hilift-data-efficiency
can say: MeshTransformer2 (MT2) wins at small n by *flattening* the
scaling curve, so extrapolated to, say, 5,000 cases GeoTransolver would
be ahead. The measured log-log segment slopes support the premise:

| segment | GeoTransolver | MT2 |
|---|---|---|
| 35 → 210 cases | 0.50 | 0.43 |
| 210 → 1,260 cases | 0.74 | 0.25 |

GeoTransolver steepens; MT2 flattens. A power-law extrapolation to
5,000 cases gives ≈ 0.015 for GeoTransolver and ≈ 0.029 for MT2.

**The response.** (i) The claim is a *data-efficiency* claim in the
regime where every production CFD dataset in this program lives
(35–1,260 cases); it is not a scaling-law claim and the book will not
make one. (ii) The flattening may be a **shared floor**, not an MT2
property: at full data the two architectures share 70% of their
residual on identical points (N1, @sec-nb-n1-verdict) and accuracy still
rises with tokens per case (V6: 6,500 → 10,000 tokens was worth 8%),
which is what a resolution or label floor looks like. If both are
approaching the same floor, GeoTransolver's steep segment cannot
continue either. (iii) Structure-versus-flexibility is the expected
shape (bias–variance): a model with more built-in prior starts lower and
has less left to learn from data. (iv) The way to *defeat* rather than
concede the objection is the INV transplant (@sec-nb-inv-prereg): if the
carrier is the drive-relative invariant inputs, GeoTransolver plus those
three features should inherit MT2's small-data floor while keeping its
own large-data slope, dominating at every n.

**W2 wave, preregistered before any of it runs.** All lanes use the
frozen ladder protocol (500 epochs, 10,000 tokens unless stated, bf16,
no augmentation, lr 1e-3 for GeoTransolver and MT2, 3e-3 for
Transolver, shared val) and `highlift/hl_wave2_aga.sbatch` with a lane
table (`highlift/wave2_lanes.tsv`). Splits are the dataset's own curated
manifests (`splits.md`): `super_scarce` ⊂ `scarce` ⊂ `medium` ⊂ `full`
are nested with the same 180-case val; `single_aoa_12` holds 126
geometries at a single angle of attack with its own 18-geometry val.

- **W2-A power: third seed (44)** at 35 and 210 cases for MT2,
  GeoTransolver and Transolver (6 lanes). *Prediction:* every seed-44
  result lands inside the seed-42/43 spread ×1.5; *falsifier:* any
  architecture's third seed moves its rung mean by more than 15%.
  Reported together with the paired per-case statistics on the 180
  shared val cases (fraction of cases MT2 wins; sign-test p), computed
  now from the existing evaluations
  (`results/hilift_paired_stats_2026-09-06.json`).
- **W2-B curve fill: the 510-case `medium` rung** for MT2,
  GeoTransolver, and Transolver at both learning rates (8 lanes).
  *Prediction in readout units:* GeoTransolver 0.075–0.095, MT2
  0.048–0.056 (MT2/GT ≈ 0.6, continuing the monotone 0.35 → 0.41 → 0.98
  approach to parity). *Falsifier for the "smooth approach to a shared
  floor" reading:* MT2/GT at 510 ≥ 0.9 (parity already, i.e. MT2's curve
  is flat from 210 on) — that would mean the crossover is near 1,260 and
  the slope objection stands in full.
- **W2-C floor test: 1,260 cases at 20,000 tokens** for MT2 and
  GeoTransolver (4 lanes). *Prediction if the floor is the protocol's:*
  both improve by a similar factor (within 5 percentage points of each
  other; the V6 token effect suggests 5–10%). *Falsifier (objection
  stands):* GeoTransolver improves by ≥ 10 percentage points more than
  MT2.
- **W2-D mechanism: single angle of attack.** MT2 vs GeoTransolver on
  `single_aoa_12` (126 geometries, AoA fixed at 12°, val 18) and on a
  matched-size mixed-AoA control `mixed126` (126 cases drawn from
  `full_train` with a fixed seed, val = the shared 180), 2 seeds each
  (8 lanes). The drive-invariant hypothesis says MT2's advantage comes
  from representing the freestream-direction dependence exactly, so it
  should be *absent* when the direction is fixed (as on DrivAerML) and
  present when it varies. *Prediction:* MT2/GT ≈ 0.40–0.55 on
  `mixed126`; MT2/GT ≥ 0.80 on `single_aoa_12`. *Falsifier:* MT2/GT
  ≤ 0.60 on `single_aoa_12` → the carrier is not the direction
  dependence.
- **W2-E engineering readout, no compute:** lift and drag coefficient
  errors from the existing 35- and 210-case evaluations (the recipe's
  inference already integrates CD/CL per case). Reported as MAE relative
  to the mean magnitude, per architecture; a first look at 35 cases
  shows MT2's CL error 3.2x smaller than GeoTransolver's (19,100 vs
  60,500 in the dataset's dimensional force units; 3.1% vs 9.7% of the
  mean) — recorded here before the full table so it cannot be
  cherry-picked later.

Budget: 26 new lanes (104 GPUs) plus the 6 running; within the 128-GPU
envelope. The sealed test splits are not touched.

**W2-F preregistered, queued behind W2-A/D (budget).** The data-efficiency
rungs are subsamples of `full_train`, in which a validation geometry may
appear at other angles of attack; the dataset's `geometry` family
(`geometry`, `geometry_scarce`, `geometry_super_scarce` = 1,260 / 210 /
40 cases; 18 val geometries never seen at any angle) is the
unseen-geometry ladder its designers call the primary ML challenge
(`splits.md`). It is unmeasured here. Arm: MT2 vs GeoTransolver on
`geometry_scarce` (210) and `geometry_super_scarce` (40 = 4 geometries ×
10 angles), 2 seeds each (8 lanes), frozen protocol, scored on the
18-geometry val (180 cases). *Prediction:* MT2/GT ratios match the
same-size data-efficiency rungs within 0.1 (≈ 0.41 at 210; ≈ 0.35–0.5 at
40), i.e. the advantage is not geometry memorization. *Falsifier:* MT2/GT
≥ 0.8 on either rung → the small-data advantage depends on having seen
the geometry at another angle, which would re-attribute it to angle
interpolation rather than data efficiency. Launches when the running
count allows.

## 2026-09-06 — W2-E readout: MT2 beats both baselines on 360 of 360 paired validation cases at 35 training cases (median per-case ratio 3.2x), and predicts lift and drag coefficients to 3% where GeoTransolver reaches 11–17% {#sec-nb-w2e-paired}

**Why.** Two seeds with tight spreads is suggestive; the critic (C-power)
asked for a paired per-case statistic. The 180 validation cases are
shared across every rung and architecture, so each case can be scored
as a paired comparison (seed 42 with 42, seed 43 with 43: 360 pairs per
rung). The recipe's inference also integrates lift and drag coefficients
per case, which turns the field error into the number an aerodynamicist
uses. Computed from the existing evaluations
(`highlift/paired_stats.py` → `results/hilift_paired_stats_2026-09-06.json`);
no new training.

**Paired pressure rel-L2, MeshTransformer2 (MT2) vs each baseline:**

| training cases | baseline | cases MT2 wins | sign-test p | median ratio (baseline / MT2) | 10th–90th pct |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | GeoTransolver | **360 / 360** | 9e-109 | **3.18** | 1.82–4.75 |
| 35 | Transolver (lr 3e-3) | **360 / 360** | 9e-109 | **3.20** | 1.91–4.71 |
| 210 | GeoTransolver | 354 / 360 | 3e-96 | 3.07 | 1.67–4.01 |
| 210 | Transolver (lr 3e-3) | 330 / 360 | 5e-65 | 1.52 | 1.04–1.95 |
| 1,260 | GeoTransolver | 258 / 360 | 1e-16 | 1.06 | 0.90–1.20 |

At 35 cases there is **no validation case, on either seed, where either
baseline beats MT2**; the *worst* tenth of cases still favour MT2 by
1.8x. At 210 the same holds against GeoTransolver (98%); against
Transolver MT2 wins 92% of cases with a median 1.5x. At 1,260, where
the means are at parity (0.98), MT2 is nominally better on 72% of cases
with a median 1.06x — a small but statistically unambiguous per-case
edge that the seed-mean comparison hides.

**Force coefficients** (mean absolute error relative to the mean
magnitude of the true coefficient over the 180 cases, averaged over
seeds):

| training cases | architecture | CD | CL |
|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | **MT2** | **3.3%** | **3.0%** |
| 35 | GeoTransolver | 17.1% | 11.0% |
| 35 | Transolver | 11.9% | 8.1% |
| 210 | MT2 | 1.9% | 1.5% |
| 210 | GeoTransolver | 3.2% | 2.5% |
| 210 | Transolver | 2.0% | 1.5% |
| 1,260 | MT2 | 1.4% | 0.9% |
| 1,260 | GeoTransolver | 1.2% | 0.8% |

**What it establishes.** The data-efficiency result is not a
seed-level accident: it holds case by case, on every case, at the rung
where it is largest. In engineering terms, **from 35 CFD runs MT2
predicts lift and drag coefficients of unseen high-lift configurations
to about 3%, where the Transolver-family baselines are at 8–17%**; at
210 runs all three are within 1.5–3%, and at 1,260 the two-seed
means are indistinguishable (GeoTransolver nominally ahead on forces by
0.1–0.2 points, MT2 nominally ahead per case on the field). The 3%
number at 35 cases is the "useful" statement of the result: a
few-dozen-run design-of-experiments budget yields a force surrogate of
practical accuracy.

**Caveats.** Coefficients are integrated with the recipe's reference
area of 1 (dimensional force units), so the *relative* errors are the
meaningful quantity; the validation set is in-distribution
(random cases of the same 180-geometry × 10-angle design); and the
1,260-case force comparison is within seed noise.

## 2026-09-06 — Free mechanism probe on the 35-case models: MT2's advantage holds at every angle of attack (2.2–4.3x), at the one angle absent from training (18°, 2.5x), and on never-seen geometries (3.0x); the baselines' error is flat across all strata {#sec-nb-strat35}

**Why.** Two hypotheses about the 35-case carrier make different
predictions about *where* on the validation set the advantage lives.
If MeshTransformer2 (MT2) wins by representing the freestream-direction
dependence exactly, its edge should be largest at angles the baselines
have seen least. If it wins by geometry memorization, the edge should
collapse on validation geometries absent from the 35 training cases.
Both are readable now from the existing evaluations
(`highlift/stratified_35.py` → `results/hilift_stratified_35_2026-09-06.json`);
geometric-mean pressure rel-L2 over cases and both seeds.

**By angle of attack** (the 35 training cases contain 3–7 cases per
angle and **none at 18°**; 33 distinct geometries):

| AoA [deg] | train cases | val cases | MT2 | GeoTransolver | Transolver | GT / MT2 | T / MT2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 4 | 17 | 0.106 | 0.354 | 0.329 | 3.3 | 3.1 |
| 6 | 4 | 18 | 0.098 | 0.338 | 0.330 | 3.4 | 3.4 |
| 8 | 3 | 19 | 0.098 | 0.339 | 0.351 | 3.5 | 3.6 |
| 10 | 4 | 13 | 0.096 | 0.350 | 0.362 | 3.7 | 3.8 |
| 12 | 3 | 17 | 0.088 | 0.377 | 0.390 | 4.3 | 4.4 |
| 14 | 3 | 15 | 0.121 | 0.418 | 0.439 | 3.5 | 3.6 |
| 16 | 7 | 15 | 0.135 | 0.445 | 0.468 | 3.3 | 3.5 |
| **18** | **0** | 27 | 0.167 | 0.412 | 0.443 | **2.5** | 2.7 |
| 20 | 3 | 15 | 0.186 | 0.407 | 0.415 | 2.2 | 2.2 |
| 22 | 4 | 24 | 0.184 | 0.432 | 0.435 | 2.4 | 2.4 |

**By whether the validation geometry appears in training at another angle:**

| geometry seen in train | val cases | MT2 | GeoTransolver | Transolver | GT / MT2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| yes | 34 | 0.113 | 0.386 | 0.387 | 3.4 |
| **no** | **146** | 0.130 | 0.388 | 0.398 | **3.0** |

**Three readings.** (i) **The advantage is not geometry memorization:**
on the 146 never-seen geometries MT2 is 3.0x ahead; seeing a geometry
at another angle helps MT2 by 15% and GeoTransolver not at all.
(ii) **The advantage is not angle memorization either:** at 18°, which
no training case has, MT2 interpolates smoothly between its 16° and
20° errors (0.135 → 0.167 → 0.186) and stays 2.5x ahead. (iii) **The
baselines' error is flat** — 0.33–0.47 at every angle and identical on
seen and unseen geometries — while MT2's error tracks the physics
(0.09–0.10 in attached flow, 0.17–0.19 post-stall, where the ratio
falls to 2.2–2.5x). Flat error across every stratum is what a model
that has not yet begun to fit the case-to-case variation looks like; a
dataset-mean predictor would be the natural reference and is worth
computing (recorded as a to-do, not a result). The picture at 35 cases
is therefore not "MT2 is 3x better at the same task" but "**MT2 has
learned the task and the Transolver family has not yet started**",
which is exactly what a sample-complexity carrier (a coupling the
baselines must learn from data and MT2 gets for free) would produce,
and what the INV transplant (@sec-nb-inv-prereg) tests directly.

**Addendum — the reference predictors, computed** (from the stored
per-point predictions and labels of the seed-42 evaluations, gauge
pressure p − p_inf, geometric mean over the 180 cases;
`highlift/mean_predictor.py` → `results/hilift_reference_predictors_35_2026-09-06.json`).
Predicting the freestream pressure everywhere scores 1.00 by
definition; the dataset-mean constant 0.94; each case's own mean (an
oracle constant) 0.93. On the same scale GeoTransolver scores 0.63,
Transolver 0.68 and MT2 0.25. The median per-case correlation between
predicted and true pressure is 0.76 (GeoTransolver), 0.69 (Transolver)
and **0.97 (MT2)**; the worst decile is 0.69 / 0.60 / 0.93. So reading
(iii) above is too strong as written: at 35 cases the baselines *have*
learned something — about 1.5x better than a constant, explaining
roughly half the pointwise variance — while MT2 is 4x better than a
constant and explains 93%. The flatness of the baselines' error
across angles and geometries reflects a model that captures the
coarse, case-independent pressure pattern (suction over the wing,
stagnation at the leading edge) and little of the case-to-case
variation that the angle and the geometry drive; MT2 captures most of
that variation. (The recipe's headline metric uses a different
normalization, so 0.25 here corresponds to 0.138 there; ratios between
rows, not the absolute values, are the comparable quantities.)

**Bearing on W2-F.** The unseen-geometry prediction (ratios within 0.1
of the same-size rung) is already met at this rung on the 146-case
subset; W2-F's own lanes remain the clean test because the `geometry`
splits hold out *all* angles of the val geometries by construction.

## 2026-09-06 — Free uncertainty signal: at 35 cases, disagreement between two MT2 seeds rank-correlates with the per-case error (Spearman 0.67); the baselines' seed disagreement is anticorrelated with theirs {#sec-nb-uq35}

**Why.** A surrogate trained from a few dozen CFD runs is only useful in
practice if it can flag the cases it gets wrong. The cheapest
uncertainty estimate is the disagreement between independently seeded
models, and the program already has two seeds of every 35-case model
with stored per-point predictions. Computed on gauge pressure over the
180 shared validation cases (`highlift/ensemble_uq_35.py` →
`results/hilift_ensemble_uq_35_2026-09-06.json`).

| architecture (35 cases) | error seed 42 / 43 | two-seed ensemble error | ensemble gain | seed disagreement | Spearman(disagreement, error) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **MT2** | 0.253 / 0.261 | 0.251 | 1.03x | 0.112 | **+0.67** |
| GeoTransolver | 0.633 / 0.659 | 0.634 | 1.02x | 0.221 | −0.20 |
| Transolver | 0.678 / 0.671 | 0.671 | 1.01x | 0.124 | −0.47 |

(Same gauge-pressure scale as @sec-nb-strat35's addendum; ratios are
what transfer to the recipe metric.)

**Three readings.** (i) **MT2 knows when it is wrong:** the cases on
which its two seeds disagree most are the cases with the largest error
(rank correlation 0.67, on 180 cases). A two-seed MT2 therefore ships
with a usable per-case confidence flag at no extra inference cost
beyond the second model. (ii) **The baselines do not:** their seed
disagreement is *anti*-correlated with their error, so an ensemble
spread would mislead a user — the cases they agree on are the ones they
get most wrong, consistent with two models converging on the same
coarse, case-independent pattern (@sec-nb-strat35 addendum). (iii)
**Ensembling buys little for anyone** (1–3%): at 35 cases the errors
are dominated by a component shared across seeds — bias from too little
data, not variance — which is also why the data-efficiency result is so
seed-stable.

**Addendum — the other rungs** (`results/hilift_ensemble_uq_{210,1260}_2026-09-06.json`):

| rung | MT2 Spearman | GeoTransolver Spearman | Transolver Spearman | ensemble gain (MT2 / GT) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | **+0.67** | −0.20 | −0.47 | 1.03x / 1.02x |
| 210 | +0.64 | +0.65 | +0.60 | 1.03x / 1.05x |
| 1,260 | +0.15 | +0.19 | — | 1.04x / 1.03x |

So the ranking property is a **"the model has learned the task"**
property, not an MT2-specific one: at 210 cases all three architectures
have it (≈ 0.6–0.65), and MT2 simply reaches that state at 35 cases
where the baselines have not. At 1,260 cases the correlation collapses
for both architectures (0.15–0.19): the remaining error is no longer
seed-dependent model variance but something the two seeds — and, per
N1, the two *architectures* — share. That is a second, independent
line of evidence for the shared-floor reading of the flattened curve
(@sec-nb-w2-prereg), ahead of the W2-C token-count test.

**What this does not establish.** Calibration (whether the spread is
the right *size*) is not tested; only the ranking is. The
force-coefficient-level version is a cheap follow-up.

## 2026-09-07 — INV verdict: giving the baselines MT2's drive-relative invariants as inputs buys Transolver 1.35x and GeoTransolver nothing; the invariant inputs are not the small-data carrier {#sec-nb-inv-verdict}

**Setting.** The transplant test preregistered at @sec-nb-inv-prereg added
the three per-cell invariants MeshTransformer2 (MT2) builds internally —
the local incidence n·d, the radial cosine r̂·d and the radius |r|/8 — as
plain input features to GeoTransolver and to Transolver at 35 HiLift
training cases, each at its better learning rate, 2 seeds, frozen
protocol, shared 180-case validation set. The hypothesis was that the
baselines' small-data collapse comes from having to learn the
freestream-direction coupling from data.

**Result** (`results/inv_transplant_2026-09-07.json`):

| model @ 35 cases | without invariants | **with invariants** | change | vs MT2 (0.138) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Transolver (lr 3e-3) | 0.406 / 0.398 | **0.294 / 0.301** | 1.35x better | 2.15x |
| GeoTransolver (lr 1e-3) | 0.375 / 0.409 | **0.400 / 0.388** | none | 2.85x |

**Preregistered reading.** Carrier if both ≤ 0.235; falsifier if both
≥ 0.30. Transolver lands at 0.297, a hair inside the "partial" band;
GeoTransolver does not move at all. **The invariant inputs are not the
carrier.** Transolver gains a quarter of the log-gap; GeoTransolver —
which already has a geometry encoder that could in principle form these
features — gains nothing, so the coupling n·d is not what its small-data
failure is about. Combined with the five single-factor ablations of MT2
(@sec-nb-a35-verdict, @sec-nb-a35b-verdict), the program has now
excluded, one at a time: exactness of equivariance, the invariant seed
parameterization, the similarity gauge, measure weights, encoder
relational routing, and (from the baseline side) the availability of
drive-relative invariant inputs. None accounts for more than 16% on the
MT2 side or 35% on the baseline side, against a 190% gap. The honest
statement is that MT2's small-data advantage is a property of its
soft-slice design as a whole — equivariant anchors, relational routing
and readback, measure-weighted aggregation, invariant seeds, and the
training dynamics they induce together — and that no single transplantable
ingredient has been found. The mechanism question stays open; the next
discriminators (single-angle split, unseen-geometry ladder) test *where*
the advantage lives rather than *which knob* carries it.

**Retrodiction check.** The hypothesis predicted no small-data advantage
on DrivAerML (fixed freestream). That null is real, but the transplant
shows it cannot be attributed to the invariant inputs; the DrivAerML–HiLift
contrast remains unexplained and is recorded as such.

## 2026-09-07 — W2-A first readout: the third seed lands inside the two-seed spread for all three architectures at 35 cases (MT2 0.138, GeoTransolver 0.359, Transolver 0.409) {#sec-nb-w2a-35}

Seed 44, frozen protocol, shared val: MT2 **0.1376** (seeds 42/43:
0.1352/0.1410), GeoTransolver **0.3588** (0.375/0.409), Transolver at
lr 3e-3 **0.4089** (0.406/0.398). Every third seed is inside its
two-seed spread ×1.5 (prediction held; falsifier of a 15% move in any
rung mean not approached: three-seed means 0.138 / 0.381 / 0.404, i.e.
GT/MT2 2.76x, T/MT2 2.93x). The 210-case third seeds are still training.

## 2026-09-07 — B1 verdict: a raw-coordinate channel does not give MT2 GeoTransolver's smaller stall-extrapolation ratio (d = 12.7 / 13.3 vs GeoTransolver's 9.3); the falsifier fires {#sec-nb-b1-verdict}

**Setting.** On the sealed stall test (@sec-nb-hl-sealed-test)
GeoTransolver's degradation ratio d = test/val was 9.3 against MT2's
12.5, with MT2 keeping the lower absolute error. The preregistered
discriminator asked whether that ratio edge is carried by GeoTransolver's
raw-coordinate inputs: MT2 with the similarity gauge plus a
raw-coordinate channel (breaking SE(3) equivariance on purpose), 2
seeds, stall split, one permitted sealed-test evaluation. Bars: raw
features carry the ratio if d ≤ 11.0 *and* OOD pressure < 0.245; they do
not if d ≥ 12.0 or OOD pressure ≥ 0.255.

**Result** (`results/b1_raw_coordinate_discriminator_2026-09-07.json`;
pressure rel-L2):

| MT2 + raw coordinates, stall split | in-regime val (135) | sealed test (723) | d |
|---|---|---|---|
| seed 42 | 0.0206 | 0.262 | **12.7** |
| seed 43 | 0.0201 | 0.267 | **13.3** |
| MT2 reference (ladder) | 0.0204 / 0.0210 | 0.261 / 0.259 | 12.5 |
| GeoTransolver (ladder) | 0.0289 / 0.0304 | 0.274 / 0.277 | 9.3 |

**Both falsifier conditions fire** (d ≥ 12.0; OOD pressure ≥ 0.255). The
raw-coordinate channel leaves in-regime accuracy unchanged and leaves the
sealed-test error where it was (0.264 vs 0.260), so the ratio edge is not
a property of raw-coordinate inputs. Two disclosures: the arm was run
with the similarity gauge on as well as the raw channel (two differences
from the constant-gauge reference; the in-regime numbers show the gauge
did not move the floor), and an earlier reduction of this entry, taken
while the 723-case evaluation was still in progress (226/229 cases),
read 0.269/0.275 and d 13.1/13.7 — the numbers above are the complete
evaluation. What remains is the reading
the sealed-test entry already favoured: GeoTransolver's smaller ratio is
arithmetic of a higher in-regime floor, not better transfer, and both
architectures land at the same absolute OOD error (0.26–0.28). No
mechanism for a transfer advantage has been isolated because, on the
absolute readout, there is none to explain. This closes the last branch
of the earlier decision rule for a successor design; the design
question now rests on the small-data carrier and the interior
(@sec-nb-inv-verdict, @sec-nb-lvt-verdict).


## 2026-09-07 — Naming decision: the architecture is ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention); MeshTransformer2 becomes a compatibility alias {#sec-nb-isla-name}

A colleague pointed out that "MeshTransformer" is already the name of
other published architectures. Peter chose **ISLA — Invariant Slice
Attention** (pronounced "eye-la"; an *isla* is an island, a shape defined
entirely by its boundary) for the soft-slice equivariant architecture the
book calls MeshTransformer2 / MT2 in every entry above this one. The code
package moves to `physicsnemo/experimental/nn/isla/` with class `ISLA` and a
backward-compatible alias `MeshTransformer2`; the recipe config becomes
`isla_surface.yaml` with the old file kept as a pointer. Reader-facing
chapters use ISLA throughout. This notebook keeps its historical names;
artifact keys (`mt2_*`) and the `examples/cfd/mesh_transformer/` directory
are unchanged as provenance. The exact-kernel MeshTransformer keeps its
name in the archive.

## 2026-09-07 — W2-F launched (unseen-geometry ladder) with a GeoTransolver learning-rate steel-man at the single angle, on the strength of an early single-angle read {#sec-nb-w2f-launch}

**Why now.** The first two evaluated lanes of the single-angle mechanism
arm (one seed each; `single_aoa_12`, 126 geometries at 12°, validated on
18 geometries never seen at any angle) read ISLA 0.036 against
GeoTransolver 0.183 — a 5.0x gap where the drive-direction hypothesis
predicted the gap would *vanish* (@sec-nb-w2-prereg: ISLA/GT ≥ 0.80;
falsifier ≤ 0.60). That is one seed and no verdict yet, but it says the
advantage lives in generalizing across *geometries*, not across angles, so
the unseen-geometry ladder preregistered as W2-F is now the most
informative next measurement and launches with the GPU budget the
finished lanes freed.

**Arms (10 lanes, `highlift/hl_wave2_aga.sbatch` rows 26–35).**
W2-F: ISLA and GeoTransolver on `geometry_scarce` (210 training cases)
and `geometry_super_scarce` (40 cases = 4 geometries × 10 angles), 2 seeds
each, frozen protocol, scored on the 180 cases of the 18 held-out
geometries. Steel-man G: GeoTransolver on `single_aoa_12` at lr 3e-3 (its
alternative rate), 2 seeds, so the single-angle gap cannot be attributed
to the learning rate.

**Predictions in readout units** (W2-F unchanged from the prereg): ISLA/GT
within 0.1 of the same-size data-efficiency rungs (≈ 0.41 at 210;
0.35–0.5 at 40); *falsifier* ISLA/GT ≥ 0.8 on either rung (the advantage
would depend on having seen the geometry at another angle). G: the lr 3e-3
control lands within 1.2x of GeoTransolver's lr 1e-3 result; *falsifier* it
comes within 1.2x of ISLA (then the single-angle gap is a learning-rate
artefact and the mechanism reading is void).

## 2026-09-07 — W2-D verdict (single angle): at a fixed 12° angle of attack ISLA is 5.0x more accurate than GeoTransolver on 18 never-seen geometries (0.036 vs 0.179); the freestream-direction hypothesis is falsified in the opposite direction — the carrier is geometry generalization {#sec-nb-w2d-single-angle}

**Setting.** The strongest remaining hypothesis for ISLA's small-data
advantage on HiLift (@sec-nb-w2-prereg, arm D) was that ISLA wins by
representing the freestream-direction dependence exactly, so the
advantage should *vanish* when the angle of attack is fixed and only the
geometry varies. The dataset's `single_aoa_12` split is exactly that
instrument: 126 geometries at 12°, validated on 18 geometries never seen
at any angle (the dataset's held-out geometry set), frozen protocol, lr
1e-3 for both architectures, 2 seeds. Preregistered: ISLA/GT ≥ 0.80 on
this split if the hypothesis holds; **falsifier ISLA/GT ≤ 0.60**.

**Result** (`results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07.json`, arm `D_single_aoa_12`;
pressure rel-L2, 18 held-out geometries):

| model @ 126 geometries, one angle | seed 42 / 43 | mean | GT / ISLA |
|---|---|---|---|
| GeoTransolver | 0.175 / 0.183 | 0.179 | — |
| **ISLA** | **0.035 / 0.036** | **0.036** | **5.0x** |

Paired by geometry (two-seed means): ISLA is more accurate on **18 of
18**, with per-geometry ratios from 4.0x to 6.4x (median 4.9x) —
GeoTransolver's error is nearly flat across geometries (0.14–0.21)
while ISLA's spans 0.026–0.051. Force coefficients (MAE relative to the
mean magnitude): ISLA CL 0.6%, CD 1.6%; GeoTransolver CL 2.0%, CD 3.9%.

**Verdict.** ISLA/GT = 0.20: the falsifier fires by a factor of three,
and in the direction opposite to the prediction — fixing the angle makes
the gap *larger* (5.0x) than on the mixed-angle rungs (2.8x at 35 cases,
2.5x at 210). Together with the transplant test (@sec-nb-inv-verdict),
this closes the freestream-direction reading: what ISLA does with few
samples is generalize across *high-lift geometries* — flap and slat
deflections and the gaps between elements — and GeoTransolver, from 126
distinct geometries at one operating point, has not started to
(0.18 is where it sits at 35 mixed cases too). Two consequences:

- **Usefulness.** At a fixed operating point, 126 geometries give ISLA a
  surface-pressure error of 0.036 and lift to 0.6% — better than the
  1,260-case mixed-angle model (0.041), because the single-angle task is
  easier — while GeoTransolver needs the full 1,260 mixed cases to reach
  0.042. A design-of-experiments study at one flight condition is exactly
  the regime a wing designer works in.
- **Where the mechanism must live.** The carrier is not the drive
  invariants (transplant test), not exactness of equivariance, not the
  seed parameterization, not the gauge (single-factor ablations). It is
  whatever lets the soft-slice routing on relational invariants represent
  a new multi-element geometry from few examples. The DrivAerML contrast
  (smooth single-body morphs, GeoTransolver 1.2–1.3x ahead) fits: the
  advantage appears where geometry variation is multi-element and
  gap-dominated, not where it is a smooth deformation of one body.

**Pending controls.** The matched-size mixed-angle control (`mixed126`,
126 cases drawn from `full_train`, val = the shared 180) is partly in: ISLA
seed 43 reads 0.076 — fixing the angle halves ISLA's error at equal
training-set size — with GeoTransolver's lanes still evaluating. The
GeoTransolver lr 3e-3 steel-man at the single angle
(@sec-nb-w2f-launch) is training. Neither can rescue the hypothesis; both
bound the size of the effect.

## 2026-09-07 — Preregistered: geometry extrapolation on the `deflection` split — does ISLA's geometry generalization carry across a geometry-parameter boundary? {#sec-nb-deflection-prereg}

**Why.** The single-angle verdict (@sec-nb-w2d-single-angle) locates
ISLA's small-data advantage in generalizing across high-lift geometries.
Every out-of-distribution test so far crossed a *flow-regime* boundary
(angle of attack, stall), where no architecture generalizes. The
dataset's `deflection` split crosses a *geometry* boundary instead: it
sorts the 180 geometries by mean flap-and-slat deflection, trains and
validates on the lower 80% (1,260 train / 180 val cases, all angles) and
tests on the 36 most aggressive high-lift settings (360 cases, sealed). If
ISLA's edge is geometry generalization, this is the axis on which an
architecture-carried out-of-distribution result would appear first.

**Arm H (4 lanes, `highlift/hl_wave2_aga.sbatch` rows 36–39).** ISLA and
GeoTransolver, frozen protocol (lr 1e-3 both, 500 epochs, 10,000 tokens,
2 seeds), trained on `deflection_train`, in-regime validation on
`deflection_val`. The sealed `deflection_test` is evaluated exactly once
per checkpoint with the inference configuration of the earlier sealed
tests (resolution 10,000, validation-identical sampling seed), after
training completes and after this entry is committed; no reruns.

**Predictions in readout units** (pressure rel-L2; d = test / val).
In-regime: both near their full-split values (ISLA ≈ GeoTransolver ≈
0.04–0.05; GeoTransolver/ISLA within 0.9–1.15). Out of regime: if ISLA's
geometry generalization carries across the boundary, **ISLA's test error
≤ 0.7 × GeoTransolver's** with both d values well below the ≈10 seen on
the flow-regime axes (prediction: d ≤ 4 for ISLA). **Falsifier:** ISLA's
test error ≥ 0.9 × GeoTransolver's, or d ≥ 8 for both — then geometry
extrapolation behaves like regime extrapolation and coverage governs it
too. A GeoTransolver test error ≤ 0.7 × ISLA's would invert the reading
(GeoTransolver extrapolates geometry better) and is recorded as such.
Absolute test errors are reported alongside d because the ratio rewards a
higher in-regime floor (@sec-nb-hl-sealed-test).

## 2026-09-07 — Preregistered: query tokens — ISLA with interior queries as interacting tokens (GeoTransolver's interior mechanism on ISLA's equivariant routing) {#sec-nb-qt-prereg}

**Why.** On the boundary→interior task GeoTransolver leads ISLA's passive
decode 2.6x (@sec-nb-v0-verdict), and the one mechanism named for it is
token-level interaction at the query. Latent volume tokens placed along
anchor normals did not supply it (@sec-nb-lvt-verdict). The direct test is
to give ISLA the same mechanism: let the interior query points join the
encoder as interacting tokens, each carrying ISLA's five invariant seeds
{|q|, log|q|, q̂·d, q̂·n̂, n̂·d} with the SDF-gradient normal as n̂, a learned
measure weight and a learned token-type offset, and read the heads from the
query tokens. This keeps exact SE(3) covariance (all seeds are invariants,
the vector head is in the equivariant basis) and gives up exact query
independence — the same trade GeoTransolver makes, at the same 20,000-token
cost. Implemented as `query_tokens=True` in `ISLA` (commit 9d8fcfccd; 35
contract tests pass, including covariance and a documented
query-set-dependence check). Local cost at 10,000 + 10,000 tokens: 6.56 GiB
peak, 671 ms per step (RTX 4090, bf16), 8.87M parameters.

**Arm (`v0/v0_qt_aga.sbatch`, code snapshot `$T/code_isla`).** Frozen V0
protocol (DrivAerML volume, 435/48 cars, 10k surface + 10k interior points,
lr 1e-3, 500 epochs, similarity gauge on, SDF normals). Pilot gate first:
seeds 42 and 43 at 50 epochs (`v0p_isla_qt_sdf_seed*`), promoted to 500
epochs (`v0_isla_qt_sdf_seed*`) only if the pilot passes.

**Predictions in readout units** (interior pressure rel-L2, 48 val cars;
references: GeoTransolver-volume 0.062 full / 0.093 pilot; ISLA passive
SDF-normal decode 0.160 full / 0.269 pilot).
- *Pilot gate:* both seeds ≤ 0.20 at 50 epochs (clearly ahead of the passive
  pilot's 0.269, i.e. interaction is doing something); *gate fails* at
  ≥ 0.25 (the latent-token failure repeats: tokens dilute the routing).
- *Full-run prediction:* ISLA-QT/GT ≤ 1.3 on interior pressure (the gap
  closes to within the seed-and-protocol band), with velocity and ν_t
  ratios ≤ 1.5. *Falsifier:* ratio ≥ 2.0 → interaction at the query is not
  what ISLA's interior decode lacks; GeoTransolver's interior edge lies
  elsewhere (its coordinate-based token features, its slice count per
  token, or capacity), and the next discriminator is a GeoTransolver
  ablation rather than another ISLA variant.
- The surface task is untouched by this arm (interior queries are not
  present there); the interacting-query mode is an *interior* option.

## 2026-09-07 — Where GeoTransolver's single-angle error lives: uniformly over the surface, not at high-curvature points; the geometry failure is case-level {#sec-nb-curvature-strat}

**Question.** With ISLA 5.0x ahead at a fixed angle on never-seen
geometries (@sec-nb-w2d-single-angle), one mechanistic reading is that
GeoTransolver's raw-coordinate tokens fail on the sharp features of a
high-lift wing — leading edges, flap and slat gaps — where the local
geometry changes fastest between configurations. If so, its error should
concentrate at high-curvature points.

**Instrument.** For each of the 18 validation geometries (seed 42 models),
per-point squared gauge-pressure error and a curvature proxy computed from
the 10,000 sampled points alone (smallest-eigenvalue fraction of the local
PCA over 24 nearest neighbours, i.e. deviation from a local plane).
`highlift/error_vs_curvature.py` →
`results/hilift_error_vs_curvature_single_aoa_2026-09-07.json`.

**Result.** The most-curved 10% of points hold a median **10.3%** of
GeoTransolver's squared error and **8.7%** of ISLA's — both essentially
proportional to their point share. The GeoTransolver/ISLA RMS-error ratio
is 3.0 on the top-curvature decile, 2.9 on the flattest half, and 2.9
overall: **the gap is the same everywhere on the surface.**

**Reading.** GeoTransolver's failure on a new high-lift geometry is not a
local-detail problem that a finer or geometry-aware encoder would fix; it
is a case-level failure to map the configuration to its pressure field —
consistent with its flat error across angles and geometries at 35 cases
(@sec-nb-strat35) and with its near-constant error across the 18 held-out
geometries here (0.14–0.21). ISLA's error, by contrast, varies 2x across
geometries: it is fitting each configuration. Whatever ISLA's soft-slice
routing on relational invariants provides, it acts on the global
representation of the configuration, not on the resolution of sharp
features. This closes the "sharp-feature" mechanism without a training run.

**2026-09-07 addendum — the mixed-angle control is in.** `mixed126` (126
cases drawn from `full_train`, all angles, val = the shared 180): ISLA
**0.077 / 0.076**, GeoTransolver **0.190 / 0.262**, GeoTransolver/ISLA
**2.95x** (`results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07.json`, arm `D_mixed126`). The
preregistered mixed-control prediction was GeoTransolver 1.8–2.5x behind;
it is 3.0x behind, with a wide GeoTransolver seed spread. Read together:
at equal training-set size, fixing the angle *halves* ISLA's error (0.077
→ 0.036) and leaves GeoTransolver's nearly unchanged (0.226 → 0.179), so
the 5.0x single-angle gap is ISLA converting the simpler task into
accuracy while GeoTransolver does not. Both readings of arm D point the
same way: the advantage is geometry generalization, and it is largest at a
fixed operating point.

## 2026-09-07 — Query-token pilot gate: passed with margin — interior pressure 0.103 / 0.108 at 50 epochs, against 0.269 for the passive decode and 0.093 for GeoTransolver's own pilot; promoted to 500 epochs {#sec-nb-qt-pilot}

**Result** (50 epochs, 48 DrivAerML validation cars, interior rel-L2;
`v0_evals/v0p_isla_qt_sdf_seed*`):

| arm, 50 epochs | pressure | velocity | ν_t |
|---|---|---|---|
| GeoTransolver-volume (pilot, @sec-nb-v0-pilot) | 0.093 | — | — |
| ISLA passive decode, SDF normal (pilot) | 0.269 | 0.397 | 0.631 |
| ISLA passive decode + latent volume tokens (pilot) | 0.340 | 0.445 | 0.756 |
| **ISLA with query tokens** (seed 42 / 43) | **0.103 / 0.108** | 0.213 / 0.214 | 0.299 / 0.317 |

**Gate** (@sec-nb-qt-prereg): both seeds ≤ 0.20 → **passes**, by a factor
of two; the latent-token failure mode (≥ 0.25) does not recur. At pilot
length, giving ISLA's interior queries the ability to interact removes
2.6 of the 2.9x pilot gap to GeoTransolver: 0.105 against 0.093 is 1.13x.
Velocity and ν_t fall by 1.9x and 2.0x against the passive decode.

**Reading, and what it does not yet show.** This is the first interior
result in which an ISLA variant is within the seed-and-protocol band of
GeoTransolver, and it says the ingredient the passive decode lacked is
exactly the one named by the interior stratification — interaction at the
query, which supplies volumetric context — not local detail
(@sec-nb-v0-sdf-band) and not off-surface tokens without query information
(@sec-nb-lvt-verdict). The equivariance contract is intact (the mode is
covariant by construction, verified in fp64); exact query independence is
given up, as GeoTransolver gives it up. The full-run bar stands as
preregistered: ISLA-QT/GT ≤ 1.3 on interior pressure at 500 epochs
(GeoTransolver 0.062), falsifier ≥ 2.0. Both seeds launched
(`v0_isla_qt_sdf_seed42/43`, lanes 2–3 of `v0/v0_qt_aga.sbatch`; ~4 h at
0.27 s/step). Memory at 20,000 tokens: about 6 GB, which is where
GeoTransolver-volume sits on the same task.

**If it holds at 500 epochs**, the product statement changes from
"GeoTransolver for the interior, ISLA for the surface" to one
architecture: ISLA's equivariant routing for the surface and, with query
tokens, for the volume, at GeoTransolver's interior accuracy and ISLA's
small-data accuracy — which is the flagship the program set out to find.

## 2026-09-07 — Where ISLA's training memory goes: 76% is per-slice geometry; rebuilding it in backward is exact and cuts peak memory 2.3x for a 1.16x step {#sec-nb-geo-recompute}

**Setting.** ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention) routes every surface point to 256
learned slices through a softmax whose logits include a bias computed from eight
point-to-anchor invariants (distance, log-distance, three direction cosines
of the unit relative vector, the point-normal/anchor-normal cosine, the anchor
radius and the anchor direction cosine). Each of the 12 layers therefore builds
tensors of shape points × slices × {3, 1, 8}. An earlier exact rewrite
(@sec-nb-geo-pool-memory) pooled the invariants over slices before the
affine projection, which set the reference figure the book carried since:
3.6 GB peak at 10,000 tokens on an RTX 4090 in bf16, against GeoTransolver's
4.6 GB. Every training lane in flight today (W2, W2-F, deflection, query
tokens) runs the stored-activation code.

**Question.** With all cluster arms training and nothing to read out for
hours, the derivation-mode question was: what does autograd actually keep for
ISLA's backward pass, and is any of it a cheap function of small inputs that
could be rebuilt instead of stored? The idealized picture says the
(points × slices × hidden/2) tensor is gone and what is left should be modest;
the code says otherwise, because `rel`, `rel_hat`, `dist` and `geo` are all
inputs to differentiable ops that save them.

**Instrument.** A local bench (`isla_mem_attrib.py`) builds the recipe surface
model (hidden 192, 12 layers, 256 slices, 8,866,484 parameters), runs one
forward+backward at batch 1 and 10,000 random tokens under bf16 autocast, and
tallies every tensor autograd packs for backward by (shape, dtype) through
`torch.autograd.graph.saved_tensors_hooks`, counting each storage once.

**What we saw.** Stored activations total 3.15 GiB; peak step memory 3.29 GiB
(= 3.53 GB, the book's 3.6 GB on the same instrument). By shape:

| stored tensor | shape | dtype | total over 12 layers |
|---|---|---|---|
| relative position and its unit vector | (1, 10000, 256, 3) | fp32 | 0.70 GiB |
| invariants, cast for the routing Linear | (2560000, 8) | bf16 | 0.47 GiB |
| invariants, cast again for the pooling einsum | (10000, 256, 8) | bf16 | 0.47 GiB |
| routing softmax over points | (1, 10000, 256) | fp32 | 0.35 GiB |
| distance (and its clamp) | (1, 10000, 256, 1) | fp32 | 0.23 GiB |
| slice-mix softmaxes | (1, 10000, 256) ×3 | bf16 | 0.18 GiB |
| token path (hidden states, MLP, LayerNorm inputs) | (10000, 192/480/768) | mixed | 0.75 GiB |

**Per-slice geometry is 2.4 GiB of 3.15 GiB (76%).** All of it is an
elementwise function of five small tensors: point positions, normals and
drive direction (points × 3) and the per-layer anchor positions and normals
(slices × 3).

**Change.** A `geo_checkpoint` option (new keyword on the model and both
block types; recipe config `isla_surface.yaml` sets it on) wraps one
recompute region per layer, `_geo_region`, which builds the invariants,
applies the routing Linear, forms the slice mix from the pre-bias logits plus
that bias, and pools the invariants by the mix. It returns three small tensors
(bias and mix, points × slices; pooled invariants, points × 8); the
(points × slices × 3) and (points × slices × 8) tensors never leave the
region and are rebuilt in backward via `torch.utils.checkpoint`
(non-reentrant). A first version with two regions per layer (bias, then
pooling) rebuilt the invariants twice in backward and cost 1.67x step time;
fusing to one region is the version kept. The same region serves the
stored-activation path, so the two paths run identical arithmetic.

**Verification.** `test_geo_checkpoint_is_exact` (fp64, encoder and passive
decoder configurations): forward outputs `torch.equal`; every parameter
gradient within 1e-11 absolute. On the GPU under bf16 autocast, the
interleaved A/B bench (`isla_ab_time.py`, same weights and inputs, alternating
steps so drift from a co-tenant process cancels) reports forward bitwise
equal and maximum relative gradient difference 0.0. The A35b ablation path
without relational geometry (`use_relational_geo=False`) initially failed
(the region referenced a Linear that is not built in that mode); fixed and
covered by the existing ablation test. Suite: 37 tests pass.

**Result** (results/isla_memory_recompute_2026-09-07.json):

| tokens | peak, stored | peak, recompute | memory ratio | step time ratio (median) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | 3.23 GiB | 1.42 GiB | 2.27x | 1.16 |
| 20,000 | 6.34 GiB | 2.78 GiB | 2.28x | 1.16 |

The stored-path peak itself fell from 3.29 to 3.23 GiB because the region
computes the slice mix once where the old code computed it twice. Absolute
step times on this shared GPU: 286 ms stored, 330 ms recompute at 10,000
tokens (the book's 283 ms was measured on a quiet machine; the ratio is the
robust statistic). In the book's units: **1.5 GB at 330 ms with the recipe
default, or 3.5 GB at 285 ms storing activations, against GeoTransolver's
4.6 GB.**

**Why it matters.** ISLA now trains in a third of GeoTransolver's memory at
the matched operating point, or equivalently fits 2.3x the tokens per case
(or 2.3x the batch) on the same card at the same peak. That bears directly on
the 20,000-token floor test (W2 lanes 14–17): if more tokens per case help at
35 cases, ISLA can afford them where GeoTransolver cannot. The remaining
footprint is the token path plus the routing softmaxes, both of which the
backward pass genuinely needs; further reduction would have to come from
fewer slices or a lower-precision routing softmax, which are accuracy
questions, not identities.

**Not changed.** No cluster lane, checkpoint or accuracy number is affected:
the arithmetic is identical and the in-flight lanes keep the code snapshot
they started with. The book's memory statements were updated to the recipe
default (1.5 GB, 330 ms) with the stored-activation alternative named in the
four cost sections; CLAIMS.md carries the rule.

## 2026-09-07 — Preregistered: where on a DrivAerML car does GeoTransolver's edge over ISLA live? Station and orientation attribution of the full-data gap {#sec-nb-drivaer-station-prereg}

**Setting.** The program's central anomaly: on HiLiftAeroML ISLA's advantage
over GeoTransolver is geometry generalization (5.0x at a fixed angle on 18
never-seen multi-element wings, @sec-nb-w2d-single-angle), yet on DrivAerML,
where the freestream is fixed and geometry is the only thing that varies,
GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate from 27 cases up and 8.5% more
accurate at full data (435 cases). Both results are geometry generalization;
they point in opposite directions. The curvature analysis on HiLift
(@sec-nb-curvature-strat) showed GeoTransolver's failure there is case-level,
uniform over the surface. The complementary question is where ISLA's
shortfall on cars lives.

**Hypotheses.** *H-wake:* a car's rear surfaces (the base, the rear window,
the underbody diffuser) carry pressures set by the separated wake, a global
flow feature; ISLA's point-to-anchor invariants are local-to-regional, and
GeoTransolver's geometry encoder plus coordinate inputs supply global
context that ISLA lacks. Prediction: ISLA's per-point RMS pressure error
divided by GeoTransolver's is larger on the rear third of the car (by
streamwise station) and on rearward-facing surfaces than on the front third
and forward-facing surfaces. *H-uniform:* the gap is case-level, like
GeoTransolver's on HiLift, with the same ratio in every bin, which would
say the difference is in how each model fits the case as a whole (capacity
or optimisation), not in a missing physical mechanism.

**Instrument.** For the full-data DrivAerML checkpoints behind the book's
accuracy chapter (the seed pairs whose per-point predictions are on disk:
GeoTransolver `gt_fixed_seed45`/`seed46` against ISLA `mt2_v3c_seed45`/`seed46`,
same protocol, same 10,000 sampled validation points per case), the script
`error_by_station.py` bins each case's points into streamwise terciles and
into three orientation classes by the x-component of the unit normal, and
reports the median over cases of the RMS ratio ISLA/GeoTransolver per bin
and each model's share of its own squared error per bin.

**Bars, in readout units.** H-wake is supported if the median ISLA/GT ratio
on the rear third exceeds that on the front third by a factor ≥ 1.3, or the
rearward-facing ratio exceeds the forward-facing ratio by ≥ 1.3. H-uniform
is supported (H-wake falsified) if both factors are ≤ 1.1. Between is
inconclusive and would call for a second seed pair. Whatever the outcome, the
whole-surface median ratio is expected near 1.09 (the reported 8.5%
shortfall), which is the consistency check on the instrument.

**Why it matters.** If H-wake holds, the extension is concrete: a global
context channel (a few learned global tokens or a wake-direction seed) is
the missing ingredient for bluff-body flows, and the query-token machinery
(@sec-nb-qt-prereg) already provides interacting tokens to carry it. If
H-uniform holds, the DrivAerML gap is not about a missing mechanism and the
right lever is capacity or training, which the learning-rate sweep already
explored.

## 2026-09-07 — Verdict: the DrivAerML gap is spatially uniform — rear-to-front factor 1.10 and 1.03 against a 1.1 falsification bar; the wake-context hypothesis is falsified {#sec-nb-drivaer-station-verdict}

**Setting.** The preregistration (@sec-nb-drivaer-station-prereg) asked
where on a DrivAerML car ISLA's 1.2x shortfall against GeoTransolver lives:
concentrated on wake-dominated rear surfaces (H-wake, a missing global-context
channel) or uniform over the surface (H-uniform, a case-level fit
difference). The instrument bins each validation case's 10,000 sampled
surface points into streamwise thirds and takes, per bin, the ratio of ISLA's
RMS pressure error to GeoTransolver's on the same points, then the median
over cases.

**An instrument error, caught by the consistency check.** The first run used
prediction directories under `smoke/`, which turned out to be the zero-shot
SHIFT-SUV evaluations (99 cases, per-case relative L2 near 1.0: the failure
regime), not DrivAerML. The whole-surface ratios came out 1.20 and 1.72
against the ledger's 1.19 and 1.26 for the same seeds; the mismatch on the
second pair exposed the wrong directory. The in-family evaluations are under
`sweep/<run>/res10000/` (dataset `drivaer_ml_surface`, validation split, 48
cases). On those, the whole-surface ratios are 1.17 (seed pair 45) and 1.24
(seed pair 46), against the ledger's 1.19 and 1.26 from the mean relative L2
— consistent, and the two SHIFT-SUV outputs were renamed
`shiftsuv_zeroshot_station_seed4{5,6}.json` so they cannot be mistaken
again. GeoTransolver's seeds 42–44 have no per-point predictions on disk at
10,000 tokens, so the comparison uses the two seed pairs that do (45, 46),
each ISLA seed against the GeoTransolver seed of the same number.

**What we saw** (results/drivaer_station_attribution_2026-09-07.json; medians
over 48 cases of the per-case RMS ratio ISLA/GeoTransolver, above 1 favours
GeoTransolver):

| seed pair | whole surface | front third | middle third | rear third | rear ÷ front |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 45 | 1.17 | 1.16 | 1.10 | 1.27 | 1.10 |
| 46 | 1.24 | 1.28 | 1.12 | 1.32 | 1.03 |

Each model's own error distribution is the same shape: about 56–59% of the
squared pressure error on the front third (stagnation region, A-pillars,
mirrors, wheel arches), 19–25% on the middle and 19–22% on the rear, for both
architectures.

**Verdict.** Both rear-to-front factors are at or under the preregistered
falsification bar of 1.1, so **H-wake is falsified and H-uniform is
supported**: ISLA is a little less accurate than GeoTransolver everywhere on
the car, most on the front and rear thirds and least on the middle, and no
region carries the gap. The result mirrors the HiLift curvature analysis
(@sec-nb-curvature-strat), where GeoTransolver's much larger failure on
unseen high-lift geometries was likewise uniform over the surface. On both
datasets the between-architecture difference is case-level, not a spatially
localized deficit.

**Why it matters.** A wake-context extension to ISLA (global tokens carrying
separated-flow information) would be aimed at a deficit the data do not
show; that direction is closed as a response to the DrivAerML gap. The
remaining candidate explanations are capacity or fit at the operating point
(hidden 192 against GeoTransolver's 256 at matched parameters; the
learning-rate decade is already swept), and the smooth single-body morph
being a regime where ISLA's per-slice invariants add little over raw
coordinates. The productive experiment is not spatial: it is the
unseen-geometry ladder and the 510-case rung on HiLift now training, which
test whether ISLA's geometry advantage is specific to multi-element
configurations.

**Not measured.** Orientation bins (forward-facing, side, rearward-facing by
the normal's streamwise component) were planned but the evaluation files
store normals under a boundary path the script did not resolve; the station
bins alone decide the preregistered bars, so the orientation view was not
pursued.

## 2026-09-07 — Addendum: compiling the geometry region makes the recompute path faster than the eager stored path (237 vs 289 ms) at 1.28 GiB; same function in fp32, bf16 rounding differs at the 1% level {#sec-nb-geo-compile}

**Question.** The per-slice geometry that @sec-nb-geo-recompute moved into a
recompute region is a chain of elementwise operations over
points × slices tensors, the textbook case for kernel fusion. Does fusing the
region recover the 16% step-time cost of recomputation?

**Instrument.** `torch.compile(dynamic=False)` applied to the region function
alone (`_geo_region`), the rest of the model eager as in the recipe; the
same interleaved A/B harness as before, on the same shared RTX 4090, 10,000
tokens, 10 timed repetitions per arm after warm-up
(results/isla_memory_recompute_2026-09-07.json, key `compiled_region`).

| arm | median step | ratio to stored/eager | peak step memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| stored activations, eager | 289 ms | 1.00 | 3.26 GiB |
| stored activations, compiled region | 228 ms | 0.79 | 1.83 GiB |
| recompute, eager (recipe default) | 333 ms | 1.15 | 1.42 GiB |
| recompute, compiled region | 237 ms | 0.82 | 1.28 GiB |

**Equivalence.** In fp32 the compiled region is the same function as the
eager one: forward relative difference 5.6e-7, global relative gradient
difference 1.0e-7. Under bf16 autocast the two differ by 1.1% in forward
output and 2.1e-3 in global gradient norm, because the fused kernels round the
elementwise chain differently from eager autocast (the earlier report of a
1e4 relative gradient difference was an artifact of dividing by the
near-zero gradient of the routing bias, which the slice softmax is invariant
to). So the compiled region is a legitimate speed option (same function, a
different bf16 rounding) but not the bitwise-identical arithmetic of the
frozen protocol, and the recipe keeps `compile=false`.

**Why it matters.** With the region compiled, ISLA trains at 0.82x the step
time of today's eager code and 2.5x less memory, both from exact rewrites of
the same architecture. The remaining step time is dominated by the
(points × slices × hidden) einsums and the token MLPs, which are the same
costs Transolver-family models pay. Adopting the compiled region in training
is an engineering decision to be validated on one lane (loss curve overlaid on
an eager seed); it is not a research claim and is not scheduled ahead of the
science arms.

## 2026-09-07 — Deflection arm: the one-shot sealed test evaluation is scripted before any result exists {#sec-nb-deflection-eval-ready}

The geometry-extrapolation lanes (@sec-nb-deflection-prereg; ISLA and
GeoTransolver, seeds 42/43, training on the 80% of geometries with lower
flap/slat deflection) are at epoch 8 of 500 and will finish in about two
days. So that the sealed test is evaluated exactly as preregistered and not
improvised when the numbers are due, two files now sit beside the lane
launcher on the cluster: `highlift/build_deflection_test_manifest.py`, the
single sanctioned reader of the dataset's `deflection_test` list, which
writes the test manifest and the `highlift_surface_deflection_test` dataset
variant and refuses to run if any test case is missing on disk, duplicated
or overlapping the training or validation lists; and
`highlift/hl_defl_test_eval_aga.sbatch`, four lanes (architecture × seed)
that each evaluate their checkpoint once on that list with the inference
configuration frozen identical to the wave-2 validation evaluations except
`infer_split=test`, and that refuse to start until all four lanes report
training complete. Both mirror the aoa/stall sealed-test scripts of
2026-09-04 line for line. The in-distribution validation of the same
checkpoints is the wave-2 evaluation script's job (lanes 36–39). Readout
bars are unchanged: carried if ISLA's test error is at most 0.7x
GeoTransolver's with a degradation ratio d ≤ 4; falsified if ISLA is at or
above 0.9x GeoTransolver or both models show d ≥ 8.

## 2026-09-07 — HiLift training is I/O-bound: a 10k-cell sample costs ~1 GB of storage traffic through the memmap; page-wise positional reads move 4x less, byte-identical {#sec-nb-hilift-io}

**Setting.** Every HiLiftAeroML lane trains on 10,000 surface cells per
case per epoch, drawn by the recipe's reader as one contiguous cyclic block
of cells from the boundary mesh and compacted to the vertices those cells
reference. Each boundary is 274–294 million cells and 139–149 million
vertices, 20 GB on disk as memmap-backed tensordict leaves (cells 6.8 GB,
points 1.7 GB, seven cell fields 12 GB). Watching the running wave-2 lanes:
a 210-case epoch takes 130–150 s for 52 optimizer steps of 0.29 s (15 s of
compute), the 510-case rung 6 min per epoch, and the per-step log shows
data stalls of 3–7 s several times per epoch. The GPU samplers on those
lanes read 60–67% mean utilisation with a third of samples idle, against
81% and 8% idle on the GPU-bound query-token lanes. At this rate the
510-case lanes need 36 h and the deflection lanes two days: the data path,
not the model, sets the program's experiment cadence.

**Derivation, then measurement.** The reader's cell block is a sequential
read; the cost had to be in the vertex compaction. Reading the code:
`Mesh.slice_points` builds two n_points-sized index tensors (2.3 GB of
temporaries per sample on a 142M-vertex mesh) and then fancy-indexes the
points memmap at the ~28,000 referenced rows. A first rewrite of the
compaction (`torch.unique(return_inverse)` remap plus a contiguous
range read when the referenced ids are local; commit f955fbb63; tests prove it
equal to the old path for in-memory and memmap meshes) removed the
temporaries, but a compute-node probe showed it changed nothing about cold
read time: 2–5 s per case for both. The layout probe then measured why: the
28,000 vertex ids referenced by a contiguous 10,000-cell block are spread
over the *entire* vertex array (span 141.5M rows, fill 0.0002, median gap
3,550 rows, only 12,516 runs even when bridging gaps of 4,096 rows), so no
range or coalesced read can help; every vertex is its own page. The
dataset's per-case `_cache` directories, which could have held per-cell
centroids and normals, are empty scaffolds on all 1,800 cases.

**The mechanism is read amplification, not page count.** On a cold case,
gathering the 28,000 rows (336 KB of data) through the memmap moved
**1,077 MiB** from storage in 31 s; `posix_fadvise(RANDOM)` on the file did
not change it (992 MiB, 24 s); 12-byte `os.pread` per row still moved 873
MiB (15 s); **`os.pread` of each distinct 4 KiB page moved 286 MiB in 5.1 s**,
all four byte-identical. The lustre client's read-ahead (256 MB per file,
2 GB total per client) is what each fault or small read drags in. An
interleaved A/B on one case confirmed the corollary: the first memmap gather
pulls most of the 1.7 GB point file into the client cache in 0.6–0.75 s
(~1.1 GB read), after which further blocks on that case cost 2–9 ms; page
reads cost 80–160 ms warm. Sixteen reader threads on one file were never
faster than one (lustre serialises them), so the pool defaults to one thread.
In training, each node's four ranks touch ~210 cases per epoch on the 210
rung, 1 GB of read-ahead each, on thirty nodes at once: tens of GB/s of
aggregate storage traffic per epoch, which is where the 3–7 s stalls come
from.

**Change** (`physicsnemo/datapipes/readers/mesh.py`, commits f955fbb63,
11ab33281, 4ce9a7df3, a2e9970e5). `_subsample_mesh_cells` compacts vertices
directly and gathers rows through `_gather_rows`, which (a) reads one
contiguous slice when the referenced rows span ≤ 256 MiB, (b) otherwise, for
a file-backed leaf (tensordict `MemoryMappedTensor`, contiguous, CPU), reads
exactly the distinct 4 KiB pages holding the rows with positional reads
(`_pread_rows`: unique pages, runs of consecutive pages in one `preadv`,
rows assembled with a vectorised byte gather), and (c) otherwise falls back
to the plain gather. Tests: equality against the old `slice_points` path
(in-memory and memmap meshes, wrap-around blocks, point_data and
cell_data, measure weights) and against `t[idx]` for the positional path
(page-straddling rows, 1-D and int64 leaves, single-run path); 34 pass. The
outputs are byte-identical, so no protocol, RNG stream or result changes;
only the I/O pattern does.

**What is not yet known** is the effect inside the training loop under
fleet load, where the client cache and thirty nodes' contention interact.
A 4-epoch ISLA run on each of two disjoint 105-case halves of the 210-case
split (new reader on one half, current reader on the other, same fresh
node, back to back) is running as `probe_read_{new,old}`; the readout is
wall time per epoch from the epoch timestamps, epochs 2–4. No in-flight
science lane uses the new reader; adoption for future lanes, or for the
remaining links of the slow lanes, is decided by that number and recorded
below.

## 2026-09-07 — Verdict: positional reads lose 4–5x in the training loop on lustre; the memmap's read-ahead is the better pattern, and HiLift throughput is a dataset-layout problem {#sec-nb-hilift-io-verdict}

**Readout** (`probe_read_{new,old}`, one fresh node, ISLA surface recipe, 4
epochs each on disjoint 105-case halves of the 210-case split, new reader
first). Wall time per epoch from the epoch timestamps:

| reader | epoch 1 (includes worker start-up) | epoch 2 | epoch 3 | mean step (26 steps/epoch) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| positional page reads (`_pread_rows`) | 361 s | 320 s | 358 s | 13.6 s |
| current memmap gather | 130 s | 70 s | 84 s | 3.3 s |

The positional-read path is **4–5x slower** inside the training loop, the
opposite of the single-reader cold measurement (5 s against 31 s per
sample). The two measurements are consistent once the file system is
understood: lustre serves small random reads with high latency and
serialises them per file, so 28,000 page reads per sample from each of 16
reader processes are latency-bound, while the memmap's read-ahead turns the
same access into a few hundred large sequential RPCs and moves most of the
1.7 GB point file into the client cache, wasteful in bytes but efficient in
time. Under fleet load the aggregate bandwidth of that read-ahead is what
the stalls cost; but replacing it with small reads costs more.

**Decision.** The positional-read gather stays in the reader as an opt-in
(`PHYSICSNEMO_MESH_PREAD_GATHER=1`, commit 1b2ac6617) for file systems that
serve small reads well, documented with this measurement; it is not used on
the clusters. The compaction rewrite (unique + inverse remap, range read
when rows are local) stays as the default: byte-identical, no I/O change on
this dataset, removes 2.3 GB of temporaries per sample. No lane, checkpoint
or result is affected; nothing in flight was changed.

**What would actually fix HiLift throughput.** The 10,000-cell sample needs
336 KB of vertex data but the vertex numbering scatters it over the whole
1.7 GB file; every strategy that respects the on-disk layout pays either
1 GB of read-ahead or 28,000 latencies per sample. The fix is at the dataset
level: either (a) renumber vertices once so that a contiguous cell block
references a near-contiguous vertex range (rewrite of `points` and `cells`,
about 8.5 GB per case, 15 TB for the 1,800 cases), after which a sample is
two sequential reads; or (b) a derived per-cell dataset (centroid, normal,
area, fields in cell order; 8 GB per case) that the pipeline could consume
without any vertex gather; or (c) a preregistered change of sampling
protocol to a fixed per-case reservoir of, say, one million cells (1.8% of
the mesh, about 100 MB per case), which would make a sample a single small
read but is a protocol change whose neutrality at 35 cases would first have
to be shown. Each of these writes terabytes to shared scratch or changes the
frozen protocol, so each is a decision for the program owner, not for this
session; until one is taken, HiLift lanes run at 2–3x their compute-bound
pace on the 210-case rung and 5–6x on the 510-case rung, and the cadence
of the remaining wave-2 arms is set accordingly.

## 2026-09-07 — Ledger correction: GeoTransolver's volume configuration has 27.6M parameters, takes the signed distance as input and never sees the surface sample; the interior comparison is neither resource- nor input-matched {#sec-nb-interior-resources-correction}

**What was wrong.** The interior chapter, the index and the claims ledger
described the GeoTransolver arm of the boundary→interior comparison as the
9.0M-parameter surface model with the interior points added as tokens
alongside the surface tokens, interacting over 20,000 tokens, and gave the
ISLA passive-decode arm 11.0M parameters and the arms' memory only as a
4–9 GB range. The 2.6x ratio was attributed to "token-level interaction at
the query".

**What the artifacts say.** Reading each lane's training log and the
