## 2026-09-08 — Sync: upstream main and PR #1966 merged; the branch-local reader compaction and the positional-read path are dropped in favour of the upstream Mesh.slice_points fix {#sec-nb-sync-1966}

The reader investigation of 2026-09-07 (@sec-nb-hilift-io,
@sec-nb-hilift-io-verdict) produced two code changes on this branch: a
vertex compaction in the reader that avoided `Mesh.slice_points`'s two
n_points-sized temporaries, and an opt-in page-wise positional-read gather
that measured 4–5x slower than the memmap path inside the training loop on
Lustre. The upstreaming session took the first to the repository as PR
#1966 and, at Peter's direction, moved the fix into `Mesh.slice_points`
itself (cell remap through the lookup table when the mesh is small,
binary search over the kept ids otherwise; memmap rows read as one range
when they span ≤ 256 MiB; bit-identical to the old implementation on every
index form; on HiLiftAeroML 63 → 2 ms per 10k-cell slice and 3.0 → 0.85 GB
peak RSS per sample). This session merged `upstream/main` (three
conflicts, all combinations of this branch's target-quadrature-measure
bookkeeping with upstream's nested-key handling, resolved by keeping both;
one upstream test now expects the private measure key) and the #1966
branch (`origin/pr/mesh-reader-cell-compaction` at 1e605e0ba), then restored
`physicsnemo/datapipes/readers/mesh.py` and its test to the upstream
versions, dropping the branch's compaction and the positional-read path.
The positional-read path was dropped rather than re-hooked because its own
measurement said so: the byte saving (0.29 vs 1.08 GB per cold sample) did
not survive contact with Lustre's per-file serialisation of small reads.
Tests after the sync: 594 (transforms, readers, recipe) and 97 (readers,
slice_points equivalence, row gather, ISLA) pass. Cluster lanes run from
frozen code snapshots and are unaffected. Commits 30338f599 (upstream
merge), dea2adcf1 (#1966 merge), c7134fe5d (reader restored).

## 2026-09-08 — Verdict: Transolver at the single angle scores 0.091 on the 18 never-seen geometries — 2.55x behind ISLA, 1.96x ahead of GeoTransolver; the fixed-angle failure is partly the geometry encoder's and partly the backbone's (inconclusive band, both bars missed) {#sec-nb-transolver-single-verdict}

**Readout** (wave-2 lanes 40–41, `mech_hl_transolver_single_aoa_12_lr3e3_seed{42,43}`;
126 geometries at 12°, validated on the 18 held-out geometries; two seeds):

| model (single angle) | pressure (42 / 43 → mean) | wall shear (42 / 43) | vs ISLA | vs GeoTransolver |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA | 0.0354 / 0.0363 → 0.0358 | 0.102 / 0.111 | 1.0 | 5.0x ahead |
| Transolver (lr 3e-3) | 0.0872 / 0.0955 → **0.0914** | 0.189 / 0.199 | **2.55x behind** | **1.96x ahead** |
| GeoTransolver (lr 1e-3, its better rate) | 0.1749 / 0.1829 → 0.1789 | 0.307 / 0.316 | 5.0x behind | 1.0 |

**Verdict against the bars** (@sec-nb-transolver-single-prereg). H-encoder
(Transolver within 2.0x of ISLA): missed at 2.55x. H-backbone (Transolver
3.5x or more behind): missed. **Inconclusive by the preregistered bands, and
informative anyway**: in log-error, removing GeoTransolver's geometry
encoder recovers 42% of its 5.0x deficit to ISLA (log 1.96 / log 5.0), and
the remaining 2.55x belongs to the slice-attention backbone that both
baselines share. The same ordering held on the mixed-angle 210-case split
(Transolver 1.8x ahead of GeoTransolver, 1.3x behind ISLA); at the fixed
angle every gap widens (1.96x and 2.55x) because the angle can no longer
carry any of the fit.

**Reading.** GeoTransolver's geometry encoder is a liability for
generalizing across multi-element geometries from ~100 training cases: its
own backbone without it does twice as well. But the backbone is not the
answer either; it is 2.5x behind ISLA at the fixed angle with a seed spread
(0.087–0.096) three times ISLA's. Whatever ISLA's soft-slice design carries
(@sec-nb-inv-verdict: not the invariant inputs alone) is worth 2.5x over the
Transolver backbone and 5x over GeoTransolver when the geometry is the only
thing that varies. The mechanism ledger now reads: geometry encoder −42%,
backbone-versus-ISLA the remaining 58%, invariant inputs not the carrier.

## 2026-09-08 — W2-F, second rung (210 cases from 21 geometries): ISLA 0.102 vs GeoTransolver 0.143 on 18 never-seen geometries, 1.40x; falsifier clear, 0.1 band missed for the same reason as at 40 cases {#sec-nb-w2f-210-verdict}

**Readout** (results/w2_reduction_2026-09-08b.json, arm `F_geometry_scarce`;
`geometry_scarce` = 210 cases from 21 geometries at all ten angles, validated
on the 180 cases of 18 geometries never seen at any angle; two seeds):

| model | pressure (42 / 43 → mean) | velocity | wall shear | GT / ISLA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA | 0.1005 / 0.1029 → **0.1017** | 0.118 / 0.121 | 0.187 / 0.193 | |
| GeoTransolver | 0.1531 / 0.1322 → **0.1427** | 0.171 / 0.156 | 0.268 / 0.241 | **1.40** (velocity 1.37, wall shear 1.34) |

**Verdict.** ISLA/GeoTransolver = 0.71: below the 0.8 falsifier, so the
advantage again does not depend on having seen the validation geometry;
0.25 above the random 210-case split's 0.46 (three seeds), so the 0.1 band
is missed, as at the 40-case rung (@sec-nb-w2f-40-verdict). The reason is
the same and now measured twice. Going from the random 210-case split
(about 126 distinct geometries) to 210 cases from 21 geometries, ISLA's
error rises from 0.065 to 0.102 (1.57x) while GeoTransolver's stays where it
was (0.141 → 0.143); at the 40-case rung the same move (33 → 4 geometries)
took ISLA from 0.138 to 0.250 and GeoTransolver from 0.381 to 0.449.
GeoTransolver's seed spread is 15% here (0.132–0.153) against ISLA's 2%.

**Reading, both rungs together.** ISLA's accuracy on high-lift geometries
is bought with distinct training geometries, not with cases: at a fixed
case count, cutting the geometries 6x costs it 1.6x in error; GeoTransolver
does not respond to geometry count at all, which is the geometry-blindness
seen in every other instrument today (@sec-nb-seen-unseen,
@sec-nb-hilift-percase). The unseen-geometry ratio (1.8x at 4 geometries,
1.4x at 21) is smaller than the random-split ratio (2.8x, 2.2x) only because
the geometry-poor splits hurt the one model that uses geometries. The
preregistered prediction (ratio within 0.1 of the random split) assumed
case count was the controlling variable; it is not, and the ladder says
which is. Per-case paired statistics on the 180 validation cases are being
reduced and are appended below when they land.

**Per-case count for the 210-geometry rung (landed).** On the 180 validation
cases ISLA is more accurate than GeoTransolver on **172 of 180** by two-seed
means (157 on both seeds individually; sign test p = 3 × 10⁻⁴¹), median
per-case ratio 1.48, 10th–90th percentiles 1.07–2.02
(results/hilift_paired_stats_case_2026-09-08.json, arm `geo210`). The same
172-of-180 count as the 40-case rung with a smaller median (1.48 against
2.24): the advantage on never-seen geometries is case-by-case at both rungs.

**Qualification from the unseen-geometry rungs.** On the two geometry-poor
splits GeoTransolver's per-case error is *not* flat: coefficient of
variation 0.41 at 4 training geometries and 0.27 at 21, against 0.15 on the
random 35-case split (ISLA 0.66 and 0.46 there), and its per-case ordering
correlates with ISLA's at 0.77 at both rungs (seed self-consistency
0.91–0.96), against 0.57–0.64 on the random splits
(results/hilift_geo_percase_correlation_2026-09-08.json). So the flat,
case-independent GeoTransolver error of @sec-nb-hilift-percase is a property
of the random splits, where 33–126 geometries each appear at few angles;
when the training set holds a handful of geometries at every angle, both
architectures find the same validation geometries hard and GeoTransolver's
error varies with them, only 1.4–1.8x higher than ISLA's. The
geometry-count reading of @sec-nb-w2f-210-verdict stands; the
"geometry-blind" phrasing should be read as "does not turn additional
geometries into accuracy", not as "insensitive to which geometry".

## 2026-09-08 — Program review: the verdict calibrated, five threads retired from the chapters, regime extrapolation folded into chapter 6, and the mechanism question restated {#sec-nb-program-review-2026-09-08}

**Setting.** The book had grown by accretion over a week of verdicts:
five places offered a summary judgment (the index paragraph, the accuracy
chapter's verdict, the limits chapter's established list and its
recommendation section, and the status chapter's opening), two of them
stale (the limits chapter still recommended GeoTransolver for the interior
and treated the unseen-geometry ladder as future; the status chapter still
named the exact-kernel MeshTransformer as a recurring architecture and the
cross-family transfer gap as the organizing question). The index paragraph
was a 400-word chain of ratios with no sentence saying how large the author
thinks the effect is.

**What changed in the chapters.** (1) The index now opens with one verdict
sentence, "a large improvement in one regime, parity elsewhere, not a new
capability", the horizontal (data-multiplier) reading of the ladder, the
three bounding facts (the multiplier shrinks with data; no transfer to
DrivAerML; part of the 2.8x is GeoTransolver's weakness, since plain
Transolver beats it at 210 cases), and a standing table
(`tbl-verdict`). (2) Chapter 5 gains a live data-multiplier table
(`tbl-data-multiplier`): GeoTransolver needs 6x the cases to reach ISLA's
35-case accuracy (two measured points); Transolver about 2x at the 0.09
level (ISLA interpolated at about 106 cases on its own 35→210 segment); the
uncertainty-signal section is one paragraph; the mechanism section states
the small-feature hypothesis (below) as not yet measured. (3) Chapter 7
(regime extrapolation) is folded into chapter 6 as a section with the same
anchors, compressed to the table, the figure, the three readings, the
raw-coordinate falsification and two sentences of practice; the
boundary-condition-content paragraph, a remnant of the exact-kernel line, is
cut. (4) The query-independence section is one paragraph. (5) Chapter 8's
"two designs" (wake-aligned probes, canonical probe lattice) are dropped
as roads, superseded by the query-token configuration. (6) Chapter 12's
established list, mechanism limit, interior limit, open questions and
recommendation are rewritten to the current state; the third-seed and
unseen-geometry questions are removed as settled; the region-stratification
and width-control questions are added. (7) Chapter 13's opening names two
architectures and the Transolver control, moves the exact-kernel line to
tree history, and reorganizes around the mechanism question; node HLREG is
added as the ready frontier.

**Why the verdict is "large improvement", not "groundbreaking".** The
program's own evidence caps it: parity at 1,260 cases and a naive
extrapolation favouring GeoTransolver 2x at 5,000; GeoTransolver 1.2–1.3x
ahead on DrivAerML at every size; no architecture crosses a regime boundary
or transfers across families; the carrier not isolated (five ablations
≤ 16%; transplant falsified for GeoTransolver). Groundbreaking would
require either a capability no baseline has (none appeared) or a located
mechanism that predicts where the advantage will and will not appear
before a dataset is trained on. The second is within reach and is the
program's ready frontier.

### Preregistered: HLREG, where on the wing does the advantage live? {#sec-nb-hlreg-prereg}

*Hypothesis.* ISLA's advantage on HiLiftAeroML is in resolving the
small-scale geometric features of multi-element wings, the slat and flap
deflections and the gaps they open, from few samples. Those features are a
few percent of the chord in size, covered by a few dozen of the 10,000
sampled points per case, and set the pressure over the element downstream of
them. DrivAerML cars differ by smooth morphs of one body with no such
features, which would explain the non-transfer without a second mechanism.
The single-angle result (5.0x at a fixed angle, so the freestream direction
is not the carrier), the geometry-count response (ISLA's error rises 1.6x
when the training geometries are cut six-fold at fixed case count;
GeoTransolver's does not move), and the uniformity of the DrivAerML gap
across streamwise thirds are all consistent with it; none tests it.

*Instrument (eval-only).* For each of the 180 shared validation cases at
the 35-case and 210-case rungs (ISLA and GeoTransolver, seeds 42/43):
partition the sampled surface points by (a) connected component of the
surface mesh (slat, main element, flap; the elements are disjoint bodies,
so connectivity identifies them without labels) and (b) distance to the
nearest point of a *different* component, in bands of 0–2%, 2–10% and
>10% of the reference chord. Readout per band: the ratio of GeoTransolver's
to ISLA's RMS pressure error over the band's points (two-seed mean
predictions), reported as the median over cases with its 10–90% range, and
each band's share of total squared error for each model. The instrument
needs per-point predictions; if the ladder evaluations did not save them,
the four 35-case and four 210-case checkpoints are re-evaluated once with
the frozen inference configuration (minutes each on one GPU).

*Bars, in readout units.* Let R_near be the GeoTransolver/ISLA ratio in
the 0–2% band and R_rest the ratio over all other points, medians over
cases at 35 cases. **Supported** if R_near / R_rest ≥ 1.5 (the advantage
is at least half again as large next to the gaps as elsewhere) and the
ordering is preserved at 210 cases. **Falsified** if 0.87 ≤ R_near / R_rest
≤ 1.15, the band within which the DrivAerML streamwise stratification
called the gap uniform. Between 1.15 and 1.5, inconclusive; a per-element
concentration (one element's ratio ≥ 1.5x the others') is then reported as
a secondary finding, not as support. A supported verdict is written as
"the advantage concentrates on the gap regions", never as "ISLA resolves
the gaps", until a discriminating ablation (for example, ISLA with the
gap-region points removed from the sample) has been run.

*What each outcome changes.* Supported: the mechanism is located on the
surface; the book gains a predictive statement (feature-scale variation
should show the advantage, smooth morphs should not) testable on a third
dataset before training; the next node is the sample-removal ablation and
a per-slice attribution of which routing slices carry the gap regions.
Falsified: the advantage is in the fit of the whole surface; the
small-feature hypothesis joins the freestream-direction hypothesis as
excluded, and the remaining candidates are the routing structure as a
whole (a slice-count and relational-routing ladder at 35 cases) and the
loss landscape at small data (a training-dynamics comparison).

**Scheduling decision.** HLREG is READY (depends on W2F and DRV-STA, both
done). It is eval-only and should run before any further training lane is
launched on the surface task. The width control (QT-SDF-h256), the 510-case
rung, the 20,000-token test and the deflection split continue as running.
Tech-tree changes: node HLREG added with edges W2F → HLREG, DRV-STA → HLREG,
HLREG → MT3; chapter 7 removed from the render (anchors preserved in
chapter 6).

## 2026-09-08 — Independent audit: verified findings, corrections applied, and reopened questions {#sec-nb-audit-2026-09-08}

**Setting.** An independent reviewer with fresh context read the book at
commit 3b73817b together with the result reductions, the ISLA
implementation, the aerodynamic recipe and the successor preregistrations,
without launching any training. The review reproduced the headline means
from the saved reductions (35 cases: ISLA 0.138, GeoTransolver 0.381,
Transolver 0.404; 210 cases: 0.065 / 0.141 / 0.087; 1,260: 0.041 / 0.042;
fixed angle: 0.036 / 0.179 / 0.091; interior with signed distance: pressure
0.057 vs 0.062, velocity 0.085 vs 0.133, viscosity 0.122 vs 0.094), called
the controls real strengths, and then argued that the mechanism and the
deployment value are less settled than the verdict said. Its finding list
was twelve items. Each was checked in this session before anything in the
book changed; the checks, the numbers and the resulting edits are below,
in the audit's order. Facts marked *verified* were reproduced here with
the probe named; nothing below is taken from the audit on its word.

**1. The baselines do not receive the drive at the same numerical scale
(verified).** ISLA's recipe consumes the unit freestream direction
(`conf/model/isla_surface.yaml`, line 32); GeoTransolver's
(`geotransolver_surface.yaml`, line 41) and Transolver's
(`transolver_surface.yaml`, line 34) consume the physical freestream
velocity, which the dataset pipelines pass through unnormalized: 2,679.5
in/s on HiLiftAeroML (inches and seconds) and 38.9 m/s on DrivAerML.
Probe: GeoTransolver's global-context projector at production dimensions
(hidden 256, 8 heads, 256 slices), untrained, fed a drive of magnitude 1,
38.9 and 2,679.5. The entropy-equivalent number of occupied slices per head
falls from 191–232 to 1.0–3.8 to 1.00–1.02, and the maximum context
magnitude rises 0.66 → 22.7 → 1,530
(results/geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json). This is a
conditioning difference at initialization. It is *not* evidence that it
explains the trained gap: training can rescale the projection, and the
transplant test (INV) kept the raw velocity and so does not answer it.
Node UDRV, the training control (GeoTransolver and Transolver with the unit
direction at 35 cases and on the fixed-angle split, same cases, seeds,
budget and rate search), is preregistered at @sec-nb-udrv-prereg and READY.
Book: chapter 4 gains a paragraph on the input scale
(`sec-part-baseline`); chapters 5 and 12 name it as the one untested
alternative to every mechanism reading; the index's does-not-claim list
carries it.

**2. The query-token configuration is not invariant to an equivalent
representation of its source measure (verified).** In `model.py` around
line 756 the routing weight of an interacting query is exp(qt_logw) times
the geometric mean of the source weights. Probe, float64, ISLA(hidden 32,
2 layers, 8 slices) with fixed queries: replacing every source token by two
copies at half weight, which leaves every integral against the discrete
source measure unchanged, moves the output by 3.7% (query tokens) and 9.1%
(query tokens with the signed-distance scalar), against 8e-16 for the plain
surface model. Consequence: source refinement, the number of queries, their
distribution and chunking can all change the predicted field, and the
existing contract test (uniform rescaling of all weights) cannot see it. A
repaired convention, `query_mass="source_total"` (query mass = a learned
fraction of the total source measure, divided by the query count), is being
added with tests; trained checkpoints keep the old convention, and their
dependence on companion-query count (fixed sentinel queries with 1k / 10k /
40k companions, plane and near-wall sets, chunk layouts) is not yet measured.
Node QMASS, RUNNING. Book: chapter 2's "what is not a contract" list gains
the refinement bullet; chapter 8's query-token description states the
dependence; chapter 12 adds the open question with the 0.005 absolute
pressure margin as the bar it must not consume.

**3. Composition failures (verified).** Similarity gauge + surface
local-feature channel: a 2.7x rescale of geometry (areas ×2.7²) changes
the output by up to 0.79 in the probe, the gauge alone at roundoff; the
patch log-mass is not normalized by the gauge. Passive queries + boundary
scalars, scale conditioning or raw seed features: shape errors whenever
source and query counts differ. Passive queries + the parity-odd vector
head: source and query normals collide when counts differ. None is behind a
reported number and the plain reference surface configuration is
unaffected; the fixes ride with QMASS. Book: chapter 2 lists them.

**4. The first-moment blind spot is broader than M3 said (verified).** M3
(@sec-nb-m3-verdict) found that geometries with a discrete rotational
symmetry about the drive collapse every slice anchor onto the axis and
argued the mechanism therefore needs such a symmetry, which no car has.
Counterexample: five equal, disjoint spherical component samples around an
axial drive at azimuths {0, 120, 240, 27, 207}° and {0, 120, 240, 43,
223}°, a triangle plus an antipodal pair each. Both have zero transverse
first moment, so within every slice the component contributions cancel and
the mean-position and mean-normal anchors stay axial, and the relational
invariants cannot recover the angular arrangement at any layer. The two are
not congruent (pairwise-distance profiles differ by 0.56) and no rotation
preserves both geometry and drive. ISLA's outputs on the common component
agree to 4e-15 (default and similarity-gauge configurations, two seeds); the
optional local-distance channel separates them by 0.039–0.063; a
second-moment contraction at the query, r̂ᵀ C r̂ with C the points' second
moment, reads 2.41 against 1.99
(results/isla_first_moment_collision_2026-09-08.json). So M3's necessity
claim is false, and "refuted as a DrivAerML-scale limitation" becomes "not
established as the cause on cars": a documented representation limitation,
not a demonstrated cause of any benchmark deficit, and not a completeness
proof either way. Node MOM2 (READY) is the cheap expressivity benchmark
below. Book: chapter 2 gains a completeness bullet; the M3 node and row
are qualified.

**5. "Sealed" was a per-checkpoint property, not a program-level one
(verified from the pinned manifest).** Intersections of case IDs in the
HiLiftAeroML manifest at revision bbec30bcfc6103309c1375c5228b3ad0a586bfaf:
full_test (360 cases) shares 179 with aoa_test ∪ stall_test, which were
evaluated on 2026-09-04 (results/hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json);
geometry_test shares 182 and deflection_test 182; geometry_test and
deflection_test also share 37 and 40 cases with full_val. aoa_test (900
cases) and stall_test (723) between them contain all 180 geometries, so no
HiLift geometry is unexposed at the level of the program. full_val's 180
cases span 118 geometries; geometry_val's 180 span 18 geometries at ten
angles. No checkpoint trained on a case it was scored on; the finding is
about what an evaluation can confirm, not about leakage. Removing the 179
already-read cases would define a new selected population and is not a
replacement confirmatory test. Node EXPO, DONE
(results/hilift_exposure_ledger_2026-09-08.json). Book: chapter 1's splits
and protocol paragraphs, chapter 4's protocol item 7, chapter 5's limits
and chapter 12's validation limit now distinguish "held out per
checkpoint" from "program-level confirmation"; the deflection question
carries the same note.

**6. The statistical unit on the unseen-geometry rungs is the geometry
(verified by inspection of the split).** The W2-F and single-angle
validation sets are 18 geometries × 10 angles; the saved paired statistics
treat 172 of 180 case wins as independent trials (p ≈ 3e-41). The test that
matches the design has n = 18 and a smallest attainable two-sided p of
7.6e-6, and 172 case signs do not determine how many geometry means
improve. On the random split the 180 cases stand for 118 geometries; the
180-of-180 ordering at 35 cases survives any grouping. Two further points
of the same kind: all seeds at a rung share one training subset, so seed
spread measures initialization and data order, not which 35 cases a
practitioner would have; and the data-multiplier reading (GeoTransolver at
210 ≈ ISLA at 35) is a comparison of two measured points, not a minimum
CFD-run count under optimized sampling. Node GEOSTAT, RUNNING (geometry-level
statistics: @sec-nb-audit-geometry-stats). Book: chapters 5 and 12 state the
unit and demote case counts to descriptive; chapter 5 adds the
training-draw caveat under its limits.

**7. Four mechanism readings compared more than the named intervention
(verified against the manifests and the code).** (a) The random-split and
geometry-ladder validation sets share only 20 of 180 cases, so 0.138 vs
0.250 and 0.065 vs 0.102 change both the training composition and the
evaluation population; they support a geometry-generalization advantage,
not "only geometry count". (b) Plain Transolver differs from GeoTransolver
in depth (8 vs 12 layers), parameters (6.0M vs 9.0M), drive injection and
learning rate, so the ~2/5 encoder / ~3/5 backbone split of the fixed-angle
log-gap is a numerical decomposition, not a causal contribution of the
geometry encoder. (c) Passive ISLA decodes through a separate four-block
read decoder (`model.py` around line 366) while query-token ISLA sends its
queries through the twelve encoder blocks with token-type and weight
parameters, and the signed-distance scalar is unavailable in passive mode;
0.160 vs 0.064 is therefore the cost of the complete passive configuration,
not a fundamental 2.6x price of query independence. The passive question is
reopened as a narrower node, PASSIVE2 (PLANNED, after QMASS): hold query
depth, readout and inputs fixed and disable only the writes from queries
into the shared state. (d) HLREG locates output error, not input
information: a slat-gap change moves the pressure over the whole element,
so a uniform ratio would not falsify a gap-information mechanism; the
node's bars stand and its verdict is graded as localization. Book: chapters
5, 8, 12 and the W2 and W2F ledger rows carry each qualification.

**8. Interior interpretation (verified by reducing the band artifact).**
From the per-band squared-error numerators in
results/v0_sdf_band_2026-09-05.json, 94.6% of the passive SDF-normal arm's
excess pressure squared error over GeoTransolver-volume and 93.7% of its
excess velocity squared error lie in the first band (below 0.01
nondimensional, about 5 cm), and over 99% within 2 m
(results/v0_interior_excess_sse_2026-09-08.json). These are fractions of the
error on the near-wall-biased sample, not volume integrals; the far-field
ratio growth is real and does not identify a missing mechanism. The
eddy-viscosity relative L2 is computed on the standardized target
(ν_t − 4.8e-4)/9.4e-4 before inverse normalization (`infer.py` line 590;
`drivaer_ml_volume.yaml` line 62), so 0.122 is not a 12.2% physical error;
orderings under the frozen metric stand, ratios of means need not survive
another centering. DrivAerML's closure is hybrid RANS/LES whose modeled
viscosity depends on a grid or filter length, so query-neighbour features
could recover discretization information rather than a wall feature: a
hypothesis to discriminate. Book: chapter 8's distance section is
rewritten around both readings; its metric paragraph states the viscosity
normalization; the "missing volumetric context" finding is withdrawn from
chapters 8 and 12 in favour of the measured statement.

**9. Forces (verified in the recipe).** `forces.py` line 296 integrates
predictions and labels on the same 10,000 sampled cells, so the 3% (35
cases) and 0.6% (fixed-angle lift) errors are against the sampled-cell
label integral, not the full-surface force, and shared quadrature cancels
sampling error common to both. A 10k / 20k / 40k / full-surface reference
ladder is node FORCE-REF (READY). The dataset revision used is
bbec30bcfc6103309c1375c5228b3ad0a586bfaf, in which six force-monitor means
were replaced by surface-field integrations; the book never used the
dataset's coefficients as reference, so no reported number changes. Book:
chapter 1's metric definition, chapter 5's force section and the index
carry the qualifier.

**10. Memory instruments (verified in the artifacts and the logger).**
ISLA's 1.5 GB subtracts resident parameter and optimizer memory from
`max_memory_allocated` (results/isla_memory_recompute_2026-09-07.json);
GeoTransolver's 4.6 GB and every "peak allocated" value in
results/v0_interior_resources_2026-09-07.json come from the training logger,
which records `torch.cuda.memory_reserved()` (`train.py` line 612), a
different and never-smaller quantity. The within-ISLA 2.28x recompute
reduction is one instrument and stands. Read on the same instrument, the
comparison reverses: every ISLA HiLift lane behind the book's accuracy
numbers (full data, 210 cases, fixed angle; trained before the activation
recompute existed) logged 9.83 GiB reserved against GeoTransolver's 4.62 GiB,
2.1x more (results/memory_instrument_audit_2026-09-08.json). Node MEM-INST then
measured both models in one harness on one GB300 (bf16 autocast, batch 1,
10,000 tokens, AdamW step included; results/matched_memory_isla_gt_2026-09-08.json):
total peak allocated memory is 4.07 GiB for GeoTransolver, 9.26 GiB for the
ISLA code that trained every checkpoint (no rewrite, no recompute), 3.40 GiB
for the current ISLA code without recompute and 1.57 GiB with it; reserved
memory 4.58 / 9.53 / 3.63 / 1.77 GiB; step time 65 / 246 / 239 / 246 ms.
The harness reproduces both trainer-log reserved figures (4.62 and 9.83 GiB)
and the RTX 4090 incremental figure (1.40 GiB), so every number in the
program was real and the disagreement was code version plus instrument. The
reading for the book: ISLA's current code is 2.6x smaller than
GeoTransolver and the trained checkpoints were 2.3x larger; the losses of
the three ISLA variants agree step for step within 1e-3, so no accuracy
number depends on the footprint, and none was produced at the small one; and
ISLA's step is 3.7x slower at this size. The "3x less memory" headline is
replaced everywhere by that sentence and the verdict table's cost row reads
"Mixed". An unplanned finding: the pool-then-project rewrite alone accounts
for 9.3 → 3.4 GiB (2.7x), more than the 2.3x that the recompute adds; the
earlier notebook entries attributed the two savings correctly but had not
measured them against GeoTransolver. Also verified: GeoTransolver-volume's blocks run at
an effective width of 448 (256 plus six 32-channel local features,
`geotransolver.py` line 542), so the h256 ISLA control (about 15.7M
parameters) is a width increase, still narrower and smaller than the 27.6M
comparator: a success shows one width increase helps, a null cannot refute
capacity. Book: every "1.5 GB against 4.6 GB" names both instruments
(index, chapters 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 12); chapter 8's table and resources
paragraph say which instrument they use; the width control is renamed and
qualified in chapters 8, 12 and 13.

Chapter 1's symmetry argument no longer derives isotropy and scale
