## 2026-09-09 — Preregistered: MEAS-METRIC, are ISLA's measure weights costing accuracy because the model fits the area measure while the metric scores points? {#sec-nb-measure-metric-prereg}

**Setting.** ISLA weights each surface point by its cell area in the slice
routing softmax (`use_measure_weights`), so slice states are quadrature
means over the surface measure. The book's pressure metric is the per-point
relative L2 over the 10,000 sampled cells, in which every point counts
equally. Turning the weights off improved the 35-case HiLift error from
0.138 to 0.122 (0.88x; @sec-mechanism), a gain the book reads as removed
gradient variance under uniform sampling. That gain is as large as ISLA's
whole deficit to the unit-drive GeoTransolver (0.124), so the reading
matters. A second reading: the weighted model is optimized for a different
functional than the one it is scored on. On a CFD surface mesh the cells
are far from uniform (fine on the wing, coarse on the fuselage), so the
area-weighted model concentrates capacity on the coarse cells, and the
per-point metric penalizes it exactly where the wing's fine cells are dense.

**Instrument (eval-only).** From the saved predictions of the 35-case arms
(ISLA weighted, three seeds; ISLA without measure weights, two seeds;
unit-drive GeoTransolver and Transolver, two seeds each; the physical-drive
baselines for reference) and the saved cell measure weights, compute per
case both the uniform relative L2 and the *area-weighted* relative L2,
sqrt(Σ w e² / Σ w t²), with seed-mean predictions; report per-arm means
under both metrics, paired per-case ratios, and the share of each model's
squared error on the finer half of the cells.

**Bars, in readout units.** Let R_u = mean error of the unweighted ISLA ÷
weighted ISLA under the uniform metric (0.88 from the reductions) and R_w
the same ratio under the area-weighted metric. *Measure–metric mismatch
supported* if R_w ≥ 0.97 (the unweighted model's 12% advantage shrinks to
within seed spread or reverses when the metric adopts the model's measure).
*Falsified* if R_w ≤ 0.91 (the advantage is essentially unchanged: the
weights are a cost under either measure, i.e. variance or a worse
optimization target). Between: partial. Consequence if supported: the fix is
to route with weights tempered toward uniform, w^α with α ∈ {0, 0.5, 1}
trained at 35 and 210 HiLift cases and on DrivAerML (the α ladder,
preregistered separately), and the book gains a rule that the routing
measure must match the scored measure. If falsified: the weights are
dropped from the reference configuration for accuracy runs and kept only
where density robustness is the target, and the book's variance reading
stands. Either way the unit-drive baselines are reported under both metrics
alongside, since a metric change that moves ISLA must be applied to them
too.

## 2026-09-09 — Verdict: MEAS-METRIC falsified — the no-weights advantage is the same under the area-weighted metric (ratio 1.116 against 1.119), so ISLA's measure weights are a cost under either measure {#sec-nb-measure-metric-verdict}

**Readout** (@sec-nb-measure-metric-prereg; 180 validation cases at 35
training cases, seed-mean predictions, gauge pressure; cell areas
recomputed from the saved triangles because the artifact's stored measure
field is a constant placeholder; results/measure_metric_35_2026-09-09.json).
Two instrument faults found and fixed before the numbers were read: the
stored `_measure_weights` are constant, and the saved pressure is absolute,
not gauge (a first pass returned relative errors of 0.009; subtracting the
artifact's p_inf restores the metric's quantity). The relative errors below
are on gauge pressure and therefore larger than the book's standardized
metric (0.262 against 0.138 for ISLA); every ratio between arms matches the
standardized reductions to within 1%.

| arm | uniform rel-L2 | area-weighted rel-L2 | share of squared error on the finer half of the cells |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA, measure weights on (three seeds) | 0.262 | 0.183 | 86% |
| ISLA, measure weights off (two seeds) | 0.234 | 0.163 | 86% |
| GeoTransolver, unit drive | 0.240 | 0.169 | 85% |
| Transolver, unit drive | 0.224 | 0.155 | 86% |

Paired, weighted ISLA ÷ unweighted ISLA: uniform metric mean ratio 1.119
(median per case 1.092; the unweighted model lower on 149 of 180), area-weighted
metric 1.116 (median 1.064; 130 of 180). R_w = 0.896 against R_u = 0.894.
Cell areas on a sampled HiLift surface span two orders of magnitude between
the 10th and 90th percentiles (0.05x to 11x the median; the largest cell
420x the median), and every model puts 85–86% of its squared error on the
finer half of the cells.

**Verdict: falsified** (R_w below the 0.91 falsifier). Adopting the model's
own measure in the metric does not recover the weighted model: the weights
cost 12% at 35 cases whichever way the error is scored. The variance reading
stands, and the area statistics say why it is so large: with a 400-fold
range of cell areas the log-area bias makes a few coarse fuselage cells
dominate every slice's quadrature, so slice states are high-variance
estimates from few effective points. Consequence, fixed in the
preregistration: measure weights leave the reference configuration for
accuracy runs, subject to the confirmation below, and are kept only where
density robustness is the target (with the similarity gauge). The
unit-drive baselines are reported under both metrics for completeness;
their ordering does not change.

### Preregistered: NOW-L, does the no-weights gain persist with more data and on DrivAerML? {#sec-nb-noweights-prereg}

*Question.* The 12% gain from dropping the routing measure weights is
measured once, at 35 HiLift cases. Before the reference configuration
changes, it must hold where the variance argument predicts a smaller effect
(more training cases average the quadrature noise) and on a mesh with a
different area distribution (DrivAerML). Two lanes each: HiLift 210 cases
(`a35_hl_mt2_noweights_scarce_seed{42,43}`, wave-2 rows 42–43, jobs
689985/689986, submitted and held until the 510-case rung frees nodes, the
program being at its 32-node budget with the interior track's lanes;
reference ISLA 0.065, three seeds 0.062–0.067) and
DrivAerML 435 cars (`now_mt2_lr1e3_seed{42,43}`, launcher nowt_aga.sbatch
from the reference lanes' own code snapshot; reference 0.0577, seeds
0.0588/0.0567; to launch when the 510-case rung frees nodes). Everything
else frozen.

*Bars.* *Persists* if the unweighted model is ≥ 5% better at both rungs
(HiLift 210 ≤ 0.0618; DrivAerML ≤ 0.0548); *fades* if within 3% at both
(HiLift 0.0631–0.0670; DrivAerML 0.0560–0.0594); otherwise reported per
rung. Prediction from the variance reading: a smaller but positive gain at
210 (2–8%) and a smaller one on DrivAerML, whose sampled cell areas are more
uniform. If it persists, the reference configuration for accuracy runs
becomes weights-off and every ISLA accuracy number in the book is
restated at the next full rerun; if it fades, the 35-case gain is recorded
as a small-data effect and the configuration is unchanged.

**Amended 2026-09-10 (@sec-nb-principle-redirect).** The consequence stated
above, that the weights-off configuration becomes ISLA's reference at four
or more of six rungs, is retired. Dropping the measure weights makes the
slice aggregate a mean over the sampled points rather than an integral over
the surface measure, so the model's answer depends on the mesher's sampling
density; the ladder continues as an ablation that prices the measure
semantics in distribution, and the bars above keep their meaning as
"persists" or "fades" for that price only.

## 2026-09-09 — Planned: POSE-BENCH (the one setting where exact equivariance can show value) and QCOUNT (query-count robustness of the interior configuration) {#sec-nb-pose-qcount-plan}

Two nodes scoped while the unit-drive ladder trains; neither is launched
(the program is at its node budget), both are written here so that their
bars exist before any run.

**POSE-BENCH.** Every benchmark in the book presents geometries in one
canonical frame, so ISLA's exact rotation covariance has never been able to
earn accuracy. The honest test is a pose-varying benchmark against the
standard remedy: DrivAerML surface pressure at 435 cars with every training
and validation case in an independent random SO(3) pose (the recipe's
`RandomRotateMesh` already supports uniform unit-quaternion rotations; the
validation pose must be deterministic per case, one small transform
option), GeoTransolver and Transolver trained *with* SO(3) augmentation and
the unit drive, ISLA without (it is invariant, so augmentation is a no-op
up to sampling). Reference: canonical-frame errors (ISLA 0.0577,
GeoTransolver at unit drive to be measured). Bars, in the posed setting:
*equivariance earns accuracy* if the unit-drive GeoTransolver-with-augmentation
error rises by ≥ 10% over its canonical-frame error while ISLA's changes by
≤ 3%, and ISLA is more accurate than both augmented baselines by ≥ 5%;
*augmentation suffices* if the augmented baselines stay within 3% of their
canonical-frame errors; between, reported. Cost: four lanes (two baselines,
two seeds), about two days.

**QCOUNT.** The interior query-token configuration's error depends on how
many queries are asked together (0.062 at 10,000, 0.077 at 2,000, 0.110 at
1,000; @sec-nb-qmass-verdict), a deployment defect. Remedy to test: the
measure-consistent query mass (`query_mass=source_total`) plus query-count
augmentation in training (a random interior subsample size per step
between 1,000 and 10,000). Readout: the error-versus-query-count curve at
1k / 2k / 5k / 10k / 40k on fixed sentinel points. Bars: *robust* if the
curve's spread (max ÷ min over the range) is ≤ 1.05 with the 10k error
within 3% of the current 0.0567; *not robust* if the spread stays ≥ 1.30.
Gated on UDRV-INT: if the interior lead does not survive the unit-drive
GeoTransolver-volume, the remedy is still worth having for deployment but
is no longer a competitive claim. Cost: two lanes, about eight hours each.

## 2026-09-09 — Preregistered: SPARSE, sparse anchor routing for ISLA (route each point to its k nearest anchors) {#sec-nb-sparse-routing-prereg}

**Setting.** Every ISLA slice block evaluates the eight relational invariants
of every point against all 256 slice anchors in every layer: the
(points × slices × 8) invariant tensor and its (points × slices × 3)
intermediates are the block's dominant cost. At 10,000 tokens ISLA's
training step is 3.7x GeoTransolver's on the same GPU (matched-instrument
measurement, @sec-nb-audit-2026-09-08), and before the exact recompute
option those tensors were 76% of saved activations (@sec-nb-geo-recompute).
The anchors are spatially local: a point's routing mass concentrates on the
anchors near it, so the invariants against distant anchors carry little.

**Hypothesis.** Routing each point to only its k nearest anchors (k of 256;
selection by Euclidean distance to the anchor position, no gradient through
the selection; invariants, routing bias and the point→slice mix restricted
to the selected anchors; unselected anchors excluded from the point's mix
and from the slices' point-assignment softmax) cuts step time and memory
roughly in proportion to k / 256 for the geometry term, at negligible
change in what the model computes. The option `anchor_topk` (default 0,
dense) is exact at k = 256 by construction and is contract-tested (SE(3)
covariance, drive degree one, measure-scale invariance, gauge scale
equivariance; test/experimental/nn/test_isla_sparse.py).

**Instrument (no training).** One GPU, the reference surface configuration
(hidden 192, 12 layers, 256 slices, 1 scalar + 1 vector output), 10,000
random anisotropic tokens, batch 1, bf16 autocast, AdamW step: median
forward+backward+step wall time over 10 iterations after 3 warm-ups, and
peak allocated memory over the resident model, for k ∈ {dense, 128, 64,
32, 16} with and without `geo_checkpoint`. Output change: the relative L2
change of the full output and of the scalar (pressure) channel between
dense and k-sparse routing *with the same weights*, at initialization on
the random cloud and on the trained HiLift 35-case checkpoint
`lad_hl_mt2_super_scarce_seed42` applied to six saved validation inputs
(points, cell normals, measure weights, unit drive from the prediction
artifacts). Script results/isla_sparse_routing_bench_2026-09-09.py;
artifact results/isla_sparse_routing_bench_2026-09-09.json.

**Bars, in readout units.** *Worth a training arm* if k = 32 gives a
step-time reduction ≥ 1.5x against dense (same checkpoint setting) with a
trained-checkpoint scalar-output change ≤ 1%. *Not worth it* if the
reduction is < 1.2x or the change is > 5%. Between: reported, and the
smallest k meeting the 1% change bar is named. A training arm, if
warranted, is the reference HiLift 35-case lane with `+model.anchor_topk=32`
(two seeds), bar: pressure within 2% of the dense reference 0.138, and is
preregistered separately before launch. The output-change readout is the
approximation error of *re-routing a model trained dense*; a model trained
sparse may differ less or more, which is what the training arm measures.

## 2026-09-09 — Verdict: SPARSE not worth a training arm — routing each point to its k nearest anchors is 8–16% *slower* than dense on a GB300 at 10,000 tokens, saves memory only where the exact recompute already does, and re-routes an untrained model's output by 21–46% {#sec-nb-sparse-routing-verdict}

**Setting and bars** (@sec-nb-sparse-routing-prereg). The `anchor_topk`
option (commit f1668bebe on branch isla-sparse-routing) restricts each
point's relational invariants, routing bias and point→slice mix to its k
nearest anchors; exact at k = 256, contract-tested (61 tests pass). Bars:
worth a training arm if k = 32 gives ≥ 1.5x step-time reduction with ≤ 1%
scalar-output change on the trained checkpoint; not worth it if < 1.2x or
> 5%.

**Readout** (one GB300, hidden 192, 12 layers, 256 slices, 10,000 tokens,
batch 1, bf16 autocast, AdamW step; median of 10 steps;
results/isla_sparse_routing_bench_2026-09-09.json):

| routing | step, recompute off | speed-up | incremental peak memory | step, recompute on | speed-up | incremental peak memory |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dense (256 anchors) | 0.230 s | 1.00 | 3.37 GiB | 0.237 s | 1.00 | 1.47 GiB |
| k = 128 | 0.273 s | 0.84 | 2.83 GiB | 0.281 s | 0.84 | 1.40 GiB |
| k = 64 | 0.261 s | 0.88 | 2.08 GiB | 0.268 s | 0.88 | 1.32 GiB |
| k = 32 | 0.256 s | 0.90 | 1.71 GiB | 0.262 s | 0.91 | 1.32 GiB |
| k = 16 | 0.253 s | 0.91 | 1.51 GiB | 0.258 s | 0.92 | 1.32 GiB |

Output change with the same weights at initialization (fp32, random
anisotropic cloud), relative L2 of the scalar channel: 21% (k = 128), 32%
(64), 42% (32), 46% (16); of the full output 26–31%.

**Verdict: not worth it, on the speed bar alone.** Sparse routing is slower
than dense at every k: the k-nearest selection (a 10,000 × 256 distance
matrix and top-k per layer), the gathers of anchors and logits, and the
scatters back to the dense (points × slices) tensors cost more than the
(points × k × 8) invariants save, because on this GPU the dense
(points × 256 × 8) geometry is a small, fused, memory-bound term (about
40 MB per layer in bf16) and not the bottleneck the step-time gap to
GeoTransolver suggested. Memory does fall as intended when nothing else
removes the geometry activations (3.37 → 1.71 GiB at k = 32, a 2.0x cut of
the incremental peak), but the exact recompute option of @sec-nb-geo-recompute
already brings dense routing to 1.47 GiB, and on top of it sparse routing
saves a further 10% only. The output change is far past the 5% bar as well:
at initialization the routing mass is spread over many anchors, so the
premise that a point's mass concentrates on its nearest anchors does not
hold for an untrained model, and excluding the other anchors from the
slice-state assignment re-routes it wholesale.

**What was not measured.** The trained-checkpoint re-routing test failed to
load `MeshTransformer2.0.96.mdlus` through `Module.from_checkpoint` in the
benchmark job (the registered class resolved from the checkpoint's name
rejected `out_scalars`; results/isla_sparse_routing_bench_2026-09-09.json,
key `checkpoint_output_change.error`), so the output change on a trained
model, where routing may well be local, is unknown. It is not needed for
the verdict: a speed-up below 1.2x fails the preregistered bar regardless of
accuracy. Where ISLA's step time actually goes at 10,000 tokens (the two
softmaxes over the (points × slices) logits, the slice-state and readback
einsums, or the per-token MLPs) is the profiling question this leaves open;
a kernel-level profile of one dense block is the right next instrument, and
is cheaper than any routing change.

**Tech-tree change.** SPARSE RUNNING → DONE (not worth it); no training arm.
The option stays in the code, flag-gated and default-off, as the runnable
record of the refuted design.

## 2026-09-09 — Verdict: UDRV-INT null — GeoTransolver-volume with the unit freestream direction changes by under 2% on every interior field; ISLA's pressure and velocity lead is not an input-scale artifact {#sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict}

**Setting and bars** (@sec-nb-udrv-int-prereg): the frozen
GeoTransolver-volume lane (27.6M parameters, 435 cars, 10,000 interior
points) with `forward_kwargs.global_embedding=global_data.U_inf_dir` in
place of the physical 38.9 m/s velocity, two seeds. Confound present if any
field improves by more than 5% over 0.0620 / 0.1334 / 0.0939; null if all
three lie within 3%.

**Readout** (results/udrv_int_reduction_2026-09-09.json; 48 validation cars):

| arm | pressure (seeds → mean) | velocity | eddy viscosity |
|---|---|---|---|
| GeoTransolver-volume, physical velocity | 0.0622 / 0.0618 → 0.0620 | 0.1335 / 0.1332 → 0.1334 | 0.0934 / 0.0944 → 0.0939 |
| GeoTransolver-volume, unit direction | 0.0615 / 0.0618 → **0.0617** | 0.1338 / 0.1282 → **0.1310** | 0.0941 / 0.0930 → **0.0936** |
| ISLA query tokens + SDF (~365 surface cells) | 0.0567 | 0.0853 | 0.1215 |
| ISLA query tokens + SDF (10,000 surface cells) | 0.0572 | 0.0848 | 0.1187 |

Paired per car (seed-mean errors): the unit-drive GeoTransolver-volume is
lower than its physical-drive twin on 27 / 41 / 26 of 48 cars (pressure /
velocity / eddy viscosity; median ratios 1.003 / 1.017 / 1.005). Against
ISLA query tokens + SDF it is higher on pressure on 44 of 48 cars (median
GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA 1.088) and on velocity on 48 of 48 (1.56), and
lower on eddy viscosity on 38 of 48 (0.91).

**Verdict: null.** Pressure −0.5%, velocity −1.8%, eddy viscosity −0.3%,
all inside the 3% band; the only field with a consistent per-car direction
is velocity (41 of 48), at a size below the bar. On the interior task the
freestream magnitude (38.9 against 2,679.5 on HiLiftAeroML, and constant
across cars) does not handicap GeoTransolver-volume the way it handicapped
the surface baselines, so the interior ordering of @sec-interior (ISLA
ahead on pressure and velocity at a third of the parameters, behind on
eddy viscosity) is not an input-scale artifact. The index's verdict
sentence, the verdict table's interior row, chapter 8's inputs paragraph
and chapter 12's limits and recommendation are updated accordingly; the
interior recommendation remains conditional only on the eddy-viscosity gap
and the query-count dependence. Tech-tree change: UDRV-INT READY → DONE
(null); QCOUNT's gate is open.

## 2026-09-09 — UDRV-L verdict, four training geometries: unit-drive GeoTransolver 0.189 against ISLA 0.250 by the mean, 9 of 18 geometries each way; the 1.8x was the input scale {#sec-nb-udrvl-geo40-verdict}

**Setting and bars** (results/udrv_ladder_preregistration_2026-09-09.md,
lanes 12–13). The `geometry_super_scarce` split: 40 training cases made of
four geometries at all ten angles, validated on 180 cases of 18 geometries
never seen at any angle. Reference: physical-drive GeoTransolver 0.449
(seeds 0.407 / 0.492), ISLA 0.250 (0.248 / 0.251), the book's 1.8x. Bars:
ISLA advantage only if unit-drive GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA ≥ 1.10 with ISLA
lower on at least two thirds of the cases and 12 of 18 geometries; parity
0.95–1.05; baseline ahead ≤ 0.90.

**Readout** (results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09c.json):

| arm | pressure (seeds → mean) | velocity | wall shear | ÷ ISLA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA | 0.248 / 0.251 → 0.250 | 0.226 | 0.353 | 1.00 |
| GeoTransolver, physical velocity | 0.407 / 0.492 → 0.449 | 0.424 | 0.606 | 1.8x behind |
| GeoTransolver, unit direction | 0.1888 / 0.1888 → **0.189** | **0.179** | **0.286** | **0.76 (ahead by the mean)** |

Paired per case (seed means): the unit-drive GeoTransolver is lower than ISLA
on 96 of 180 cases and on 9 of 18 geometries (median ISLA ÷ GeoTransolver
1.03; 10–90% range 0.78–2.06; sign test p = 0.41). Against its own
physical-drive twin it is lower on 180 of 180 cases and 18 of 18 geometries
(median factor 2.4). Its two seeds agree to 0.02%.

**Verdict: no ISLA advantage; baseline ahead by the mean, even by
geometry.** The mean ratio 0.76 meets the "baseline ahead" bar; the
per-geometry count is a coin toss (9 of 18) with a wide spread: on half the
held-out geometries ISLA is the more accurate model, and on a tail it is up
to twice as bad, which is what drives the mean. Either way the
preregistered condition for "ISLA generalizes across wing geometries from
few samples" (≥ 1.10 and two thirds of the cases) is not approached at four
training geometries, and the book's 1.8x was the input scale. Three of six
HiLift rungs are now re-measured with unit-drive baselines (35 cases, the
fixed angle, four geometries); at all three the baselines match or beat ISLA
by the mean. Remaining: 210 cases (GeoTransolver and Transolver), 21
geometries, 1,260 cases, and the deflection and floor replacements.

## 2026-09-09 — Preregistered and launched: WAVE-3, completing the fair-comparison picture in one pass (unit-drive baselines on every rung and dataset, ISLA weights-off on every rung, third seeds, steel-men for the new baselines) {#sec-nb-wave3-prereg}

**Why one wave.** The cluster has idle capacity and the program's open
comparisons are all cheap, well-defined lanes whose bars are already
written. Running them serially would take weeks for no scientific reason.
Every lane below is the frozen ladder protocol (10,000 sampled points, 500
epochs, bf16, no augmentation, final checkpoint, each split's own
validation set) with the drive at unit scale for every architecture, and
differs from an existing lane in exactly one declared way. Launch
increases the program to about 66 GPU nodes.

**Arms and bars.**

1. *ISLA weights off on every rung* (`now_hl_mt2_<split>_seed{42,43}` for
   the 1,260-case, 4-geometry, 21-geometry, fixed-angle and deflection
   splits; plus a third seed 44 at 35 cases). Bars per rung as in
   @sec-nb-noweights-prereg: persists if ≥ 5% better than weighted ISLA,
   fades if within 3%. If weights-off persists at ≥ 4 of 6 rungs, it becomes
   ISLA's reference configuration for accuracy and every ISLA-versus-baseline
   statement is made with it.
   *Amended 2026-09-10:* the reference-configuration consequence is retired
   (@sec-nb-principle-redirect); the arm is an ablation of the routing
   measure and its gains are read as the in-distribution price of
   discretization invariance.
2. *Unit-drive Transolver on the rungs it lacks* (4 geometries, 21
   geometries, 1,260 cases; lr 3e-3; seeds 42/43). Bars: the UDRV-L bars
   (ISLA advantage only if baseline ÷ ISLA ≥ 1.10 with two thirds of cases;
   parity 0.95–1.05; baseline ahead ≤ 0.90).
3. *Third seeds (44) for the unit-drive GeoTransolver and Transolver at 35
   and 210 cases*: no bar; the seed spread is reported and every two-seed
   statement at those rungs becomes three-seed.
4. *Steel-men for the new baselines at 35 cases*: unit-drive GeoTransolver
   at lr 3e-3 and unit-drive Transolver at lr 1e-3, seeds 42/43. Per the
   protocol's best-learning-rate rule, a rung's baseline number moves to the
   better rate if it improves by ≥ 5% (GeoTransolver ≤ 0.118, Transolver
   ≤ 0.109); the comparison is then restated at that rate.
5. *DrivAerML unit-drive baselines at 435 cars* (`uw_gt_unit_lr1e3_seed{42,43,44}`;
   `uw_transolver_unit_lr{1e3,3e3}_seed{42,43}`, Transolver's first DrivAerML
   lanes, both rates because it has no prior on this dataset; plus ISLA's
   third seed `iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed44`). Bars: the GeoTransolver confound is
   present if the unit-drive lane beats the physical-drive 0.0548 by ≥ 5%
   (≤ 0.0521), null within 3%; Transolver is reported at its better rate
   against ISLA (0.0577) with the UDRV-L bands.
6. *Interior third seeds*: ISLA query tokens + SDF seed 44 and unit-drive
   GeoTransolver-volume seed 44 (interior bars unchanged; spread reported).

The pose-varying benchmark (POSE-BENCH, @sec-nb-pose-qcount-plan) is run
by the transfer-program session (research/transfer_program) under its own
preregistration, together with a geometry-stratified multi-draw study at 35
and 210 cases; its results are offered to the book when they land.
Launchers: HiLift lanes as rows 44–68 of highlift/wave2_lanes.tsv
(hl_wave2_aga.sbatch); DrivAerML lanes uw_aga.sbatch (cloned from
instwave_aga.sbatch); interior seeds through v0/v0_qt2_aga.sbatch lane 2 and
v0/v0_udrvint_aga.sbatch lane 2.

## 2026-09-09 — NOW-L, DrivAerML rung: measure weights off scores 0.0561 against 0.0577 (2.8% better, 41 of 48 cars), inside the preregistered "fades" band; the 210-case HiLift rung is pending {#sec-nb-noweights-drivaer-verdict}

**Setting and bars** (@sec-nb-noweights-prereg). ISLA's reference DrivAerML
surface configuration at 435 cars with `use_measure_weights=false`
(`now_mt2_lr1e3_seed{42,43}`, the reference lanes' own code snapshot) against
the weighted reference `iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed{42,43}` (0.0588 / 0.0567 →
0.0577). Bars: persists if ≥ 5% better (≤ 0.0548); fades if within 3%
(0.0560–0.0594).

**Readout** (results/nowt_reduction_2026-09-09.json; 48 validation cars):

| arm | seed 42 | seed 43 | mean | vs weighted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA, measure weights on | 0.0588 | 0.0567 | 0.0577 | 1.00 |
| ISLA, measure weights off | 0.0569 | 0.0553 | **0.0561** | **0.972** (2.8% better) |
| GeoTransolver, physical velocity (reference) | 0.0546 | 0.0550 | 0.0548 | 0.950 |

Paired per car: the unweighted model is lower on 41 of 48 (median weighted ÷
unweighted 1.025, 10–90% range 0.99–1.09).

**Verdict for this rung: fades, narrowly.** The gain is 2.8%, inside the 3%
band by 0.2 percentage points, but it is consistent (41 of 48 cars, both
seeds) and in the predicted direction: the variance reading predicted a
smaller gain on DrivAerML, whose sampled cell areas are more uniform than
HiLift's, and 12% → 2.8% is that. On DrivAerML the unweighted ISLA sits 2.4%
behind the physical-drive GeoTransolver (0.0561 against 0.0548) instead of
5.3%; the unit-drive GeoTransolver (WAVE-3, `uw_gt_unit_lr1e3_*`) is the
reference that matters and is training. The NOW-L decision (reference
configuration change) waits for the 210-case HiLift rung
(`a35_hl_mt2_noweights_scarce_seed{42,43}`, epoch ~110) and the WAVE-3
weights-off ladder; the rule stays "persists at ≥ 4 of 6 rungs".

## 2026-09-09 — Preregistered: SCALE, width and token-count scaling of ISLA, GeoTransolver and Transolver at full data on both datasets {#sec-nb-scale-prereg}

**Why now.** Every lane in the program runs under 20 GB on a 288 GB
device: the frozen protocol's operating point (about 9M parameters, 10,000
sampled cells per case) was chosen for an earlier cluster, and the accuracy
ordering the book reports has only ever been measured there. Whether the
ordering, the absolute errors and the cost frontier change when the models
are given the memory they have is an open question with an idle cluster
able to answer it in days.

**Design.** Full-data splits only, where capacity can matter (HiLiftAeroML
1,260 cases; DrivAerML 435 cars), every architecture with the freestream at
unit scale, the frozen protocol otherwise (500 epochs, bf16, no
augmentation, final checkpoint, the reference learning rates 1e-3 for
ISLA and GeoTransolver, 3e-3 for Transolver, two seeds). Per architecture
and dataset, five arms against the existing or running reference arm
(reference width, 10,000 cells):

| arm | ISLA (`model.hidden`) | GeoTransolver (`model.n_hidden`) | Transolver (`model.n_hidden`) | cells per case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| reference | 192 (8.9M) | 256 (9.0M) | 256 (6.0M) | 10,000 |
| width ×2 | 384 | 384 | 384 | 10,000 |
| width ×2.7 | 512 | 512 | 512 | 10,000 |
| tokens ×4 | 192 | 256 | 256 | 40,000 |
| tokens ×8 | 192 | 256 | 256 | 80,000 |
| corner | 384 | 384 | 384 | 40,000 |

Sixty lanes (3 architectures × 2 datasets × 5 arms × 2 seeds), plus four
ISLA lanes at width 384 with the routing measure weights off (both datasets,
two seeds) as an *ablation* that separates the width effect from the
weights effect; the weights-off configuration is discretization-dependent
(it reads the mesher's density) and is never a reference configuration, so
every reference ISLA number in this study is the measure-weighted model. ISLA arms run from the code snapshot at 52eb29ec5
(default forward bitwise the reference model) with the exact activation
recompute enabled on the 40,000- and 80,000-cell arms; the existing
20,000-cell lanes (floor_hl_mt2_full_20k_seed{42,43}, udrv_hl_gt_full_20k_seed{42,43})
are the 20k rung of the token ladder. Learning
rates are not retuned for width; a run that diverges is reported as a
divergence at the protocol rate, not silently retuned. Each arm records
parameters, peak memory and step time from its own training log, so every
accuracy point carries its cost.

**Readouts and bars, in the validation pressure relative L2 of each
dataset.** Let e_ref be the reference arm's two-seed mean for an
architecture on a dataset (HiLift: ISLA 0.041, unit-drive GeoTransolver and
Transolver from UDRV-L lanes 16–17 and wave-3 rows 58–59; DrivAerML: ISLA
0.0577, unit-drive GeoTransolver and Transolver from the uw lanes).

1. *Width scales* for an architecture on a dataset if the 512-wide arm is
   ≥ 5% better than e_ref; *saturated* if within 3%; between, reported.
2. *Resolution-limited* if the 80,000-cell arm is ≥ 5% better than e_ref at
   the reference width; *sample-limited* if within 3%.
3. *Scale changes the ordering*: with r = (baseline ÷ ISLA) at matched arm,
   scale *favours ISLA* if r at the corner arm exceeds r at the reference by
   ≥ 0.05; *favours the baselines* if it falls by ≥ 0.05; otherwise the
   ordering is scale-independent over this range.
4. *Cost frontier*: for each architecture the (GPU-hours, error) points of
   its six configurations; the useful statement is which architecture
   reaches a given error cheapest, read off the frontier, not the endpoint.

**Consequences.** If width or tokens move errors by more than 5% for the
baselines but not ISLA (or the reverse), the book's accuracy ordering is
labelled as an ordering at 9M parameters and 10,000 cells and the
recommendation section gains a scale clause. If everything saturates within
3%, the protocol's operating point is vindicated as data-limited and the
program's next data investment, not its next model, is the lever.

**Ownership.** One agent per architecture runs its twenty lanes from its
own lane table and launcher (highlift/scale_lanes_<arch>.tsv,
highlift/hl_scale_<arch>_aga.sbatch cloned from hl_wave2_aga.sbatch), after
a ten-minute probe of its three heaviest configurations for memory and step
time; verdict entries per architecture follow, and one synthesis entry.
Job-name prefix scale-<arch>-; run ids scale_<arch>_<dataset>_<arm>_seed<s>.

## 2026-09-09 — SCALE launched: 64 lanes accepted; the cost half of the study is already measured, and it is step time, not memory, that scales {#sec-nb-scale-launch}

**State.** Every lane of @sec-nb-scale-prereg is training (ISLA 24, including
the weights-off pair; GeoTransolver 20; Transolver 20), each after a first-link
acceptance check of steps advancing, memory recorded and no fault. The
per-architecture agents' own launch entries carry the per-lane detail
(@sec-nb-scale-launch, @sec-nb-scale-gt-launch).

**What the first links measured** (four GPUs per lane, bf16, peak memory
per GPU from the training log; reference operating point 10,000 cells):

| architecture | arm | parameters | peak memory | step time | projected wall time (HiLift 1,260) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA | width 512 | 60.2M | 6.1 GB | 1.28 s | ~2.3 days |
| ISLA | 80,000 cells (exact recompute) | 8.9M | 13.0 GB | 3.44 s | ~6.3 days |
| GeoTransolver | width 512 | — | 6.0 GB | 0.15 s | hours |
| GeoTransolver | 80,000 cells | — | 31.9 GB | 0.19 s | ~7 hours |
| Transolver | width 512 | — | 4.2 GB | 0.08 s | hours |
| Transolver | 80,000 cells | — | 22 GB | 0.10 s | hours |

No configuration in the grid exceeds 32 GB of the 288 GB available, so the
study is bounded by step time, not memory. The two baselines' step times are
nearly flat in both width and token count at this scale (their attention is
over 256 slices, so the token dimension enters only through linear
projections); ISLA's grows about 5.6x from width 192 to 512 and about 15x
from 10,000 to 80,000 cells, because its per-slice relational geometry
(points × slices × 8 invariants per layer) scales with tokens and the
per-token MLP with width. Whatever the accuracy half of the study returns,
the cost frontier (bar 4) will be read against this: at 80,000 cells the
baselines complete an epoch in the time ISLA completes a fraction of one,
and the sparse-routing route to closing that gap was already measured as
not worth it (@sec-nb-sparse-routing-verdict). The remaining speed lever is
kernel-level (a fused slice-block kernel), which is an engineering item, not
a research node.

**Next.** Each agent evaluates its lanes as they train, reduces, and writes
its verdict on bars 1–2; the coordinator writes the cross-architecture
synthesis on bars 3–4 when all three are in. The heaviest ISLA arm sets the
study's horizon (about six days); the GeoTransolver and Transolver grids and
the ISLA width arms land within a day, so a partial synthesis at that point
covers width scaling fully and the token ladder up to 40,000 cells.

## 2026-09-09 — Ops: every DrivAerML interior lane hung from about 12:14; root cause a hang inside host-memory pinning in the reader's prefetch thread, not Lustre; workaround `dataloader.pin_memory=false` at +35% step time {#sec-nb-interior-pin-stall}

**Symptom.** From about 12:14 every training lane on the DrivAerML volume
dataset, across three sessions (the density and neighbour arms, the
interior third seeds, the transfer companion's D1 and campaign-D lanes),
stopped advancing within minutes of starting or resuming, with fresh lanes
hanging before their first checkpoint and resumed lanes at the same epochs
on every attempt; HiLift and DrivAerML *surface* lanes were unaffected. Each
hung link idled until the 3,600 s distributed timeout, restarted from its
checkpoint and hung again.

**Diagnosis** (density track; tools `highlift/qtdens_thread_dump.sh`,
`highlift/qtdens_probe_stripes.sh`, a faulthandler `sitecustomize` that
dumps every thread's stack every ten minutes). Not a hung read: on a
stalled link no thread on any rank was in D state, no dataset file was
open, and every training file and every stripe of every interior memmap
read cleanly from a healthy allocation. The stack dump of the stuck rank
shows its main thread waiting without timeout in the DataLoader prefetch
hand-off (`physicsnemo/datapipes/protocols.py:366` ←
`datapipes/dataloader.py:459/499/306` ← `train.py:548`), and the prefetch
worker it waits for inside `TensorDict.pin_memory` called from
`physicsnemo/datapipes/readers/mesh.py:690` (`dm = dm.pin_memory()` in
`DomainMeshReader.__getitem__`). The other three ranks spin in the recipe's
step-failure barrier all-reduce, which is what the NCCL watchdog then names.
Why host pinning hangs on these lanes is not established (driver or
pinned-memory level; it began at a fixed time and affects only the volume
pipeline).

**Workaround and cost.** The hydra override `dataloader.pin_memory=false`
(recipe/conf/base.yaml sets it true) on the train.py command line. A probe
lane resumed from epoch 310 stepped normally for fifteen minutes past the
point where four pinned attempts hung, at **0.388 s per step against 0.287 s
pinned (+35%)** for the 10,000-query ISLA configuration on GB300. Every
interior lane launched or resumed from 2026-09-09 onward runs with the
override, and every interior step time from then on is a pageable-copy
number, stated as such wherever it is quoted. Held chains (mine, the
density track's, the transfer companion's ten) were released with the
override after the probe's acceptance.

**What it says about the tooling.** A prefetch hand-off with no timeout
turns any producer fault into an hour of idle GPUs per link; a bounded wait
that raises a named error (and the recipe's step-failure barrier reporting
the *cause* rather than the collective) is a datapipe fix worth making
independent of the pinning cause. Recorded as an upstream candidate.

## 2026-09-09 — Preregistered: ISLA-PERF, profile the training step, then buy scale with the savings {#sec-nb-isla-perf-prereg}

**Why.** The SCALE launch (@sec-nb-scale-launch) measured ISLA's step at
0.23 s (hidden 192, 10,000 cells), 1.28 s (512, 10k) and 3.44 s (192, 80k
with the exact geometry recompute) on GB300s, four GPUs per lane, against
GeoTransolver's 0.15–0.19 s and Transolver's 0.08–0.10 s over the same grid.
Peak memory never exceeded 13 GB of 288. Step time, not memory, is what
stops ISLA from being trained at the scale the hardware allows, and the
token scaling (15x for 8x cells) is superlinear where the arithmetic
(points × slices × 8 invariants per layer) is linear; something in the
implementation, not the model, is paying that. Earlier speed work: the
exact recompute trades 1.16x step for 2.3x less incremental memory;
compiling the geometry region gave 0.82x step with bf16 rounding
differences (not adopted); sparse anchor routing was slower at every k
(@sec-nb-sparse-routing-verdict).

**Instrument, written before running.** One GB300, bf16 autocast, AdamW
step, batch 1, synthetic anisotropic cloud (no data loading), the reference
surface configuration (12 layers, 256 slices). Median step time over ten
steps after three warm-ups, peak allocated and reserved memory, and a
torch.profiler trace of three steps with CUDA kernel time bucketed by
operator family (point softmax, slice softmax, slice einsums, geometry
elementwise and cat, Linear/MLP GEMMs, LayerNorm and GELU, optimizer,
other), at (192, 10k), (512, 10k), (192, 80k) and (512, 40k); plus the
log-log slopes of step time in tokens (10k–80k at hidden 192) and in hidden
(192–512 at 10k), with and without the recompute. Readout 1 is the ranked
bucket table and the named term behind the superlinear token scaling.

**Optimization rule.** Every change must reproduce the reference forward to
bf16 roundoff (the observed maximum relative difference is stated) or
bitwise; a change that is exactly equivalent in fp32 arithmetic may become
the default with an exactness test; anything beyond roundoff is a flag-gated
option with its own test, default off. Candidates to be measured, not
assumed: never materializing the (B, N, S, 8) invariants (a fused region
with recompute in backward), chunking over slices, avoiding (B, N, S)
intermediates in bf16 copies, fp32 accumulation only where needed, removing
the duplicated point softmax, contiguity and memory format, the passive
readout's chunk size.

**Bars, in readout units.** *Worthwhile for merge* if the step time at
(192, 80k) or at (512, 10k) falls by ≥ 1.3x at equal outputs, or peak
memory falls by ≥ 30% at ≤ 1.05x step time (quoted against both the plain
path, 3.37 GiB incremental at (192, 10k), and the recompute path, 1.47 GiB).
*Not worthwhile* if < 1.15x and < 15%. Between: reported, merged only if
exact. Readout 3 is the largest (hidden, cells) configuration trainable in
the reference lane's budget (500 epochs of HiLift's 1,260 cases on four
GPUs in ≤ 3 days) before and after. If the gain is ≥ 1.5x, one scaled
training pilot is proposed with its exact flags (not launched here).

## 2026-09-09 — Verdict: ISLA-PERF — one kernel was 85–95% of the training step; reducing the point softmax along a contiguous dimension makes ISLA 3.6x faster at 10k cells and 18.7x at 80k, exactly {#sec-nb-isla-perf-verdict}

**Profile readout** (@sec-nb-isla-perf-prereg; one GB300, bf16 autocast,
AdamW step, batch 1, reference surface configuration with 12 layers and 256
slices; CUDA kernel time per step from torch.profiler;
results/isla_profile_2026-09-09.json). At every configuration one kernel
dominated: PyTorch's `cunn_SpatialSoftMax`, which serves a softmax over a
*middle* tensor dimension. ISLA normalizes its point-to-slice assignment
over the points, `softmax(logits + log_w, dim=1)` on a (B, N, S) tensor,
twice per slice block; the spatial kernel parallelizes over the B × S = 256
columns only and walks the N points serially.

| configuration (hidden, cells) | step | point softmax (fwd + bwd) | share of step | geometry elementwise | everything else |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 192, 10,000 | 0.238 s | 203 ms | 85% | 35 ms | 27 ms |
| 512, 10,000 | 0.243 s | 204 ms | 84% | 37 ms | 27 ms |
| 512, 40,000 | 1.245 s | 1,128 ms | 91% | 121 ms | 85 ms |
| 192, 80,000 | 3.507 s | 3,321 ms | 95% | 219 ms | 226 ms |

Step time was independent of width (0.238 → 0.243 s from hidden 192 to 512,
exponent 0.02) and superlinear in tokens (exponent 1.28), because the
dominant kernel's cost grows with N at fixed, tiny parallelism. The model's
arithmetic is a small fraction of the step: the Linear and MLP GEMMs total
2–8 ms, the slice einsums 5–45 ms.

**The fix** (commit 3abd0ff58; `fast_point_softmax`, default on): compute
the point softmax on the transposed (B, S, N) tensor along its last,
contiguous dimension and transpose the result back, at every point-softmax
site (both in the slice block, the latent-token assignment, the passive
decoder's final assignment, the odd head's source assignment). Same
arithmetic, different floating-point summation order. `fast_point_softmax=False`
reproduces the original kernel bitwise.

**Exactness** (results/isla_perf_round2_2026-09-09.json, same weights, same
inputs): in float64 the two paths agree to 10⁻¹¹ on every configuration that
owns a point softmax (surface, gauge + recompute, passive decoder, latent
tokens, odd head, query tokens; test/experimental/nn/test_isla_perf.py, 9
tests; all 82 ISLA tests pass). Under bf16 autocast on the GPU the relative
L2 difference between the fast and the original path is 1.05% (192, 10k),
1.08% (192, 40k) and 1.49% (512, 10k), against 0.98%, 0.98% and 1.32% for
the same model evaluated in bf16 versus fp32: the change is at bf16
roundoff, as the bar requires, and not below it (a summation-order
difference of 10⁻⁷ is amplified through twelve layers to ~5 × 10⁻⁴ in fp32
with TF32 matmuls). Trained checkpoints therefore evaluate to within their
own bf16 noise, not bitwise; `fast_point_softmax=False` is the switch for a
bitwise reproduction.

**Speed and memory after the fix** (results/isla_profile_fast_2026-09-09.json;
median of 10 steps; incremental memory over the resident model and
optimizer; plain path / exact geometry recompute):

| configuration (hidden, cells) | step before | step after | speedup | tokens/s after | incremental memory (unchanged) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 192, 10,000 | 0.238 / 0.274 s | 0.065 / 0.115 s | **3.6x / 2.4x** | 153k / 87k | 3.20 / 1.37 GiB |
| 192, 20,000 | 0.570 / 0.585 s | 0.086 / 0.117 s | 6.7x / 5.0x | 233k / 171k | 6.34 / 2.74 GiB |
| 192, 40,000 | 1.233 / 1.262 s | 0.105 / 0.134 s | 11.7x / 9.4x | 381k / 297k | 12.6 / 5.5 GiB |
| 192, 80,000 | 3.507 / 3.568 s | 0.188 / 0.245 s | **18.7x / 14.6x** | 427k / 327k | 25.2 / 11.0 GiB |
| 256, 10,000 | 0.240 / 0.247 s | 0.085 / 0.115 s | 2.8x / 2.2x | 117k / 87k | 3.5 / 1.6 GiB |
| 384, 10,000 | 0.242 / 0.249 s | 0.086 / 0.117 s | 2.8x / 2.1x | 117k / 85k | 4.0 / 2.1 GiB |
| 512, 10,000 | 0.243 / 0.251 s | 0.085 / 0.116 s | **2.9x / 2.2x** | 118k / 86k | 4.5 / 2.5 GiB |
| 512, 40,000 | 1.245 / 1.275 s | 0.118 / 0.147 s | 10.6x / 8.7x | 339k / 272k | 17.8 / 10.2 GiB |

The token exponent falls from 1.28 to 0.49 (0.35 with recompute): at 10,000
cells the step is now launch-bound (about 60 ms of CUDA time for roughly a
thousand kernels), so tokens per second *rises* with the token count until
about 80,000 cells. The remaining cost is the per-slice geometry (the eight
invariants built from (B, N, S, 3) intermediates and concatenated) at about
60% of the step, the slice einsums at about 12%, and kernel launches.

**Bars.** Worthwhile for merge required ≥ 1.3x at (192, 80k) or (512, 10k)
at equal outputs: measured 18.7x and 2.9x. Memory is unchanged (the fix
touches no saved activation), so the memory bar is not claimed; the
recompute option remains the memory lever (2.3x at 1.16x → now 1.8x step
cost at 10k, converging to 1.3x at 80k).

**Round 2, measured and not adopted.** Compiling the geometry region
(`torch.compile` on `_geo_region`, dynamic=False) is *slower* at 40,000 and
80,000 cells (0.56–0.72x) and 1.17–1.21x faster only at 10,000 cells with
recompute, while changing outputs by 1–3% relative L2 in bf16; consistent
with the earlier compile trial. It stays out. The next exact lever is
building the invariants without (B, N, S, 3) intermediates (the dot products
against the drive and the normals are bilinear and can come from small
batched matrix products); it would remove most of the remaining 60% but
introduces cancellation in the distance term for points near their anchor,
so it belongs behind a flag with its own tolerance test, not in this pass.

**What the savings buy.** The reference lane's budget (500 epochs of
HiLiftAeroML's 1,260 cases on four GPUs in ≤ 3 days, about 157,500 steps)
admits a step of about 1.6 s. Before: the SCALE grid's (192, 80k) arm did
not fit (3.5 s, about 6 days) and (192, 40k) did (1.2 s, 2.3 days). After:
every arm of the grid fits with a wide margin (the heaviest, (192, 80k),
takes about 9 hours; (512, 40k) about 6 hours), and by the measured token
exponent the budget reaches roughly (512, 320,000 cells) at about 0.35 s
per step with 140 GB of memory on the plain path or 80 GB with recompute,
an extrapolation to be confirmed by measurement. GPU-hours for the (192,
80k) arm fall from about 610 to 33.

**Proposed pilot (not launched here), as the bar's ≥ 1.5x clause asks.**
One pair of lanes from a snapshot containing 3abd0ff58: HiLift 1,260 cases,
`model.hidden=512`, `sampling_resolution=80000`, `+model.geo_checkpoint=true`
(11 GB, about 0.3 s per step, about 13 hours), seeds 42/43, frozen protocol
otherwise, graded with the SCALE bars against the (512, 10k) and (192, 80k)
arms; and, for the SCALE ISLA lanes already training at the slow kernel,
the coordinator's call whether to let the six-day 80k arm finish or restart
it from the fast snapshot (a restart changes numerics at bf16 roundoff and
must be declared in the arm's provenance).

**Addendum (2026-09-09, coordinator).** Two amendments before the merge.
*Default.* The fast kernel ships with `fast_point_softmax=False` as the
default: under bf16 its outputs differ from the old kernel by 1.0–1.5%
relative L2, the same order as several comparisons in the book (ISLA
against the unit-drive GeoTransolver at 35 cases is 10%; the DrivAerML
weights-off difference is 2.8%; interior seed spreads are about 1%), and
every checkpoint and evaluation in the book used the old kernel. The scaled
lanes and the neutrality control enable it explicitly
(`+model.fast_point_softmax=true`). The default flips only after two checks
land: the DrivAerML neutrality pair (`scale_isla_dr_kernelctrl_seed{42,43}`,
within 3% of 0.0577) and an evaluation-only check of an existing trained
checkpoint (`iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed42`) with both kernels showing the metric
moves by ≤ 0.3%; both numbers are written here when they land.
*Attribution.* The sparse-routing entry (@sec-nb-sparse-routing-verdict)
attributed ISLA's step cost to the per-slice geometry tensors and concluded
that routing to fewer anchors could not recover it; the profile shows the
cost was the softmax kernel's launch geometry, not the invariant tensors, so
that entry's mechanism was wrong while its verdict (sparse routing is not the
lever) stands.

4.58 GiB and 65 ms). One GB300, one process, batch 1, bf16 autocast, fp32
parameters, AdamW(lr 1e-3), MSE on a random 9-channel target, three warm-up
and five measured steps, the same synthetic inputs, and the same four
readouts per step: incremental peak allocated (the book's ISLA instrument),
total peak allocated, memory reserved after the step (the trainer's
instrument), and the CUDA-synchronized step time (median of five); memory
summaries are the maximum over the five steps. Every architecture at its
recipe surface configuration (ISLA 12 layers × hidden 192, GeoTransolver 12
× 256 without local features, Transolver 8 × 256; 256 slices; 3 scalar + 2
vector outputs). ISLA rows are labelled by kernel: *reference kernel* is the

(`fast_point_softmax=False`, the branch default); *fast kernel* is

Artifact: results/isla_vs_baselines_cost_fastkernel_2026-09-09.json.

| architecture (hidden) | cells | parameters | incremental peak | total peak | reserved | step |

| Transolver 512 | 10,000 | 23.9M | 3.29 GiB | 3.62 GiB | 4.08 GiB | 31 ms |

**Reading, for the cost row.** On one GPU and one instrument, at the
reference operating point (10,000 cells, about 9M parameters): the
reference-kernel ISLA is 3.5x slower per step than GeoTransolver and 7.1x
slower than Transolver at 0.83x GeoTransolver's incremental memory (0.36x
with the exact recompute, at 3.6x GeoTransolver's step); the fast-kernel
ISLA is **1.09x** GeoTransolver's step and **2.2x** Transolver's at the same
memory (0.83x GeoTransolver's), or 1.5x GeoTransolver's step at 0.36x its
memory with the recompute. At 80,000 cells the fast-kernel ISLA is 1.11x
GeoTransolver's step at 0.81x its memory (1.45x at 0.35x with recompute).
At width 512 the three architectures differ in parameter count for the same
width (ISLA 60M, GeoTransolver 36M, Transolver 24M) and ISLA's step is again
1.09x GeoTransolver's. The audit's earlier "1.6 GiB against 4.1 GiB"
compared ISLA with recompute (total peak, here 1.57 GiB) against
GeoTransolver's total peak (4.07 GiB); on the incremental instrument the
same pair reads 1.41 against 3.91 GiB. Memory is unchanged by the kernel;
the "3.7x slower" clause of the current cost row is what the fast kernel
removes.

**Default policy.** The branch ships `fast_point_softmax=False` so that the
trained checkpoints evaluate bitwise as before; the flip to True is gated on
neutrality on a trained checkpoint (the DrivAerML reference
iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed42 evaluated through the recipe with the fast kernel; bar:
every validation metric within 0.3% of its reference-kernel value), reported
in the addendum below when its evaluation lands.

**Addendum: neutrality on a trained checkpoint — bar not met; the default
stays `fast_point_softmax=False`.** The DrivAerML reference checkpoint
`iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed42` (epoch 500) was evaluated through the recipe's
inference path from the current code snapshot twice, identical except for the
kernel (the recipe resolves the model file by class name, so the checkpoint's
`MeshTransformer2.0.500.mdlus` was exposed as `ISLA.0.500.mdlus` through a
symlinked copy of its checkpoint directory; both runs report "Loaded model
state dictionary"). Control, reference kernel: pressure 0.06235, wall shear
0.09100 (x 0.06837, y 0.16191, z 0.13073). Fast kernel: 0.06197, 0.09068
(0.06828, 0.16060, 0.13070). Relative change of the means: −0.61%, −0.35%,
−0.13%, −0.81%, −0.02%; the largest per-case change is 20% on pressure and
26% on wall shear y (results/isla_fastkernel_checkpoint_neutrality_2026-09-09.json).
Two of five metrics exceed the 0.3% bar, so the default is not flipped: a
trained ISLA is sensitive enough to the summation order of its point softmax
that a roundoff-level perturbation moves individual cases by tens of
percent, in both directions, with the means moving under 1%. The fast kernel
is therefore the kernel to *train* with (models trained and evaluated with
it are self-consistent, and the SCALE study's cost frontier is measured with
it), while the book's existing checkpoints keep the reference kernel for
evaluation.

**A second finding, outside this track and flagged for the coordinator.**
The same checkpoint evaluated with the reference kernel from the current
code snapshot and the current recipe copy scores pressure 0.06235 against
the 0.05875 recorded at training time from the snapshot it was trained with
(+6.1%; wall shear +6.1%, x +5.4%, y +9.1%, z +3.5%; per-case changes up to
31–51%; results/isla_checkpoint_snapshot_discrepancy_2026-09-09.json). The
kernel is not the cause (it is held fixed in that comparison). The per-case
spread suggests the two evaluations did not see the same sampled validation
points (the reader path changed between snapshots), rather than a model
difference; either way, the numbers a checkpoint produces depend on the
evaluation snapshot at the 6% level, which is larger than several of the
book's stated margins, and needs its own instrument before any
cross-snapshot comparison is read.

## 2026-09-09 — WAVE-3 arm 5 verdict: on DrivAerML the unit drive does not help GeoTransolver (0.0556 against 0.0548, null); unit-drive GeoTransolver, Transolver and ISLA are at parity within 4% at 435 cars, within 1% with ISLA's weights off {#sec-nb-uw-verdict}

**Setting and bars** (@sec-nb-wave3-prereg, arm 5). DrivAerML surface
pressure, 435 training cars, 48 validation cars, frozen protocol, every
architecture fed the unit freestream direction:
`uw_gt_unit_lr1e3_seed{42,43,44}`, `uw_transolver_unit_lr{1e3,3e3}_seed{42,43}`
(Transolver's first DrivAerML lanes, both rates because it had no prior on
this dataset). References: physical-drive GeoTransolver 0.0548

where the freestream magnitude is 38.9 m/s and constant across cars, the

the book stand as fair measurements and the "lower bound" qualifier is
retired. Transolver: 0.0563 at its better rate, parity with ISLA (0.98x,
inside 0.95–1.05). The full-data DrivAerML picture is therefore three
architectures within 4% of one another, and within 1% once ISLA drops its
measure weights: GeoTransolver 0.0556, ISLA (weights off) 0.0561, Transolver
0.0563, ISLA (weights on) 0.0577. Chapter 6's full-data paragraph, chapter
12's limits and recommendation, chapter 5's DrivAerML ladder note, the index
paragraph and the verdict table's DrivAerML rows are rewritten; "8.5%
behind" is retired. ISLA's third DrivAerML seed (`iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed44`,
training) is added to the reference when it lands. Tech-tree change: WAVE-3
arm 5 measured.

**Correction (later the same day).** With pinning off, the same lanes stalled
again (twice more on the probe lane, once across every interior lane at
19:22–19:25 in three sessions), and the new stack dumps place the stuck rank
inside the host-to-device copy of the loaded sample
(`physicsnemo/mesh/domain_mesh.py:1686` → `TensorDict.to(device)`), with the
other ranks in the step barrier. Pinning was a *site* of the hang, not its
cause: on one rank the CUDA context stops completing host-side operations
at a random point, on DrivAerML interior lanes only, with synchronized onset
across nodes and sessions, which is a GPU-driver or shared-infrastructure
condition outside user space (py-spy attach is denied on the nodes). The
chains do progress between stalls. Mitigation adopted on every interior
launcher: `PHYSICSNEMO_DIST_TIMEOUT_S=600` so a stalled link dies and
resumes from its checkpoint in ten minutes rather than sixty, link
recycling at 15 minutes idle, and `dataloader.pin_memory=false` kept
because it removes one hang site. The +35% step-time caveat stands for
unpinned lanes. Open question for the cluster team: what changed on the
GB300 nodes' CUDA or driver side around 12:14 PDT on 2026-09-09 for jobs
performing large host-to-device copies.

## 2026-09-09 — Preregistered: SNAPSHOT-LADDER, which code or recipe change moves the evaluation of a fixed checkpoint by 6%? {#sec-nb-snapshot-ladder-prereg}

**Symptom.** The DrivAerML reference checkpoint `iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed42`
scored a validation pressure relative L2 of 0.05875 at training time, from
the code snapshot that trained it; evaluated through the recipe's inference
path from the current snapshot with the same (reference) kernel it scores
0.06235 (+6.1%; wall shear +6.1%; per-case changes up to 31–51%;
@sec-nb-cost-matched-fast). Every comparison in the program that reads a
checkpoint through a different snapshot than the one that trained it rests
on knowing where that 6% comes from.

**Instrument (eval-only).** The same checkpoint, the reference kernel, the
same recipe copy ($T/recipe), dataset drivaer_ml_surface, validation split,
10,000 sampled cells, evaluated under each cluster code snapshot in turn:
`code` (trained it; produced 0.05875), `code_isla2`, `code_isla3`,
`code_isla4`, `code_isla5`, `code_perf`; then, if $T/recipe_support (the
transfer session's recipe copy) differs from $T/recipe, `code` with
recipe_support. The checkpoint directory is exposed through a symlinked copy
carrying both class-derived file names (`MeshTransformer2.0.500.mdlus`,
`ISLA.0.500.mdlus`) so every snapshot loads the same weights, and each
evaluation must log "Loaded model state dictionary". For two fixed
validation cars the sampled point coordinates are read from each
evaluation's prediction artifact and compared across snapshots (identical,
a permutation, or a different sample).

**Readouts.** Per snapshot: mean pressure, velocity and wall-shear relative
L2 over the 48 cars; the largest per-case relative change against the
`code` evaluation; identity of the sampled point sets. **Bars.** The
discrepancy is *attributed to a snapshot step* if exactly one adjacent pair
in the ladder moves the mean pressure error by ≥ 3% while every other
adjacent pair moves it ≤ 0.3%. If the point sets differ across that pair,
the attribution is *the validation sample changed*, and the change is named
from the git history of physicsnemo/datapipes/readers/mesh.py and
physicsnemo/mesh between the two snapshots' recorded commits. If all
snapshots agree with one another (≤ 0.3%) but not with the 0.05875 recorded
at training time, the discrepancy lies *between the training-time validation
pass and infer.py*, and that is the finding. Anything else is reported as
measured.

## 2026-09-09 — Verdict: SNAPSHOT-LADDER — the +6% is bf16 evaluation rounding, not code, data or recipe: in float32 every snapshot scores the fixed checkpoint at 0.05682 to five digits, while bf16 gives 0.05875 under the training class and 0.06235 under every later one {#sec-nb-snapshot-ladder-verdict}

**Ladder** (@sec-nb-snapshot-ladder-prereg; checkpoint `iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed42`,
reference kernel, recipe $T/recipe, DrivAerML validation, 10,000 cells, bf16
autocast unless stated; results/snapshot_ladder_2026-09-09.json):

| evaluation | pressure | wall shear | wss x / y / z | largest per-case change vs `code` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| training-time record (snapshot `code`) | 0.05875 | 0.08580 | 0.0649 / 0.1483 / 0.1263 | — |
| `code` | 0.05875 | 0.08580 | 0.0649 / 0.1483 / 0.1263 | 0 (bitwise) |
| `code` with recipe_support | 0.05875 | 0.08580 | 0.0649 / 0.1483 / 0.1263 | 0 |
| `code_isla2` | 0.06235 | 0.09100 | 0.0684 / 0.1619 / 0.1307 | 31% |
| `code_isla3`, `code_isla4`, `code_isla5`, `code_perf` | 0.06235 | 0.09100 | identical to `code_isla2` | 31% |
| **float32**, `code` | **0.05682** | **0.08300** | 0.0627 / 0.1427 / 0.1229 | — |
| **float32**, `code_perf` | **0.05682** | **0.08300** | identical to fp32 `code` (per case ≤ 0.001%) | — |

Exactly one adjacent pair moves the mean (`code` → `code_isla2`, +6.1%);
every other pair is bitwise identical; the recipe copy is exonerated. The
sampled points, cells, normals, freestream and reference length saved by
every evaluation are bit-identical across all snapshots for both fixed cars
(results/snapshot_ladder_2026-09-09.json, `point_identity_ladder`), so the
sample did not change.

**What the step is.** With the training snapshot and the `code_isla2`
snapshot grafted into one process and the same checkpoint weights loaded
into both classes (no missing or unexpected keys), the old
`MeshTransformer2` and the new `ISLA` agree in float32 to 3.6 × 10⁻⁶
relative L2 with every one of the twelve blocks' hidden states bitwise
identical, and disagree under bf16 autocast by 3.3% relative L2 (each
class's own bf16-versus-fp32 difference is 2.5%;
results/snapshot_model_diff_2026-09-09.json). The two forwards are the same
arithmetic; the refactor pooled the eight relational invariants over slices
before projecting them instead of after, an exact reordering in real
arithmetic, which moves the bf16 rounding points. The float32 evaluation
under both snapshots agrees per case to 0.001%
(results/snapshot_ladder_fp32_code_vs_perf_2026-09-09.json).

**Verdict.** The discrepancy is *bf16 evaluation rounding sensitivity of the
trained model*, exposed by an exactly equivalent code reordering: the same
weights on the same points score 0.0568 in float32, 0.0588 in bf16 under
one rounding pattern and 0.0624 under another (+3.4% and +9.7% over the
float32 value; per case up to 31%;
results/snapshot_ladder_fp32_vs_bf16_2026-09-09.json). Neither bf16 number
is "the" checkpoint's error. The same mechanism produced the earlier
findings that a summation-order change (the fast point softmax,
@sec-nb-cost-matched-fast) moves single cases by 20% and the means by
under 1%.

**Consequences.** (1) Within-family comparisons in the book are sound as
long as every arm was evaluated by the same snapshot in the same precision,
which the pair matrix confirms for every program comparison pair checked
(points identical; results/snapshot_ladder_2026-09-09.json, `pair_matrix`),
but their bf16 numbers carry a common rounding offset of several percent
relative to the float32 error, of unknown sign per checkpoint. (2) Any
number read across snapshots (a checkpoint evaluated by later code) is not
comparable at the few-percent level in bf16. (3) The reproducible
instrument is float32 inference (`precision=float32` in infer.py; the cost
is inference-only and small): the recommendation is to re-evaluate every
reported checkpoint in float32 once, eval-only, and to state evaluation
precision alongside every number; whether GeoTransolver and Transolver
checkpoints carry a comparable bf16 offset is untested here and is the
first thing that pass would show. (4) Training with the fast kernel is
unaffected (models trained and evaluated with one kernel are
self-consistent); the `fast_point_softmax` default stays off for evaluating
existing checkpoints, and would be moot under float32 evaluation, where the
two kernels agree to 10⁻⁶.

## 2026-09-09 — Protocol change: float32 inference becomes the reporting instrument; every bf16-evaluated number carries a per-checkpoint rounding offset of a few percent {#sec-nb-fp32-instrument}

**Finding** (scaling session's snapshot ladder, merged at d2ea6fa04). The
+6.1% "cross-snapshot" discrepancy on `iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed42` is bfloat16
*evaluation* rounding of the trained checkpoint, not code, data or recipe:
on bit-identical points the same weights score 0.05875 under the original
snapshot's bf16 graph, 0.06235 under every later snapshot's bf16 graph (the
refactor that pooled the invariants before projecting is exact in real
arithmetic and moves the bf16 rounding points), and 0.05682 in float32 under
either snapshot (per case identical to 0.001%). The two bf16 patterns differ
by 3.3% on the same weights, and per case by up to 31%. Neither bf16 number
is "the" error. Every within-family comparison in the book is on identical
points and therefore sound as a bf16 comparison, but each bf16 number carries
a common few-percent offset relative to float32 whose sign is unknown per
checkpoint, and it is not known whether GeoTransolver and Transolver (whose
graphs have no long bf16 reductions over 10,000 points) carry a comparable
offset.

**Decision.** Float32 inference (`precision=float32` in infer.py) is the
program's reporting instrument from now on; every reported checkpoint is
re-evaluated once in float32 (eval-only campaign, outputs under
`*_evals_fp32/`, existing bf16 artifacts untouched, sampled points asserted
identical per case); precision is stated beside every number; the
per-checkpoint bf16 → float32 shift is tabulated so the architectures'
offsets can be compared. Re-grading order: the 35-case HiLift rung, the
fixed angle and 4-geometry rungs, DrivAerML surface, the interior family,
then the rest. Until group one lands, no new comparative verdict is written.
Under float32 the two softmax kernels agree to 1e-6, so the kernel question
of @sec-nb-isla-perf-verdict disappears for reporting; `fast_point_softmax`
stays default off and is the kernel to train with.

## 2026-09-09 — Float32 first look (campaign E, transfer session): the bf16 offset is architecture-dependent, penalizing GeoTransolver and Transolver 8.5–9.7% and ISLA 2.8–4.0%; the density-robustness claim holds with the similarity gauge as the mechanism; weights off is the least robust configuration {#sec-nb-fp32-first-look}

**Source.** The transfer session's density-bias probe (campaign E,
research/transfer_program, #sec-nb-campe-verdict), rerun in float32 under
the reporting rule of @sec-nb-fp32-instrument on the DrivAerML surface
checkpoints (48 validation cars, pressure relative L2, uniform two-stage
control against the 10:1 biased sample). These are float32 numbers from the
same launcher configuration as the book's evaluations
(research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_e_evalonly/campaign_e_density_fp32_2026-09-09.json,
merged at ddd58d24b; bf16 twin alongside); the formal re-evaluation
campaign (FP32-EVAL) will reproduce them for the book's tables.

| arm (435 cars) | uniform, bf16 | uniform, float32 | bf16 − float32 | biased ÷ uniform (float32) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GeoTransolver, unit drive (three seeds) | 0.0554 | **0.0505** | +9.7% | **9.5x** (11.8 / 7.9 / 8.8) |
| Transolver, unit drive, lr 3e-3 | 0.0561 | **0.0517** | +8.5% | **3.9x** (2.2 / 5.5) |
| ISLA, constant gauge (weights on) | 0.0579 | **0.0558** | +3.8% | 12.1x |
| ISLA, measure weights off | 0.0566 | **0.0544** | +4.0% | **19.1x** |
| ISLA, similarity gauge | 0.0633 | **0.0616** | +2.8% | **1.21x** (1.208 / 1.214) |

**Two consequences.** First, the bf16 evaluation offset is
architecture-dependent: the baselines' float32 errors are 8.5–9.7% below
their bf16 numbers, ISLA's only 2.8–4.0%, so every bf16 comparison in the
book has penalized GeoTransolver and Transolver by about five percentage
points more than ISLA. On DrivAerML surface at 435 cars the float32 ordering
is GeoTransolver 0.0505 < Transolver 0.0517 < ISLA weights off 0.0544 <
ISLA 0.0558: GeoTransolver leads ISLA by 10% in float32 where bf16 showed
4%. The 35-case HiLift margins are expected to widen the same way; the
formal campaign's group 1 decides by how much. Second, the
density-robustness result stands against input-matched baselines with its
mechanism named and its cost stated: the similarity gauge holds ISLA to 1.21x
under a 10:1 sampling bias where the unit-drive GeoTransolver degrades 9.5x
and Transolver 3.9x, and the gauge pays 10–20% on the uniform draw (0.0616
against 0.0505 for GeoTransolver and 0.0558 for constant-gauge ISLA).
Dropping the measure weights, the configuration that gains 12–17% at small
HiLift data, degrades 19.1x under the bias (worse than predicting zero),
so NOW-L's decision is a trade between small-data accuracy and density
robustness, not a free gain.

**Interior stall, third reading.** Restarted interior links re-hang at
exactly the same training step (identical loss value at successive stalls),
and the hang sites found so far (pinning, the host-to-device copy) are the
two places where the reader's memory-mapped tensors are first faulted in;
a stuck Lustre file or stripe therefore appears as a copy hang, which unifies
the earlier readings and is the hypothesis to give the cluster team: specific
volume-dataset files, intermittent, roughly hourly since 12:14 PDT.

## 2026-09-09 — Preregistered: FP32-REEVAL, re-evaluating every reported checkpoint under float32 inference {#sec-nb-fp32-reeval-prereg}

**Why.** The snapshot ladder (@sec-nb-snapshot-ladder-verdict) showed that
the same ISLA checkpoint on bit-identical validation points scores 0.0568 in
float32 and 0.0588 or 0.0624 under two bf16 rounding patterns (per case up
to 31%). The program has therefore adopted float32 inference as its
reporting instrument (@sec-program-status, node FP32-EVAL); every reported
checkpoint is re-evaluated once, the bf16 artifacts stay in place, and the
precision is stated beside every number from now on.

**Instrument.** For every run with a completed bf16 evaluation, the
evaluation is repeated with the recipe's `precision=float32` (the trainer's
and infer.py's shared `precision` key, which selects the autocast context)
and no other change: the same code snapshot the run's own training and
evaluation used (`code`, `code_isla2`–`code_isla5`, `code_perf`), the same
model flags, forward-kwargs, dataset variant and sampled-cell count, the
reference point-softmax kernel. This is done by cloning each existing
evaluation launcher with two edits, the output root (`hl_evals` →
`hl_evals_fp32`, `iw_evals` → `iw_evals_fp32`, `v0_evals` →
`v0_evals_fp32`) and the added `precision=float32`, so override parity with
the bf16 evaluation holds by construction. After each evaluation the saved
sampled points are compared with the bf16 artifact's per case
(`np.array_equal` on interior points and, where present, boundary points);
a mismatch stops that family for inspection.

**Order.** (1) the 35-case HiLiftAeroML arms (ISLA weighted and weights
off, unit-drive and physical-drive GeoTransolver and Transolver including
the learning-rate steel-men); (2) the fixed angle and the four-geometry
split; (3) DrivAerML surface; (4) the interior arms and ladder; (5)
everything else with a bf16 evaluation (210, 510 and 1,260 cases, ladders,
wave-2 arms, 21 geometries). Skipped: runs whose training has not
finished, the transfer-program session's runs, and the scaling grid (its
agents evaluate under float32 themselves).

**Readouts and bars.** Per run and field (pressure, velocity, wall shear or
eddy viscosity): bf16 mean, float32 mean, relative shift, per-case maximum
absolute relative shift, and the point-identity result. A family's bf16
numbers are *reporting-equivalent* if every run's shift is within 1% and
every per-case maximum within 5%; otherwise the family carries an *offset*.
The offset is *architecture-dependent* if the per-architecture medians of
the shift differ by more than 1 percentage point; that decides whether the
book's cross-architecture ratios move under the new instrument. Verdicts:
one entry for the 35-case rung as soon as it is reduced (the rung is
re-graded from it), then one for all groups. Artifacts:
results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_2026-09-09.json and the reducer
results/fp32_reeval/reduce_fp32_2026-09-09.py.

**Verdict.** No DrivAerML arm is reporting-equivalent by the mean bar: the
unit-drive GeoTransolver's float32 error is 9.3–9.6% below its bf16 error
(physical-drive 9.1%), the unit-drive Transolver's 7.6–8.3%, and ISLA's
3.0–4.4% in every configuration (weights on or off, similarity gauge,
second-moment channel, 6,500 cells); per-case changes reach 17–21% for the
baselines and 5–12% for ISLA. The architecture-dependence bar fires (medians
differ by 5–6 points), so the book's DrivAerML surface comparisons, all
measured under bf16, understated the baselines' lead: under float32
GeoTransolver-unit ÷ ISLA falls from 0.96 to 0.90, GeoTransolver-physical ÷
ISLA from 0.95 to 0.89, Transolver-unit (3e-3) ÷ ISLA from 0.97 to 0.93,
i.e. ISLA is about 10% behind GeoTransolver and 8% behind Transolver on
DrivAerML surface pressure, not 4–5%. Within-ISLA comparisons move little:
weights-off stays 3% better (0.971), the second-moment channel stays free
(+0.2%), the similarity gauge stays 10% worse. The two learning-rate
outliers (GeoTransolver at 1e-2, ISLA's odd head) shift by under 1.5%
because their errors are dominated by large-scale failure, not rounding.
Mechanism as far as this instrument shows it: the offset is a property of
the trained checkpoint on this dataset (it was 0.1–0.3% for the same
architectures at 35 HiLift cases), consistent with bf16 rounding in the
baselines' 256-slice attention over 10,000 tokens at DrivAerML's tighter
error levels (0.05) mattering where at 0.12–0.40 it did not. The transfer
session's first look (float32 8.5–9.7% below bf16 for the baselines, 2.8–4.0%
for ISLA) is reproduced here on the program's own evaluations.

## 2026-09-09 — SCALE, GeoTransolver arm launched: twenty unit-drive lanes (widths 384/512, 40k/80k cells, corner) on HiLift 1,260 and DrivAerML 435; heaviest configurations accepted at 6 and 32 GB {#sec-nb-scale-gt-launch}

**Lanes** (@sec-nb-scale-prereg; table highlift/scale_lanes_gt.tsv rows
0–19, launcher highlift/hl_scale_gt_aga.sbatch cloned from the wave-2
launcher with its 3600 s stall timeout and per-link guard, the reference
`code` snapshot, `forward_kwargs.global_embedding=global_data.U_inf_dir` on
every row, learning rate 1e-3, seeds 42/43): w384 (`model.n_hidden=384`),
w512 (`model.n_hidden=512`), t40k and t80k (width 256 at 40,000 and 80,000
sampled cells), c384x40k (384 at 40,000), on `highlift_surface` and
`drivaer_ml_surface`. Run ids `scale_gt_{hl,dr}_<arm>_seed{42,43}`.

**Launch acceptance** (first link, step 19, "Mem:" is the recipe's logged
peak): DrivAerML w512 0.14–0.15 s per step at 5.9 GB; DrivAerML t80k 0.18 s
at 31.9 GB; HiLift w512 0.15 s at 6.0 GB; HiLift t80k 0.19 s at 31.9 GB
(one seed showed a transient 1.2 s step at step 19). Every heavy
configuration fits with an order of magnitude to spare on a 288 GB device,
and GeoTransolver's step time is nearly flat in token count and width at
this scale, so the lanes complete in about 3 h (DrivAerML) and 7 h
(HiLift) of wall clock per seed at 108 and 315 steps per epoch. The
remaining twelve lanes were submitted after the heavy ones were accepted.

**Reference arms** (not rerun): HiLift unit-drive GeoTransolver
`udrv_hl_gt_full_seed{42,43}` (UDRV-L lanes 16–17, training) with the
physical-drive `gt_hl_lr1_seed{42,43}` = 0.042 as the labelled fallback;
