`iw_gt_lr1e3_seed{42,43}` = 0.0548 as fallback. Evaluation:
`sbatch -q short -t 01:30:00 --array=<idx> highlift/hl_scale_gt_eval_aga.sbatch`
(80k lanes -t 02:00:00); reduction `highlift/reduce_scale_gt.py`
(results/scaling/reduce_scale_gt.py) writes hl_evals/scale_gt_reduction.json
with per-run metrics, parameters, peak memory, median step time and
GPU-hours. Verdict entry to follow as @sec-nb-scale-gt-verdict.

**Instrument amendment (program-wide, adopted before any lane is
evaluated).** Float32 inference is the reporting instrument: bf16
evaluation moves a trained ISLA checkpoint's error by several percent, and
whether GeoTransolver carries a comparable offset is one of the things
these lanes measure. Every GeoTransolver SCALE lane is evaluated twice, with
the bf16 launcher (hl_evals/<run>/) and with
highlift/hl_scale_gt_eval_fp32_aga.sbatch, which adds `precision=float32`
to the inference command and writes hl_evals_fp32/<run>/. The reducer
asserts per case that the two artifacts sampled bit-identical points,
reports fp32 as the headline with bf16 alongside and the per-run shift
(mean and per-case maximum of the relative pressure difference), and uses
the unit-drive references' fp32 re-evaluations (hl_evals_fp32/,
iw_evals_fp32/) when the re-evaluation campaign has produced them,
otherwise labels the comparison fp32-versus-bf16 explicitly.

## 2026-09-10 — SCALE, GeoTransolver on DrivAerML: width scales (0.045 at 512 against 0.050), tokens help (0.046 at 80,000), the corner gives 12% at unchanged step time; bf16 evaluation had inflated every GeoTransolver error by about 10% {#sec-nb-scale-gt-verdict}

**Scope.** The DrivAerML half of the GeoTransolver arm of @sec-nb-scale-prereg
(ten lanes, all trained and evaluated in both precisions). The HiLift half
is training: its lanes are I/O-bound on the 285M-cell boundary meshes (step
times 1.4–14 s against 0.15 s of GPU compute, the known HiLift reader
behaviour), so they finish in about five days, not the seven hours the
launch record estimated from the first steps; that estimate is withdrawn.

**Instrument.** Float32 inference is the headline (program-wide protocol);
bf16 alongside. On every one of the ten lanes the two evaluations sampled
bit-identical points (0 of 48 cars differ), and the fp32 error is 8.8–10.2%
*lower* than the bf16 error on the case mean, with per-case differences up
to 21%. The same offset holds for the reference lanes (unit-drive
`uw_gt_unit_lr1e3_seed{42,43,44}`: 0.0500 / 0.0508 / 0.0502 in fp32 against
0.0553 / 0.0561 / 0.0554 in bf16; physical-drive `iw_gt_lr1e3`: 0.0497 /
0.0500 against 0.0546 / 0.0550). GeoTransolver's bf16 evaluation offset is
therefore about 10% on DrivAerML surface pressure, consistent across width,
token count and drive input; every GeoTransolver DrivAerML figure quoted
under bf16 elsewhere in the book is about 10% too high and the coordinator
re-reads the ISLA comparison under fp32.

**Readout** (48 validation cars, two seeds each, fp32; reference = unit-drive
GeoTransolver at width 256 and 10,000 cells, three seeds, fp32 0.0503;
results/scaling/gt_scale_reduction_2026-09-09.json; parameters counted by
instantiating the surface configuration):

| arm | width | cells | parameters | pressure fp32 | ÷ reference | pressure bf16 | peak memory (logged) | step | GPU-hours / run |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| reference (uw_gt_unit) | 256 | 10,000 | 9.0M | 0.0503 | 1.000 | 0.0556 | 4.1 GB | 0.15 s | 8.7 |
| w384 | 384 | 10,000 | 20.2M | 0.0461 | **0.915** | 0.0512 | 5.4 GB | 0.167 s | 10.0 |
| w512 | 512 | 10,000 | 35.8M | 0.0450 | **0.893** | 0.0498 | 6.1 GB | 0.173 s | 10.4 |
| t40k | 256 | 40,000 | 9.0M | 0.0475 | 0.943 | 0.0520 | 16.4 GB | 0.167 s | 10.0 |
| t80k | 256 | 80,000 | 9.0M | 0.0461 | **0.916** | 0.0507 | 32.2 GB | 0.206 s | 12.4 |
| c384x40k | 384 | 40,000 | 20.2M | 0.0442 | **0.878** | 0.0486 | 18.9 GB | 0.174 s | 10.5 |

Seeds agree to within 1% on every arm (per-run values in the artifact).
GPU-hours = 500 epochs × 108 steps × median step × 4 GPUs; the reference
row's memory and step are from the uw lanes' logs at the same operating
point.

**Verdict, DrivAerML, GeoTransolver.** Bar 1: *width scales* — 512 wide is
10.7% better than the reference (bar ≥ 5%), 384 wide 8.5%. Bar 2:
*resolution-limited* — 80,000 cells is 8.4% better at the reference width
(bar ≥ 5%), 40,000 cells 5.7%. The corner (384 wide, 40,000 cells) is
12.2% better, more than either knob alone, so the two effects are largely
additive over this range. Cost: GeoTransolver's step time is nearly flat in
both knobs (0.15 → 0.21 s) because attention is over 256 slices and the
per-point work is a linear map, so the whole 12% comes at 1.2x the
GPU-hours; memory rises with tokens (4 → 32 GB), not with width (4 → 6 GB),
and every configuration fits a 288 GB device with an order of magnitude to
spare. The cost frontier is therefore monotone: on DrivAerML the cheapest
way to a given GeoTransolver error is the largest configuration tried, and
nothing suggests saturation at 512 wide or 80,000 cells. The protocol's
operating point (9M parameters, 10,000 cells) is not data-limited for
GeoTransolver on 435 cars; it left about 12% on the table.

**What this does not say.** Nothing about ISLA (its arm is a separate
track), nothing about HiLift (pending), and nothing about learning-rate
retuning (all arms at the protocol's 1e-3; none diverged). Bars 3 and 4 of
the preregistration (cross-architecture ordering, frontier comparison) are
the coordinator's, once the ISLA and Transolver arms land under fp32.

| arm (fp32) | width | cells | pressure | ÷ reference | 10:1 density-bias probe, biased ÷ uniform (fp32) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| reference (uw_gt_unit, three seeds) | 256 | 10,000 | 0.0503 | 1.000 | 11.8 / 7.9 / 8.8 (uniform 0.0503 / 0.0510 / 0.0504; biased 0.592 / 0.401 / 0.445) |

**Discretization invariance, GeoTransolver.** Neither configuration passes
the probe: the reference loses an order of magnitude under a 10:1 sampling
bias and the corner loses 1.9–6.5x, with a seed spread larger than any
accuracy difference in this study (seed 42 collapses to 0.274, seed 43 to
0.079 from the same 0.042). The larger model at eight times the cells is
less density-sensitive than the reference, which is consistent with a
per-point map that sees more of the surface, but a factor of 2–6.5 is still
a shortcut on the sampling distribution, not invariance. Under the
program's redirect the corner's accuracy is therefore reported with this
property attached and is not an adoptable configuration on its own; the
probe pool for the 80,000-cell variants is 320,000 cells (4x), shared with
the ISLA track. Provenance: 52 evaluation and probe logs checked, zero
skipped loads; summary-range guard silent on every corner and probe log
(zero "inconsistent" lines).

**HiLift half: training; I/O-bound, weeks.** The ten HiLift lanes advance
25–44 epochs per day (2.5–3.4 s per step against 0.15 s of GPU compute, the
285M-cell boundary reads), so they complete in two to three weeks at full
protocol; per the coordinator's decision they run unshortened and unheld,
and the HiLift half of this verdict is written when they land. The
DrivAerML half above is complete.

**Sample-frame probe (2026-09-10, program ruling).** The pool-frame probe
datasets centred the mesh *before* the biased draw, so GeoTransolver and
Transolver, which consume absolute centred coordinates, were handed the
unbiased pool mean; a biased mesher would deliver the sample's own mean.
The canonical sample-frame datasets (`drivaer_probe_{biased3,unif2}_sf`, 40k
pool, and `_sf_80k`, 320k pool; the pool-frame files with the CenterMesh
block moved to directly after the sampler) are run in float32 under

the reference: 9–12x at its own 80,000 cells and 9–11x at the 10,000-cell
design point, against 12x for the reference. The apparent improvement in the
pool-frame probe (6.5 / 1.9) was the centring artifact, not a property of
the larger model; the seed asymmetry disappears with it. Two further facts
from the same runs: evaluating the 80,000-cell-trained corner at 10,000
cells costs 8% on the uniform draw (0.0454 against 0.0421), so the corner's
accuracy is tied to its training resolution; and GeoTransolver at every
scale tried loses an order of magnitude under a 10:1 sampling bias once the
frame is the sample's own. Under the program's redirect, no GeoTransolver
configuration in this study passes the invariance test, and the width and
token gains are reported as capacity, not as adoptable configurations.

**Reproduction.** The four runs the transfer session re-evaluated in
float32 (#sec-nb-fp32-interior-regrade) reproduce here to the last digit:
ISLA query tokens + SDF 0.0547 / 0.0796 / 0.1116, GeoTransolver-volume
0.0514 / 0.1088 / 0.0879.

**Verdict.** No interior arm is reporting-equivalent by the mean bar, and
the architecture-dependence bar fires by a wide margin: bf16 inflated
GeoTransolver-volume's pressure and velocity errors by 17–18% and its eddy
viscosity by 6%, the ISLA query-token arms by 3–4% (pressure), 6–10%
(velocity) and 4–12% (eddy viscosity), the passive ISLA arms by 0.5–2%,
and the exact-kernel MeshTransformer not at all. Under float32 the
book's interior ordering changes on pressure and stands on the other two
fields: GeoTransolver-volume leads on pressure (ISLA ÷ GT 1.06–1.07 against
0.91–0.93 under bf16), ISLA leads on velocity (0.73–0.74 against 0.64–0.65),
GeoTransolver-volume leads on eddy viscosity (1.27–1.30, unchanged). The
width-256 arm is the only ISLA configuration within 2% of
GeoTransolver-volume on pressure under float32 (1.02) and it narrows the
eddy-viscosity gap to 1.17 (from 1.26); the surface-local-feature arm stays
falsified (1.36 on eddy viscosity either way); the query-token arm without
the SDF scalar trails on every field (1.19 / 1.28 / 1.61). The passive
decoders' deficit widens (pressure 3.7x and 3.1x against 3.1x and 2.6x),
so the "2.6x passive" figure becomes 3.1x under float32. On the ladder the
GeoTransolver-volume inflation grows with training-set size (pressure
−7.8% at 54 cars, −12.1% at 109, −17% at 435) while ISLA's stays at 2–4%,
so every ladder ratio moves against ISLA by 0.08–0.14 on pressure and
0.10–0.17 on velocity; the pressure crossover the bf16 ladder placed between
109 and 435 cars does not occur under float32 (ISLA ÷ GT 1.19, 1.18, 1.06 at
54, 109, 435 cars). The density and neighbour arms have no bf16 evaluation
yet (their lanes were still training); their float32 evaluation is queued
with the same launcher and is reported when it lands.

**Mechanism, as far as the shifts show it.** The hypothesis that
GeoTransolver-volume's inflation is specific to its six-radius ball-query
local features is not what the field pattern shows: the field most tied to
local geometry, eddy viscosity, shifts least (−6%), while pressure and
velocity shift most (−17 to −18%). In absolute terms GeoTransolver-volume's
bf16 excess is nearly constant across the ladder (0.008, 0.010 and 0.011
in pressure relative L2 at 54, 109 and 435 cars), which is the signature
of an additive rounding floor in its graph rather than a multiplicative
one, and its surface configuration, which has no local features, inflates
by 9% on DrivAerML surface pressure; the volume configuration's extra
inflation may come from the local features, from its interior inputs
(signed distance and its gradient over a 3D domain), or from both. The
direct test is the transfer session's `v0_gt_vol_nolocal_seed{42,43}`
(GeoTransolver-volume without local features): those runs have trained but
have no bf16 evaluation yet, so the bf16/float32 pair that would decide it
is not available in this reduction and is noted as the next step. Four of
the ladder GeoTransolver-volume logs carry a "FAILED" line from the first,
hung submission (cancelled after the pin-memory prefetch hang of
@sec-nb-interior-pin-stall); the resubmitted evaluations with
`dataloader.pin_memory=false` completed in 2–4 minutes each, and their
complete metrics are the ones reduced.

**Verdict on DrivAerML: width scales and the model is resolution-limited.**
Bar 1: the 512-wide arm is 8.7% better than the reference (≥ 5% bar met);
the gain is already 7.2% at width 384, so most of it comes from the first
doubling. Bar 2: 80,000 cells improve the reference-width model by 7.9%
(≥ 5% bar met), with 40,000 cells giving 6.8% of it. The corner arm shows
the two knobs are close to additive (−12.0%). Cost: because Transolver's
attention runs over 256 slices, widening from 6M to 24M parameters costs
under 10% in step time and 1 GB of memory, and 40,000 cells cost nothing
in step time; only the 80k arm is slower (1.4x) and heavier (22 GB). On
this device the DrivAerML Transolver frontier point is width 384 at 40,000
cells: 12% lower error for 10% more GPU-hours than the protocol's
operating point, at 13 GB. The bf16 instrument inflates every Transolver
configuration's error by 0.0042–0.0046 (8–9%), the same size as ISLA's
reported bf16 offset, so the offset is an instrument property and not an
architecture property; per-case shifts reach 0.011.

**Pending.** The ten HiLift lanes (1,260 cases) are at epoch 13–20 of 500
and need about a day and a half; their verdict and the cross-dataset
reading are appended here when they land, against the unit-drive
references udrv_hl_transolver_full_lr3e3_seed{42,43}.

*Density-bias probe* (program redirect of 2026-09-10: accuracy must come

first pass did exactly that and was discarded (moved to

therefore probed twice: at the probe design point (10,000 cells, like for
like with the reference) and at its own 80,000 cells with a 320,000-cell
pool (`drivaer_probe_{unif2,biased3}_80k`, the same 4x ratio).

seed-fragile), and its biased-sample error (0.20) is the reference's. The
probe at 10,000 cells also measures the resolution shift for a model trained
at 80,000: its uniform error rises from 0.0430 to 0.0465 (+8%), which is what
a deployment that samples fewer cells than training would pay. Under the
program's redirect, the corner arm's 16.7% gain is capacity and resolution,
not a physically principled improvement, and it fails the invariance test
as the reference does.

*Provenance.* Every arm's sampled points are bit-identical between the bf16
and float32 evaluations on all 48 cases (checked for all 12 DrivAerML runs);
44 evaluation and probe logs were checked for skipped or missing checkpoint
loads and for the inference summary range guard (added to infer.py on
2026-09-10): zero hits. The ten first-wave DrivAerML lanes were evaluated
under the `code` snapshot; the corner lanes and all probes under the
program-wide evaluation snapshot `code_eval` (identity check by the main
session: Transolver uw_transolver_unit_lr3e3_seed42 bitwise identical in
float32 under both). Training launchers are unchanged. Reference density
probes are the transfer campaign's (transfer/campaign_e_fp32/).

*HiLift half: training, I/O-bound, weeks.* The ten HiLift lanes (1,260
cases) run at 66–68 epochs per day for the width arms and 38–46 per day for
the 40k/80k-cell arms under the HiLift reader contention (measured over the
first 15 h), so they finish in about one to two weeks at the full protocol;
per the coordinator no epoch cut is applied. Their verdict is appended here
when they land.

**Addendum (2026-09-10): sample-frame density probe.** The pool-frame probe
datasets centre the mesh *before* the biased draw, so models that consume
absolute centred coordinates (Transolver, GeoTransolver) were handed the
unbiased pool's mean; a biased mesher would deliver the sample's own mean.
The program's canonical sample-frame variants (`drivaer_probe_{biased3,unif2}_sf`
with a 40,000-cell pool for 10,000-cell probes, `_sf_80k` with a 320,000-cell
pool for 80,000-cell probes; CenterMesh moved to directly after the sampler,
nothing else changed) were run in float32 under `code_eval` with the snapshot
sidecar in every output directory (hl_evals_probe_fp32/transolver_sf/), two
seeds each. Readout: biased ÷ uniform pressure error, **sample frame (pool
frame)**.

| arm | probe cells | uniform fp32 | biased fp32 | biased ÷ uniform, seed 42 | seed 43 | mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| reference (256, 10k) | 10,000 | 0.0518 | 0.601 | **10.2** (2.2) | **13.0** (5.5) | **11.6** (3.9) |
| c512x80k at the design point | 10,000 | 0.0467 | 0.642 | **12.2** (3.9) | **15.3** (4.9) | **13.7** (4.4) |
| c512x80k at its own resolution | 80,000 | 0.0433 | 0.644 | **13.0** (4.2) | **16.8** (5.1) | **14.9** (4.6) |

The reference's sample-frame ratio (10–13x) reproduces the generalization
session's independent measurement within seed noise, which validates the
launcher. The pool-frame probe under-reported every ratio by 2.5–3x by
leaking the unbiased centre. In the honest frame the largest Transolver is
*more* sensitive to sampling density than the reference (13–17x against
10–13x), with the same seed fragility; its biased-sample error (0.64) is
fifteen times its uniform error, so the corner arm's 16.7% accuracy gain
carries no discretization invariance and slightly worsens it. Provenance:
56 logs checked, zero skipped-load or summary-guard hits; sidecar present in
all six output directories.

**Is the offset additive?** Median bf16 excess (bf16 − float32, in units of
10⁻³ relative L2) on the HiLift surface rungs, split by the bf16 error level:

| architecture | runs with error ≥ 0.08 | excess (×10⁻³) | runs with error < 0.08 | excess (×10⁻³) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GeoTransolver | 23 | 0.2 | 6 | 1.4 |
| Transolver | 17 | 3.3 | 6 | 7.2 |
| ISLA | 3 | 0.2 | 9 | 0.8 |

**Verdict.** (1) The bf16 evaluation offset is real, negative on almost
every run (float32 is the lower error), and its size is set by the error
level rather than the dataset: on HiLift it is within 0.7% at 35, 210, 4 and
21 geometries where errors are 0.1–0.4, and grows to 2–5% for ISLA and 3–6%
for GeoTransolver at 1,260 cases and on the angle and stall tests where
errors are 0.02–0.05; on DrivAerML, whose errors are 0.05–0.06, it is 3% for
ISLA and 8–10% for the surface baselines; on the interior task 17–18% for
GeoTransolver-volume. Transolver's physical-drive checkpoints at 210, 510
and the fixed angle carry the largest surface offsets (9–24%). (2) The
offset is architecture-dependent wherever it is large (the bar fires on
DrivAerML surface, on the interior task and on the 210/510 HiLift rungs
where Transolver's checkpoints inflate 11–12% against ISLA's 0.7–1.4%), and
it is always larger for the baselines than for ISLA: every comparison in
the book that bf16 called close or favourable to ISLA moves toward the
baselines under float32, by 0.01–0.14 in ratio on the HiLift rungs (the
largest for the physical-drive Transolver at 210 and 510 cases, 1.34 →
1.20) and 0.05–0.15 on DrivAerML; the only movement the other way is the
210-case physical-drive GeoTransolver ratio, by 0.01. The interior
pressure ordering flips to GeoTransolver-volume; the HiLift orderings do
not change sign. (3) Within ISLA, the offset is nearly configuration-
independent (weights on or off, gauge, second-moment channel, query
tokens: 3–4% on DrivAerML, 0.1–0.7% on small HiLift rungs), so every
within-ISLA statement in the book survives unchanged; the passive decoders'
offset is smallest (0.5–2%), the exact-kernel MeshTransformer's zero. (4)
The per-case picture is worse than the means: single cases move by 5–25%
for the baselines and 5–17% for ISLA, so per-case paired statistics
computed under bf16 (win counts, medians of per-case ratios) are not
reproducible to the stated precision and must be recomputed from the
float32 artifacts before they are quoted again.

**What follows.** Precision is stated beside every number from here on, the
float32 artifacts under `hl_evals_fp32`, `iw_evals_fp32` and
`v0_evals_fp32` are the reporting record, and the scaling grid is evaluated
in float32 from the start. Three float32 evaluations are still owed:
the unit-drive GeoTransolver at 210 cases, at 21 geometries and at 1,260
cases (their bf16 evaluations had not completed when this campaign ran), and
the interior density and neighbour arms; each is one launcher clone away.
The offset is not a constant additive floor: the bf16 excess grows as the
error falls (GeoTransolver 0.2 → 1.4 × 10⁻³ and Transolver 3.3 → 7.2 × 10⁻³
from the high-error to the low-error HiLift rungs, ISLA 0.2 → 0.8 × 10⁻³),
so it scales more than proportionally with accuracy, and it is largest for
Transolver's physical-drive checkpoints. Why the two slice-attention
baselines round harder than ISLA's routing at the same error level is a
question for a numerics study of one block under bf16, not for this
instrument.

## 2026-09-10 — Campaign A at 35 cases: the unit-drive ordering stands on three further training draws; between-draw spread is 3–11x the seed spread {#sec-nb-campa-35-merged}

The cross-dataset companion program (research/transfer_program) asked whether
the 35-case standing of @sec-de-unit-drive is a property of the particular 35
training cases. The four unit-drive arms (GeoTransolver at 3e-3, Transolver
at 3e-3, ISLA with measure weights on and off) were retrained on three
further geometry-stratified 35-case draws from the 1,260-case pool, three
seeds each, and evaluated in float32; the curated draw enters as draw 0 from
the float32 re-evaluations of @sec-nb-fp32-35-regrade. Artifact:
`research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n35_fp32_2026-09-10.json`.

**Every ordering stands on every draw.** GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA is 0.881, 0.892
and 0.957 (curated 0.895; mean 0.910, 90% t-interval 0.840–0.979); Transolver
÷ ISLA 0.846, 0.852 and 0.900 (curated 0.829; 0.866, 0.816–0.916); ISLA with
weights off ÷ on 0.896, 0.898 and 0.947 (curated 0.885; 0.914, 0.865–0.963).
The preregistered "between" band for the weights-off effect (0.93–0.97)
holds on two draws; the third lands at 0.947, past 0.93 but short of the 0.97
"fades" bar, so the weights-off gain at 35 cases is written as 5–10% and
draw-dependent. Absolute seed-mean pressure errors by draw: GeoTransolver
0.1155 / 0.1309 / 0.1434, Transolver 0.1109 / 0.1249 / 0.1349, ISLA 0.1311 /
0.1467 / 0.1498, ISLA weights off 0.1175 / 0.1317 / 0.1419; the curated draw
is typical, at the easy end, for every arm.

**What changes practice** is the variance decomposition. The between-draw
standard deviation of an arm's error is 8.8 (GeoTransolver), 10.9
(Transolver), 3.4 (ISLA, whose seed spread is two to three times the
others') and 8.4 (weights-off ISLA) times its between-seed standard
deviation; the hardest draw is 24% harder than the easiest for
GeoTransolver. A two-seed 35-case number therefore carries 3–11x more
uncertainty than its seed spread shows. Adopted: every 35-case ratio in the
polished chapters is quoted with the interval above (@sec-de-unit-drive), and
new HiLift rungs are judged over geometry-stratified draws, not extra seeds.
The 210-case rung of the same campaign (36 lanes) is at about epoch 125 of
500; its verdict decides whether the 210-case unit-drive comparison inherits
the same caveat.

## 2026-09-10 — Step-schedule hazard: the frozen recipe's learning rate is ÷10 every 100 epochs, so "500 epochs" is about 300 useful ones and the doubled-epoch control was a low-rate tail {#sec-nb-steplr-hazard}

The single-sample overfitting track (a companion session) found that its
20,000-epoch lanes, with one sample per epoch, reached a learning rate of
10⁻⁶ by step 300 and then sat flat for 19,700 steps (loss 0.036 at step 319
and at step 19,999 alike; float32 relative L2 0.59 on their own training
sample). The cause is the frozen recipe's scheduler: `StepLR` with
`step_size=100` epochs and `gamma=0.1`, advanced once per epoch, verified in
the resolved configs of every reported run. Under the standard protocol (500
epochs at a peak rate of 10⁻³) epochs 300–500 run at 10⁻⁶ or less, so the
effective budget is about 300 epochs, and any run whose epoch count differs
from 500 gets a different effective schedule unless the step is rescaled.

Two consequences for this book. First, the GeoTransolver "doubled epochs"
steel-man of @sec-de-controls (the `ctrl_hl_gt_*_ep1000` lanes) kept
`step_size=100`, so its second 500 epochs ran at 10⁻⁶ and below: it tested a
longer low-rate tail, not a doubled optimization budget, and its 210-case
improvement (0.140 against 0.159) is within the two seeds' spread (0.152 /
0.128). The control's conclusion is unaffected in substance, because the
small-data deficit was later identified as the freestream input scale
(@sec-de-unit-drive), but the caption now says what the lanes actually
tested. Second, every comparison in the book is at equal epoch counts (the
ladder rungs, the WAVE-3 and UDRV lanes, and the scaling study's larger-token
arms all run 500 epochs of the same schedule), so no reported ratio is
affected; the hazard applies to future runs with other epoch counts, which
must set `training.scheduler.step_size` to keep the schedule proportional.
The single-sample track's attempt is archived as not a result and relaunched
with `step_size=4000` (fixed cached sample and 64 cycled cached views, twelve
lanes each, float32-training arms included). Protocol statement amended in
@sec-protocol; rule recorded in CLAIMS.

## 2026-09-09 — SCALE, ISLA arm launched: 24 lanes; the heaviest configurations fit with room to spare (width 512 at 6.1 GB, 80,000 tokens at 13 GB) {#sec-nb-scale-isla-launch}

model and which exposes the exact activation recompute; the token arms
(40,000, 80,000 and the 384 × 40,000 corner) run with

80,000-token lanes would not fit at width 512); and one de-confounding pair

weights *on*, the reference configuration. The existing 20,000-token ISLA
lanes `floor_hl_mt2_full_20k_seed{42,43}` (physical-drive era; ISLA's drive
input is the unit direction regardless) serve as the 20k rung of the HiLift
token ladder when they land.

**Acceptance of the heaviest arms** (first link, four B300 GPUs per lane;
from each lane's train.log):

| arm | parameters | peak memory per GPU | step time | steps per epoch | projected training time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HiLift width 512, 10k | 60.2M | 6.1 GB | 1.28 s | 315 | ~2.3 days |
| HiLift width 192, 80k (recompute) | 8.9M | 13.0 GB | 3.44 s | 315 | ~6.3 days |

No lane exceeded 13 GB of the 288 GB available; the study is bounded by
step time, not memory. HiLift's step is four times DrivAerML's at equal
width and token count (five target fields and a heavier data pipeline), so
the HiLift 80,000-token arm is the long pole. Remaining sixteen lanes
(width 384, 40,000 tokens, the corner, the weights-off pair; both datasets)
launched after acceptance. Evaluation: highlift/hl_scale_isla_eval_aga.sbatch
per lane; reduction results/scaling/reduce_scale_isla.py.

**Amendment after the performance track's result (same day).** The
performance track found the point-over-slices softmax kernel to be 85–95% of
ISLA's step and replaced it (`fast_point_softmax`, default on; exact to
1e-11 in float64; 1.0–1.5% relative L2 against the old kernel under bf16,
the size of the model's own bf16-versus-fp32 difference). Three changes,
each stated with its provenance: the four 80,000-cell lanes were cancelled
a few hours into a six-day run, their partial run directories deleted, and
resubmitted from the snapshot `code_perf` (5eaee07e7) through a launcher
clone, highlift/hl_scale_isla_perf_aga.sbatch, that differs from the
original only in `CODE`; the width and 40,000-cell arms stay on
`code_isla5`, whose numerics match the book's checkpoints. Rows 24–27 add
the largest configuration in the grid, `c512x80k` (width 512 with 80,000
cells, both datasets, seeds 42/43), and rows 28–29 add a kernel control,
the DrivAerML reference configuration (width 192, 10,000 cells, weights
on, lr 1e-3) trained from `code_perf`; all six from the fast kernel.
**Bar for the kernel control:** the fast kernel is *training-neutral* if
its two-seed mean pressure error is within 3% of the reference 0.0577
(seeds 0.0588 / 0.0567); if it differs by 5% or more, every fast-kernel arm
is reported as a separate numerics family and not pooled with the
reference-kernel arms. Every arm trained from `code_perf` is labelled
"trained with the fast point-softmax kernel; numerics differ from the
reference checkpoints at bf16 roundoff" in the reduction and the verdict.

**Second amendment (same day).** The merged code ships the fast kernel
opt-in (`fast_point_softmax` default False until training neutrality is
shown); the `code_perf` snapshot predates that flip. Every lane run from
`code_perf` therefore carries `+model.fast_point_softmax=true` in its lane
row so the hydra override in its log names the kernel explicitly (rows 6,
7, 16, 17 and 24–29 of highlift/scale_lanes_isla.tsv); the ten lanes had
started a minute earlier without the flag and were cancelled, their run
directories (startup logs only) deleted, and their chains left to restart
from the flagged rows. All other ISLA lanes in this study run the
reference kernel.

**Acceptance of the fast-kernel lanes** (first link, four GPUs per lane):

| arm (fast point-softmax kernel) | peak memory per GPU | step time | projected training time |
|---|---|---|---|
| DrivAerML kernel control (width 192, 10k) | 3.7 GB | 0.11 s | ~1.7 hours |
| HiLift width 192, 80k | 12.3 GB | 0.31 s | ~13.5 hours (was ~6.3 days) |
| DrivAerML width 192, 80k | 12.3 GB | 0.26 s | ~4 hours (was ~2.1 days) |
| HiLift width 512, 80k | 22.4 GB | 0.34 s | ~15 hours |
| DrivAerML width 512, 80k | 22.4 GB | 0.29 s | ~4.5 hours |

The point-over-slices softmax was the step, not the invariants: with it
replaced, an 80,000-token ISLA at width 512 costs a tenth more per step
than the reference configuration did, at 22 GB of the 288 available.

**Third amendment: float32 as the reporting instrument.** Following the
program-wide protocol change (@sec-nb-snapshot-ladder-verdict: bf16
evaluation moves a trained ISLA checkpoint's error by several percent with
the rounding pattern), every SCALE lane is evaluated twice: with the
existing bf16 launcher (hl_evals/<run>/) and with a float32 clone
(highlift/hl_scale_isla_eval_fp32_aga.sbatch and its code_perf twin,
`precision=float32`, hl_evals_fp32/<run>/). The reducer asserts per case
that the two artifacts sampled bit-identical points, reports the float32
numbers as the headline with the bf16 numbers and the per-run shift
alongside, and takes the reference arms' float32 re-evaluations from the
re-evaluation campaign when they exist, otherwise their bf16 numbers with
that label. Reference-kernel lanes are evaluated with the fast kernel off;
code_perf lanes with it on, as trained (under float32 the two kernels agree
to 1e-6).

**First readout (DrivAerML, width 512; float32 instrument).** ISLA at width
512 (60.2M parameters) scores 0.0508 against the reference width's 0.0557
(float32 re-evaluation of `iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed{42,43}`; bf16 0.0577), a ratio
of 0.91: the width-scaling bar (≥ 5% better) is met on DrivAerML. The cost
of the 6.8x parameter increase is 2% in step time (0.278 against 0.273 s)
and 22.7 against 21.3 GPU-hours, at 6.1 GB peak memory: at 10,000 tokens
and width 192 the B300 is not compute-bound, so width is nearly free here.
Both evaluations sampled bit-identical points; the fp32-over-bf16 shift is
0.949 for the wide model and 0.965 for the reference. Partial artifact
results/scaling/isla_scale_reduction_2026-09-09.json (overwritten as arms
land).

**DrivAerML width ladder complete (float32 instrument; 48 validation cars,
two-seed means).** Reference width 192 (8.9M) 0.0557 → width 384 (34.2M)
0.0516 (0.93x) → width 512 (60.2M) 0.0508 (0.91x); bf16 evaluations
0.0577 / 0.0544 / 0.0536 with fp32-over-bf16 shifts 0.965 / 0.949 / 0.949.
Step times 0.273 / 0.274 / 0.278 s and peak memory 9.8 (older code) / 5.2 /
6.1 GB: the 6.8x parameter increase is free in wall-clock at 10,000 tokens.
The width-384 arm with the routing measure weights off, an *ablation*
(discretization-dependent; never a reference configuration), scores 0.0505
(0.979 of the weighted width-384 arm, within the 3% "fades" band of
@sec-nb-noweights-prereg): at full DrivAerML data and width 384 the weights
cost 2%, against 12% at 35 HiLift cases, so the two knobs are nearly
independent here and the width gain is not a weights artifact. The
reference ISLA in every table of this study is the measure-weighted
configuration. Width bar 1
on DrivAerML: **scales** (0.91 ≤ 0.95).

**Kernel control: the fast point-softmax kernel is training-neutral.** The
DrivAerML reference configuration trained from `code_perf` with
`+model.fast_point_softmax=true` scores 0.0567 in float32 against the
reference lanes' 0.0557 (+1.8%, inside the 3% bar; bf16 0.0596 against
0.0577, +3.3%), at 0.161 s per step against 0.273 and 3.9 GB against 9.8 GB
(the reference lanes ran older code). The fast-kernel arms (80,000 tokens
and the 512 × 80,000 pilot) are therefore pooled with the reference-kernel
arms in the verdict, each still labelled with its kernel.

## 2026-09-10 — Fast point-softmax kernel passes its training-neutrality control (+1.8% in float32, inside the 3% bar) and becomes the default {#sec-nb-fast-kernel-default}

The point-over-slices softmax was 85–95% of every ISLA training step under
PyTorch's middle-dimension kernel (@sec-nb-cost-matched-fast); reducing along
a contiguous last dimension gives the same arithmetic in a different
summation order at a fraction of the cost. The option shipped default-off
with two preregistered conditions for flipping it: a trained-from-scratch
neutrality check and an evaluation identity check. The scaling session ran
the first as the DrivAerML reference configuration (435 cars, 10,000 cells,
learning rate 1e-3, 500 epochs) trained with the fast kernel on two seeds
(scale_isla_dr_kernelctrl_seed42/43, code_perf snapshot). **Float32 pressure
error 0.0567 against the reference lanes' 0.0557, a 1.8% offset inside the 3%
bar** (bfloat16 0.0596 against 0.0577), at 0.161 s per step and 3.9 GB
against 0.273 s and 9.8 GB for the reference lanes, which also ran older
code, so the cost ratio is an upper bound on the kernel's share.

The second condition, evaluation identity on a trained checkpoint, failed
under bfloat16 (1.0–1.5% between kernels, per case up to 26%,
@sec-nb-fp32-instrument) and passes under float32, where the two kernels
agree to 10⁻⁶. Since float32 is the book's reporting instrument
(@sec-nb-fp32-instrument), that failure no longer bears on any reported
number. Decision: `fast_point_softmax` defaults to True in the model
(commit on psharpe/mesh-transformer), with three rules recorded in CLAIMS:
every checkpoint trained before 2026-09-10 used the reference kernel; float32
evaluation needs no kernel flag; a bfloat16 evaluation of an older checkpoint
must still request the reference kernel. The scaling study pools its
fast-kernel arms (80,000 tokens and the 512 × 80,000 corner) with the
reference-kernel arms, each labelled. The 1.8% offset is a two-seed number on
one configuration; a third seed and a HiLift repeat would tighten it, and it
is small against every effect the book argues over (the smallest quoted is
5%).

**DrivAerML token arms and the 512 × 80,000 pilot (float32; fast kernel,
labelled).** At the reference width, 80,000 cells per car give 0.0468
against the reference's 0.0557 (0.84x; bf16 0.0484): the
resolution-limited bar (≥ 5%) is met by a wide margin. The largest
configuration, width 512 with 80,000 cells, gives **0.0428** (0.77x; bf16
0.0441), at 22.8 GB peak and 0.285 s per step: 22.5 GPU-hours against the
reference's 21.3. With the fast kernel, the whole DrivAerML ladder costs the
same wall-clock as the reference configuration, so on this dataset the
protocol's operating point left a 23% pressure-error reduction on the table.
Every fp32-versus-bf16 shift lies between 0.94 and 0.97; all sampled points
bit-identical across the two instruments. The DrivAerML 40,000-cell arms
(reference kernel) and the width-384 × 40,000 corner are still training.

**HiLift lanes are input-bound by fleet contention.** With about seventy
HiLift lanes reading the 285-million-cell boundary meshes from Lustre at
once, the HiLift SCALE lanes' recent median step is 2.8 s at 80,000 cells
(first link, before the fleet filled: 0.31 s) and 1.9 s at width 512 (first
link 1.28 s), with 90th percentiles of 6–10 s; the DrivAerML lanes, whose
meshes are 30x smaller, are unaffected (40,000-cell arm 1.29 s per step,
flat). The HiLift arms therefore project to five to seven days rather than
the 13–15 hours of the acceptance table; the coordinating session decides
whether to accept that, thin the fleet, or wait for the dataset-level read
fix (@sec-nb-hilift-io-verdict). Nothing about the lanes' numerics is
affected; only their wall-clock and the GPU-hours column, which for the
HiLift arms measures the filesystem, not the model, and is reported with
that label.


**Decision on the HiLift half (coordinating session).** The week is
accepted: the concurrent HiLift lanes are the program's fair-comparison
ladder and are not thinned, and the SCALE arms are not held for the
dataset-level read fix. The watcher's stall threshold on the HiLift lanes
is raised from 20 to 45 minutes so that input-throttled links (a 10 s step
at 315 steps per epoch is slow, not hung) are not cancelled as stalls; the
DrivAerML lanes keep 20 minutes. The throttling above is the cost caveat
for every HiLift row of this study; the DrivAerML half is the study's
headline so far and its verdict is written when the 40,000-cell and
384 × 40,000 arms land.

**Program redirect (2026-09-10) applied to this track.** Accuracy must come
from physically principled means that generalize; discretization-dependent
shortcuts are never adopted on accuracy alone. Accordingly: the reference
ISLA in every table here is the measure-weighted configuration, and the
weights-off width-384 pair is labelled an ablation (discretization-dependent;
never a reference configuration) in the reduction and above. Width and token
count are capacity, not shortcuts, and stand. A discretization-invariance
evaluation is added beside the accuracy row: the program's 10:1
density-bias probe on DrivAerML (`drivaer_probe_biased3` against the uniform
control `drivaer_probe_unif2`, 10,000 cells, float32, each run's own
snapshot and flags; highlift/hl_scale_isla_probe_fp32_aga.sbatch, cloned from
the transfer session's campaign E launcher) on the width 512 × 80,000-cell
arm, the width 512 × 10,000-cell arm, and the reference (whose float32 probe
campaign E already produced). Readout: biased ÷ uniform pressure error per
arm, so the cost frontier carries the invariance property.

**Density-bias probe, float32, 10,000 cells (biased ÷ uniform pressure
error, two-seed means).** Reference width 192: uniform 0.0558, biased 0.675,
ratio **12.1x**; width 512: 0.051 → 0.739, **14.5x**; width 512 × 80,000
cells: 0.0663 → 0.721, **10.9x**. Width leaves the constant-gauge
configuration's density sensitivity where the book found it (13–14.5x,
@sec-robustness-density); none of the scaled arms is more invariant than
the reference. The probe also exposes a second dependence: the model
trained at 80,000 cells, queried at 10,000, scores 0.0663, worse than its
native 0.0428 and worse than the reference's 0.0558 at the same 10,000. Part
of the token-scaling gain is therefore tied to the training sampling density
and does not transfer to a coarser query set, which under the program's
redirect counts against it until the mirror test settles how much: the same
probe at 80,000 cells for both the 80k-trained model (its own density) and
the 10k-trained reference (queried 8x denser) is running
(highlift/hl_scale_isla_probe80k_fp32_aga.sbatch). Bar for the mirror test,
stated now: token scaling is *resolution-general* if the 80k-trained model
keeps ≥ 80% of its in-distribution gain over the reference when both are
evaluated at the other's density (i.e. the mean of its 10k-cell and 80k-cell
uniform errors is ≤ 0.0531, halfway between 0.0428 and the reference's
0.0558 adjusted for the reference's own 80k behaviour); *resolution-bound*
if its 10k-cell error stays above the reference's 10k-cell error, as
observed, and the reference queried at 80k does not degrade by more than
5%.

**Preregistered before launch: the similarity-gauge corner, `g512x80k`
(rows 30–31).** The constant-gauge 512 × 80,000 configuration's 0.0428 is
not adoptable on its own under the redirect: its density sensitivity is
10.9x and its gain is partly tied to the training density. The similarity
gauge is the program's only configuration that is nearly density-invariant
(1.20x under the 10:1 bias, @sec-robustness-density, against 11–15x for the
constant gauge at every width measured here), so scaling *it* is the
principled scaling. Arm: `model.hidden=512 +model.similarity_gauge=true
+model.geo_checkpoint=true +model.fast_point_softmax=true`, 80,000 cells,
DrivAerML, seeds 42/43, from `code_perf` (run ids
`scale_isla_dr_g512x80k_seed{42,43}`, jobs 699985/699986). Evaluated in
both precisions plus the density probe at its native 80,000 cells and at
10,000. **Bars (float32):** *principled scaling* if the gauge corner
reaches within 5% of the constant-gauge corner (≤ 0.0449) **and** its
biased ÷ uniform ratio at 80,000 cells is ≤ 1.5; *gauge fails at scale* if
that ratio is ≥ 3; *gauge costs accuracy* if the ratio is ≤ 1.5 but the
error exceeds 0.0470 (5% worse than the constant corner). The DrivAerML
verdict waits for this pair (about a day at 0.29 s per step).

**Mirror probe, first run: two instrument facts, one reading struck.**
First, both probe datasets read a 40,000-cell pool from each mesh before
subsampling to the requested count, so a request for 80,000 cells returns
the whole pool from both the biased and the uniform sampler: the two
columns are identical (ratio exactly 1.0) and the count is 40,000, not
80,000. The uniform column is a valid convergence reading at 40,000 cells;
the biased column is not. Relabelled as such (results key `@40k`), and the
true 80,000-cell probe defined on dataset variants with a 320,000-cell
pool (`drivaer_probe_{biased3,unif2}_80k.yaml`, the base probe's 4x ratio,
shared with the GeoTransolver track), including the similarity-gauge
reference `iw_mt2_gauge_seed{42,43}` as the principled control. Second, the
reference lanes `iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed{42,43}` are legacy checkpoints
(`MeshTransformer2.0.500.mdlus`); evaluated under the `code_isla5` snapshot
the loader looked for `ISLA.0.500.mdlus`, logged "Could not find valid
model file … skipping load" and evaluated the seeded initialization. The
40,000-cell reference reading of 1.5667 that this run produced (identical to
six digits on both seeds, the signature of a failed load) is therefore
**struck**; it is not a measurement of the model. Every other evaluation in
this study loaded its checkpoint (0 skipped loads in the fp32 headline,
bf16 and 10k-probe logs of all SCALE arms; the reference's 10k probe came
from campaign E under the snapshot that wrote it).

| model (float32, uniform sampling) | 10,000 cells | 40,000 cells |
|---|---|---|
| reference, trained at 10,000 (constant gauge) | 0.0558 | struck (load failure); re-run pending under snapshot `code` |
| width 512 × 80,000, trained at 80,000 (constant gauge) | 0.0663 | 0.0447 |

What stands: the 80k-trained constant-gauge model degrades 1.5x when
queried at an eighth of its training density and improves toward its native
error as the count rises; the resolution-generalization question for the
reference and for the similarity gauge is open until the corrected 80k
probe lands. Guards adopted: legacy checkpoints are evaluated under the
snapshot that wrote them (`code`); the ISLA-class evaluation snapshots used
by this track's float32 and probe launchers carry the raising loader
(c50b87e0a: a training checkpoint whose model weights file is missing
raises instead of skipping); and the reducer refuses any run whose
evaluation log contains a skipped load.

**Evaluation snapshot policy (from here on).** All ISLA SCALE evaluations
(bf16, float32 and both density probes) now import a single evaluation-only
snapshot, `code_eval`, exported from worktree-scaling-study 0e41b9ee1: it
carries the raising checkpoint loader (a training checkpoint whose model
weights file is missing raises instead of skipping) and the legacy
class-name search (ISLA declares `MeshTransformer2`, so the reference
lanes' `MeshTransformer2.*.mdlus` files load into ISLA with a warning), its
default-flag forward is bitwise the reference, and float32 evaluation is
kernel-independent, so legacy and current checkpoints alike are valid under
it. Provenance of what was already evaluated: the fp32/bf16 headline
numbers and the 10k probes of the SCALE arms were produced under
`code_isla5` / `code_perf` (checkpoints loaded; 0 skipped loads in every
log); the reference's 10k probe under `code` (campaign E); the running true
80k probe (job 700105) evaluates the constant-gauge corner under
`code_perf_eval` (= `code_perf` + the raising loader) and the two legacy
references under `code`, all valid. The reducer's skipped-load guard applies
to every path regardless of snapshot.

**True 80,000-cell probe (float32; 320,000-cell pool; every checkpoint
loaded, logs clean, seeds distinct).** Two-seed means, uniform sampling
unless stated:

| model | trained at | 10,000 cells | 80,000 cells | biased ÷ uniform at 10k | at 80k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| reference, constant gauge | 10,000 | 0.0558 | **0.814** (seeds 0.8146 / 0.8141) | 12.1x | 1.54x |
| reference, similarity gauge (`iw_mt2_gauge`) | 10,000 | 0.0616 | **0.892** (0.8924 / 0.8916) | **1.21x** | 1.00x |
| width 512 × 80,000, constant gauge | 80,000 | 0.0663 | 0.0427 (its native) | 10.9x | 16.7x |

Three readings. (1) Queried at eight times their training count, *both*
10k-trained references collapse to near a mean-field predictor (0.81 and
0.89; the biased ÷ uniform ratio near 1 at 80k is the signature of a model
that has stopped depending on the sample). The similarity gauge, which
removes the 10:1 *bias* sensitivity at fixed count (1.21x against 12.1x),
does not remove the *count* sensitivity: bias robustness and count
generalization are different properties, and the program's density-robustness
result (@sec-robustness-density) speaks only to the first. (2) The
80k-trained constant-gauge model is the mirror image: 1.5x worse at an
eighth of its count and native at 80k. (3) Bias sensitivity of the constant
gauge is as large at 80k as at 10k (16.7x), so width and count change none of
it. Under the redirect, the constant-gauge token-scaling gain remains
inadmissible on its own, and the open question for the similarity-gauge
corner `g512x80k` is now sharper: whether a gauge model trained at 80,000
keeps its accuracy at 10,000 (count generalization), not only whether it
holds its 1.2x bias robustness. A 40,000-cell re-probe of the two references
under the corrected snapshot is running to place the middle point of the
count curve (the earlier 40k reference reading was a failed load).

**HiLift half: training, input-bound, weeks.** Measured epoch rates under
the fleet's reader contention (first link to 2026-09-10 06:00 PDT): width
384 and 512 at 10,000 cells, and width 384 with weights off, about 65
epochs per day (41–44 epochs in 15.5 hours; 500 epochs in about eight
days); 40,000-cell arms about 32 per day (about 16 days); 80,000-cell arms
(fast kernel) about 40 per day (about 12 days). The coordinating session's
decision stands: full protocol, no hold, no epoch cut; the HiLift half of
this study is reported when it lands, and the DrivAerML half is written as
complete once the 40,000-cell arms (epoch 328 of 500 at this writing) and
the similarity-gauge corner finish.

**Count curve, second point: the reference is fine at 40,000 cells.**
Re-probed under the corrected snapshot (loads clean, seeds 0.0535 / 0.0531),
the 10k-trained constant-gauge reference scores **0.0533** at 40,000 cells,
*better* than its 0.0558 at 10,000, and 0.814 at 80,000. The count failure
is therefore a cliff between 4x and 8x the training count, not a gradual
drift, and the 80k-trained model's 0.0427 on the same 80,000-cell datasets
says the datasets themselves are sound. Two explanations remain and are
being separated: something in the model's constant-gauge routing breaks
between 40,000 and 80,000 points (a count cliff), or the 320,000-cell pool
variant used only at 80k differs from the base 40,000-cell pool in a way
that matters to a 10k-trained model (a dataset-variant effect). Three probes
of both 10k-trained references are running (jobs 700317–700319): 20,000
cells on the base pool, 40,000 cells on the 320,000-cell pool variant, and
60,000 cells on that variant. If the 40k-on-variant reading matches 0.0533
and 60k sits between it and 0.81, the cliff is in the count; if 40k on the
variant already collapses, the variant is the cause and the 80k readings of
the two references are struck pending a dataset fix. The similarity-gauge
reference's 40k reading is added to the curve when reduced.


**Count curve to 60,000 cells, and the cliff is at 80,000.** Float32,
uniform sampling, two-seed means (biased ÷ uniform in parentheses):

| cells evaluated | constant-gauge reference (trained at 10k) | similarity-gauge reference (trained at 10k) |
|---|---|---|
| 10,000 (base pool) | 0.0558 (12.1x) | 0.0616 (1.21x) |
| 20,000 (base pool) | 0.0545 (12.3x) | 0.0594 (1.07x) |
| 40,000 (base pool, exhausted) | 0.0533 (n/a) | 0.0582 (n/a) |
| 40,000 (320,000-cell pool) | 0.0530 (12.6x) | 0.0579 (1.03x) |
| 60,000 (320,000-cell pool) | 0.0529 (12.6x) | 0.0577 (1.01x) |
| 80,000 (320,000-cell pool) | **0.814** (1.54x) | **0.892** (1.00x) |

Both 10k-trained models improve monotonically with the evaluation count up
to six times their training count, the 40,000-cell readings on the two
pools agree to 0.6%, so the dataset variant is not the cause, and the
similarity gauge's bias ratio falls toward 1 as the count grows (1.21 →
1.01). Then both collapse at exactly 80,000, to outputs that no longer
depend on the sample. A cliff between 60,000 and 80,000 with that signature
points at the evaluation path, not the models: 65,536 = 2¹⁶ lies in the
interval, and the one 80,000-cell evaluation that behaved (the 80k-trained
corner, 0.0427) ran on the fast point-softmax kernel while the two
references ran on the reference kernel. Bracket probes are running: both
references at 65,000 and 70,000 cells (jobs 700343/700344), and a kernel
swap at 80,000 (job 700345: the constant-gauge reference on the fast
kernel; the 80k-trained corner on the reference kernel). Outcomes stated
in advance: if 65k is healthy and 70k collapses, and the reference on the
fast kernel is healthy at 80k while the corner on the reference kernel
collapses, the cliff is a reference-kernel defect above 2¹⁶ points, every
reference-kernel evaluation at more than 65,536 points is struck, and the
count-generalization statements of the previous entries are withdrawn in
favour of "monotone improvement to at least 60,000 cells"; if 70k is
healthy and only 80k fails regardless of kernel, the cliff is a model
property at 8x count and stands. The 80k-trained models' own 80k numbers
(fast kernel) are unaffected either way.

**CPU control on the kernel hypothesis.** On CPU in float32, with identical
weights and inputs, the reference and fast point-softmax kernels agree to
3.5 × 10⁻⁷ relative at 60,000, 65,536, 65,537 and 70,000 points (one-layer
ISLA, hidden 64, 256 slices; outputs finite, standard deviation unchanged):
there is no CPU defect above 2¹⁶ points. If the cliff is a kernel defect it
is specific to the GPU path; the coordinating session's one-GPU softmax
micro-test and the bracket probes decide.


**Bracket verdict: the 80,000-cell collapse was the legacy snapshot's
evaluation path, not the models and not the kernel; the two readings are
struck.** Under `code_eval` the constant-gauge reference scores 0.0529 at
65,000, 0.0529 at 70,000 and **0.0528 at 80,000 cells** (on the fast
kernel, seeds distinct, loads clean), and the 80k-trained corner scores
0.0427 at 80,000 on the *reference* kernel; the similarity-gauge reference
scores 0.0577 at 65,000 and 0.0576 at 70,000. The 2¹⁶ kernel hypothesis is
falsified three ways: the coordinating session's one-GPU micro-test found
no cliff in `torch.softmax` over dim 1 at any N from 40,000 to 100,000 in
either precision (results/scaling/softmax_dim1_test_2026-09-10.json), the
CPU control agreed to 3.5 × 10⁻⁷ across 65,536, and the kernel swap is clean
in both directions. The only two evaluations that collapsed (0.814 and
0.892) were the two references evaluated at 80,000 cells under the legacy
`code` snapshot in job 700105; the same checkpoints under `code_eval` at the
same count on the same datasets are healthy. Those two readings are struck
as an artifact of that snapshot's evaluation path at 80,000 cells (the
mechanism inside the legacy snapshot is not identified and is not pursued:
every evaluation now runs on `code_eval`). The earlier statements that
"both 10k-trained references collapse at 8x count" and "bias robustness
and count generalization are different properties" are **withdrawn**; the
corrected count curve for the 10k-trained references (float32, uniform):

| cells evaluated | constant-gauge reference | similarity-gauge reference |
|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | 0.0558 (bias 12.1x) | 0.0616 (bias 1.21x) |
| 20,000 | 0.0545 (12.3x) | 0.0594 (1.07x) |
| 40,000 | 0.0530 (12.6x) | 0.0579 (1.03x) |
| 60,000 | 0.0529 (12.6x) | 0.0577 (1.01x) |
| 65,000 | 0.0529 (12.6x) | 0.0577 (1.01x) |
| 70,000 | 0.0529 (12.6x) | 0.0576 (1.01x) |
| 80,000 | 0.0528 (12.7x) | pending (job 700404) |

Both 10k-trained models improve monotonically with evaluation count to
eight times their training count and plateau from about 40,000 cells; the
constant gauge's 10:1 bias sensitivity is flat at 12–13x across counts and
the similarity gauge's falls to 1.01. Count generalization upward is
therefore a property of both configurations. The asymmetry that stands is
the 80k-trained corner's 0.0663 at 10,000 cells (its native 0.0427): a
model trained at high count loses accuracy when queried at an eighth of
it, while a model trained at low count gains when queried denser. A
further finding from the micro-test, recorded beside the kernel-neutrality
control: in float32 the reference (middle-dimension) softmax kernel is
about 1,000x less accurate than the transposed fast kernel (1 × 10⁻⁴
against 1 × 10⁻⁷ absolute on softmax weights), so the model docstring's
"agree to 1e-6" is generous; no verdict changes.

**Kernel labels corrected, the gauge reference's 80,000-cell point, and the
structural guard.** Correction to the previous entry's kernel columns: the
recipe instantiates the model from the hydra configuration, not from the
checkpoint's stored arguments, so every evaluation under `code_eval` of a
legacy checkpoint runs the *fast* point-softmax kernel (that snapshot's class
default) unless the override says otherwise. "Reference on the fast kernel
at 80,000" was therefore simply "reference under `code_eval` at 80,000";
the one reference-kernel datum in the swap pair is the 80k-trained corner
with `+model.fast_point_softmax=false` (0.0427, equal to its fast-kernel
0.0427). The "numerics" column of the reduction describes *training*
numerics; the evaluation kernel is named per evaluation from here on (the
instantiated model's flag is logged). The similarity-gauge reference at
80,000 cells under `code_eval` scores **0.0574** (bias ratio 1.012),
completing its curve: 0.0616 → 0.0594 → 0.0579 → 0.0577 → 0.0577 → 0.0576
→ 0.0574 from 10,000 to 80,000 cells.

Every 80,000-cell reading of a 10k-trained reference, with its snapshot
(struck rows kept visible):

| checkpoint | evaluation snapshot | job | float32 uniform error | standing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| constant-gauge reference | `code` (legacy) | 700105 | 0.8144 | **struck**: legacy snapshot's evaluation path at 80,000 cells |
| similarity-gauge reference | `code` (legacy) | 700105 | 0.8920 | **struck**: same |
| constant-gauge reference | `code_eval` | 700345 | 0.0528 | stands |
| similarity-gauge reference | `code_eval` | 700404 | 0.0574 | stands |
| width 512 × 80k corner | `code_perf_eval` | 700105 | 0.0427 | stands |
| width 512 × 80k corner (reference kernel) | `code_eval` | 700345 | 0.0427 | stands |

**Structural guard, so this cannot recur.** No evaluation in this track runs
under `code` or any pre-`code_eval` snapshot: every evaluation and probe
launcher imports `code_eval`; each launcher writes the snapshot it imported
into the evaluation directory (`SNAPSHOT_USED`) before `infer.py` runs; the
reducer records the snapshot of every number (from the sidecar, or for the
evaluations made before the sidecar existed from a manifest of the launcher
versions in force at the time, results/scaling/reduce_scale_isla.py) and
refuses a number whose snapshot cannot be named, the way it refuses one
whose log records a skipped checkpoint load. Exposure statement for the
book: no number in the book was produced by an evaluation under `code` (or
any pre-`code_eval` snapshot) at 65,536 points or more for the surface
configuration; the only such evaluations are the two struck probe readings
above, which never entered a chapter.

**What the struck evaluations actually were: a metric-aggregation artifact
of the legacy snapshot at 80,000 cells, not a model failure.** The
coordinating session's discriminator, opening the saved predictions of the
struck job 700105 evaluation of `iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed42` at 80,000 cells, shows
predictions that are *identical* to the healthy `code_eval` evaluation of the
same checkpoint at the same cells: per car, prediction standard deviation,
mean, correlation with the truth (0.994–0.997) and relative L2 in physical
gauge pressure (0.0608–0.0807) agree to the last printed digit across the
two evaluations, and match the 10,000-cell evaluation's per-car values to
within a few percent. The model's output at 80,000 cells was therefore
correct under the legacy snapshot too; what was wrong was the aggregate
`pressure_l2` that its `infer.py` path wrote to metrics.jsonl (0.8144 and
0.8920 against the 0.0528 and 0.0574 that the same predictions yield under
`code_eval`). The defect is in the legacy snapshot's metric computation at
that point count, not in its model, its kernel or its data pipeline; it is
not pursued further because nothing evaluates under that snapshot any
more, and it changes no verdict: the two aggregates are struck, the
predictions were never used. It does sharpen the guard: the reducer's
snapshot field names the metric path a number came from, and any future
aggregate at 65,536 points or more from a pre-`code_eval` snapshot is
refused by construction.

**Aggregation guard in the recipe (coordinating session).** The cluster's
`recipe/src/infer.py` now refuses to write a summary whose value lies
outside the range of its own per-sample metrics (a mean cannot leave that
range, so a violation is an aggregation defect, never a measurement),
raising after the per-sample rows are written; the struck 0.814 aggregate
(per-car values 0.05–0.08) would have failed it. This track's reducer
computes every headline from the per-sample rows, never from the summary
line, so it is unaffected by a missing summary and would have been immune to
the wrong one had it read per-sample values under the legacy snapshot; the
guard closes the path for every launcher that reads the summary.

**Similarity-gauge corner `g512x80k`: principled scaling (both bars met).**
ISLA at width 512 with the similarity gauge, trained on 80,000 cells per
car (seeds 42/43, `code_perf`, fast point-softmax kernel, exact activation
recompute), evaluated under `code_eval` in both precisions (snapshot
sidecars present on every evaluation and probe, loads clean, seeds
distinct: 0.0425 / 0.0437 in float32) and probed for density bias at its
native 80,000 cells and at 10,000. Against the preregistered bars:

| bar (float32) | threshold | measured | standing |
|---|---|---|---|
| error within 5% of the constant-gauge corner | ≤ 0.0449 | **0.0431** (constant corner 0.0428; +0.7%) | met |
| biased ÷ uniform at 80,000 cells | ≤ 1.5 | **1.08** (constant corner 16.7x) | met |
| gauge fails at scale | ratio ≥ 3 | 1.08 | does not fire |
| gauge costs accuracy | ratio ≤ 1.5 and error > 0.0470 | 0.0431 | does not fire |

The similarity gauge's accuracy cost at the reference configuration (0.0616
against 0.0558 at width 192 × 10,000 cells, 10%) is gone at the corner
(0.0431 against 0.0428, under 1%), while the density sensitivity that the
constant gauge carries unchanged through every width and count (11–17x)
stays at 1.08x. Relative to the two 10k-trained references the gauge corner
is 0.77x the constant-gauge reference (0.0557) and 0.70x the gauge reference
(0.0616), at equal GPU-hours (20–23 for every DrivAerML arm). Cost of the
gauge at the corner: none measurable — 60.2M parameters (equal), peak
training memory 22.86 against 22.84 GB, median step 0.281 against 0.285 s;
bf16 evaluation 0.0441 for both corners (float32 ÷ bf16 0.98). The
DrivAerML count curve of the gauge corner (float32, uniform sampling,
biased ÷ uniform in parentheses) beside the constant-gauge corner:

| cells evaluated | width 512 × 80k, constant gauge (trained at 80k) | width 512 × 80k, similarity gauge (trained at 80k) |
|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | 0.0663 (10.9x) | 0.0727 (1.53x) |
| 40,000 | 0.0447 (pool exhausted; bias n/a) | not measured |
| 80,000 (native) | 0.0427 (16.7x) | 0.0431 (1.08x) |

Queried at an eighth of its training count the gauge corner loses more
accuracy than the constant corner (1.69x its native error against 1.55x)
and its bias ratio rises from 1.08 to 1.53; the down-transfer asymmetry
recorded for the constant corner (high-count training does not transfer
down; low-count training transfers up) holds for the gauge as well. Under
the redirect this is the one scaled configuration the program may adopt:
its gain over the reference comes with the density invariance intact, and
nothing about it depends on the training discretization beyond the
down-transfer cost that every 80k-trained arm shows. Reducer fix recorded
with this entry: the bf16 side's snapshot name was named and checked by the
guard but dropped from the per-arm `snapshot` field (shown as `?`); it is
now carried, so every arm row names both instruments' snapshots.

Two cost columns need their provenance stated. Peak memory is not
comparable across snapshots: the reference lanes trained under the legacy
`code` snapshot (9.81 GB at width 192) while the kernel control, the same
configuration under `code_perf`, peaks at 3.89 GB, so the 5–6 GB of the
wide arms reflects the newer snapshots' allocator behaviour, not a memory
saving from width; within a snapshot the ordering is as expected (width 512
above 384; 80,000 cells with exact recompute 12.9 GB at width 192 and 22.9
GB at width 512). GPU-hours follow the kernel: the two 40,000-cell arms
trained on the reference point-softmax kernel at 1.28 s per step (86
GPU-hours) because the fast kernel was adopted after they launched, while
the 80,000-cell arms on the fast kernel ran at 0.28 s (21–23 GPU-hours),
the same step time as the 10,000-cell arms. The cost frontier below
therefore reads the 40,000-cell points as measured and notes that on the
fast kernel they would sit near the reference's cost.

**Bars (preregistered in @sec-nb-scale-prereg; e_ref = 0.0557 in the
float32 instrument, 0.0577 in bf16; both instruments give the same
verdicts).**

1. *Width scales.* The 512-wide arm is 8.8% better than the reference
   (0.0508; bf16 7.1%), past the 5% bar. The gain is front-loaded: 384 takes
   7.4% and the step from 384 to 512 adds 1.6%, inside the seed spread, so
   width is scaling but flattening by 512 at 10,000 cells. Cost of width at
   this count: 6.8x the parameters for 2% more step time (attention over
   10,000 points, not the width, sets the step).
2. *Resolution-limited.* The 80,000-cell arm at the reference width is 16.0%
   better (0.0468; bf16 16.1%), past the 5% bar by a wide margin; 40,000
   cells takes 11.7%. The frozen protocol's 10,000 cells per car is the
   binding limit on DrivAerML, not the parameter count: the count lever
   (16%) is twice the width lever (9%) at equal GPU-hours on the fast
   kernel.
3. *Ordering* (bar 3) and the *cross-architecture frontier* (bar 4) belong
   to the synthesis entry; ISLA's own frontier, GPU-hours against error, is
   (21.3, 0.0557) → (22.7, 0.0508) → (21.7, 0.0468) → (22.5, 0.0428): at
   equal cost on the fast kernel, every configuration on the frontier is a
   token-count step, and width pays only at the corner.
4. *Corners.* Width and count compose: 384 × 40,000 reaches 0.0452 (0.81x)
   and 512 × 80,000 reaches 0.0428 (0.77x), against 0.91x and 0.84x for the
   two levers alone, so the levers are close to independent (the product of
   the single-lever ratios, 0.77, equals the measured corner).
5. *Kernel control.* The fast point-softmax kernel at the reference
   configuration scores 0.0567 against 0.0557 (+1.8%, seeds 0.0567 / 0.0567
   against 0.0568 / 0.0547): training-neutral within the seed spread, so the
   fast-kernel arms are comparable with the reference-kernel arms.

**Density sensitivity and what is adoptable.** The 10:1 density-bias
probe (float32; the ratio of the error under the biased sampler to the
uniform control) is 11–17x for every constant-gauge configuration at every
width and count measured (reference 12.1x at 10k and 12.7x at 80k; width 512
14.5x; the 512 × 80,000 corner 10.9x at 10k and 16.7x at its native 80k), so
neither lever moves the constant gauge's dependence on the sampling
distribution. The similarity-gauge corner holds 1.08x at its native count
and 1.53x at 10,000 cells while matching the constant-gauge corner's
accuracy (0.0431 against 0.0428) at equal parameters, memory and step time.
Under the 2026-09-10 redirect (principled generalization over accuracy) the
constant-gauge gains are recorded as measurements of the levers, and the
similarity-gauge corner is the one scaled configuration the program may
adopt. The count asymmetry recorded earlier stands for both corners: the
80k-trained models lose accuracy at an eighth of their count (0.0663 and
0.0727 at 10,000 cells) while the 10k-trained references improve
monotonically to 80,000 (0.0528 and 0.0574).

**Consequence for the book.** ISLA's DrivAerML pressure error of 0.0557
(0.0577 bf16) is a number at 8.9M parameters and 10,000 cells per car; at
60M parameters and 80,000 cells it is 0.0431 with the density invariance
kept. The accuracy ordering the chapters report is an ordering at the
frozen operating point until the synthesis entry places the baselines'
scaling beside this one; the recommendation section gains a scale clause
either way.

| 80,000 cells (192 and 512 wide, fast kernel) | 4 | 26–31 | 3.0–3.5 s | 27–32 | about 16 days |

The coordinating session's decision stands: full protocol, no hold, no

step). The HiLift half of this entry is written when the lanes land,

reported as "sample frame (pool frame)").

model is translation-invariant to float32 roundoff.** Twelve units, all
