The WAVE-4 ladder (@sec-nb-wave4-prereg) trains the similarity-gauge ISLA
(centroid and reference length taken from the measure-weighted point set,
so the routing geometry is normalized per sample) on every HiLiftAeroML
rung the constant-gauge reference has, at the same learning rate (1e-3),
seeds, token count and epochs, with `+model.similarity_gauge=true` the only
change. The fixed-angle rung is the dataset's `single_aoa_12` split: 126
geometries at 12° angle of attack for training, 18 never-seen geometries at
the same angle for validation, so it isolates geometry generalization from
angle generalization. Two lanes (w4_hl_mt2_gauge_single_aoa_12_seed{42,43},
snapshot code) finished 500 epochs and were evaluated in float32 under the
same snapshot (jobs 708622_8/9; bf16 twins 708621_8/9; no loader warnings,
no "skipping load"). Constant-gauge twins: mech_hl_mt2_single_aoa_12_seed{42,43}
(lr 1e-3 confirmed in their resolved configs).

| model, fixed angle (18 never-seen geometries) | pressure rel-L2, float32 (42 / 43 → mean) | vs constant-gauge ISLA | vs unit-drive GeoTransolver 0.0270 | vs unit-drive Transolver 0.0298 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA, similarity gauge (lr 1e-3) | 0.0411 / 0.0385 → **0.0398** | **1.144x** | 1.47x | 1.33x |
| ISLA, constant gauge (lr 1e-3, reference) | 0.0342 / 0.0353 → **0.0348** | 1 | 1.29x | 1.17x |

The bf16 evaluation reads 0.0418 / 0.0391 → 0.0405 for the gauge, the
usual 2% offset for ISLA (@sec-nb-fp32-first-look).

**Against the bars.** +14.4% is inside the preregistered 5–15% "known
price" band, at its top, and is the largest in-distribution price on the
ladder: 35 cases +7.6% (three seeds), 4 training geometries +7.4%,
DrivAerML −2.5% (parity, @sec-nb-wave4-drivaer-note). The fixed angle is
already the rung where ISLA is behind the baselines (the unit-drive
GeoTransolver 0.78x and Transolver 0.86x of the constant-gauge ISLA in
float32, @sec-nb-udrv-single-verdict), and the gauge widens that gap to
1.47x and 1.33x.

**Reading, with its discriminator.** The rung where the gauge costs most is
the one whose whole task is geometry generalization at a fixed drive
direction, and the gauge is the one configuration on the ladder that
discards the absolute size of the geometry (it divides positions by the
measure-weighted root-mean-square radius of the sample). The
Latin-hypercube wing geometries differ in span, chord and flap settings,
and at a fixed angle those size differences are a large part of what
distinguishes one case's pressure field from another's; a model that sees
every wing at unit radius must recover the size from secondary cues. This
is a hypothesis, not a result. The discriminating experiment is the pair of
frames that remove the plain-mean centroid but keep the absolute scale: the
measure-centred constant-length frame (center_mode=measure,
@sec-nb-center-lanes-verdict) and the relative frame with the stated
reference length (RELFRAME "ref", @sec-nb-relframe-verdict), neither of
which has been trained at the fixed angle. If either lands within 5% of
0.0348 there, the gauge's fixed-angle price is its scale normalization; if
both pay 10–15% as well, the price is the centroid (the mesh-density
content of the plain-mean frame, 0.131 body lengths on HiLift), the same
reading FRAME-FULL is testing at 35 cases. Not launched: the reference
decision is governed by Peter's frame ruling and FRAME-FULL, and the gauge
is a sample-statistic frame either way; the pair is the first follow-up
once the reference is settled.

**Consistency half.** The constant-gauge ISLA at the fixed angle is the
benchmark's worst-behaved trained arm: D_area +960% and D_biased +1385% at
40,000 cells (10.6x and 14.9x; results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json,
arm mech_hl_mt2_single_aoa_12). The gauge checkpoints' 30 BENCH lanes
(three samplers, five counts, two seeds; lane table bench/bench_lanes_w4fa.tsv,
jobs 708692 and 708718, float32) are running; the prereg's decision rule for this rung
is that the gauge passes the consistency bars where the constant gauge
fails them, at a stated price of 14%.

*Ladder status.* Seven of thirteen HiLift lanes trained and read
(super_scarce ×3, geometry_super_scarce ×2, single_aoa_12 ×2); scarce and
geometry_scarce at epoch ~280 of 500; full and deflection at epoch ~50
(days). Evaluations follow each pair as it lands.

## 2026-09-09 — Preregistered and launched: OVERFIT-1, train each architecture on one case to separate representational capacity from data limits {#sec-nb-overfit-prereg}

**Why.** With fair inputs ISLA trails the unit-drive Transolver by 17% and
GeoTransolver by 10% at 35 HiLift cases, and by 8.5% behind GeoTransolver
on DrivAerML at full data. Two readings are open: ISLA *cannot represent*
these fields as well (capacity), or it *generalizes* worse from few cases
(inductive bias and optimization). Training on a single case removes
generalization from the problem: the floor each architecture reaches on one
field, given unlimited passes over it, is a direct measure of representational
capacity for this data, and where the residual sits (gap regions against open
surfaces; pressure against wall shear) says which capacity is missing. The
same run tests the measure-weight variance reading with the data held fixed:
if weights-off is still better on one field, the cost is not a few-sample
effect.

**Instrument.** One HiLift case (`geo_LHC020_AoA_12`, a validation case at
the middle angle) and one DrivAerML car (`run_112`, a validation car), each
used as both the training and the validation set (manifests under
$T/overfit/, dataset variants `highlift_surface_overfit`,
`drivaer_ml_surface_overfit`, `drivaer_ml_volume_overfit`; pipelines
otherwise identical to the frozen ones). Every step draws a fresh 10,000-cell
sample of the case, so the model fits the *field*, not a fixed point set;
validation draws its own fresh sample every 1,000 epochs. 20,000 single-step
epochs (one case, batch 1, one GPU per lane), the reference learning rates
(ISLA and GeoTransolver 1e-3, Transolver 3e-3 on HiLift and 1e-3 on
DrivAerML), bf16, no augmentation, unit drive for every baseline,
`dataloader.pin_memory=false` throughout. Arms (seed 42): ISLA weights on,
ISLA weights off, GeoTransolver, Transolver on each dataset (8 lanes); and
on the DrivAerML interior task ISLA query tokens + SDF against
GeoTransolver-volume with the unit drive (2 lanes; ~365 surface cells as in
every interior arm). Readouts: the training loss curve; the recipe's
per-point relative L2 of standardized pressure (and velocity, wall shear) on
the same case at 10,000 and at a dense 40,000 sampled cells; the
facing-distance band split of the residual (instrument of
@sec-nb-hlreg-amendment) on the HiLift arms.

**Bars, in readout units (10k-sample relative L2 on the training case).**
*Capacity-limited* if ISLA's floor is ≥ 1.5x the unit-drive Transolver's on
the same case (the 35-case gap is 1.2x, so a single-case gap larger than the
data-limited gap says representation, not data). *Not capacity-limited* if
ISLA's floor is within 1.15x of the better baseline's (then the 35-case gap
is generalization). Between: partial, with the band split deciding whether
the missing capacity is local (gap regions ≥ 1.5x the open-surface ratio) or
global. *Weights are a representational cost* if weights-off beats weights-on
by ≥ 5% on one field; *a few-sample effect* if within 2%. Interior:
*capacity-limited on ν_t* if ISLA's single-car ν_t floor is ≥ 1.25x
GeoTransolver-volume's; not if within 1.10x. Every floor is also reported
against zero (a field that no architecture fits below 0.02 says the sampled
metric itself has a floor at 10k points).

**Launch.** Launcher $T/overfit_aga.sbatch (array 0–2, four single-GPU lanes
per node), evaluation $T/overfit_eval_aga.sbatch; job prefix ovf-, run ids
ovf_*; code snapshot code_isla5. About two hours per lane.

**Amendment before readout (2026-09-09).** The first launch was
input-bound: with one case per epoch the pipeline re-read a fresh 10,000-cell
sample from the full boundary mesh every step, at 11.3 s per step on
HiLiftAeroML and 2.5 s on DrivAerML (the HiLift arms would have taken 63
hours). Those lanes were cancelled at epochs 46–94 and their run directories
archived (`runs_ovf_attempt1/`, not used). The instrument now matches the
literal form of the test: `MeshDataset` gained a `cache_host` option (a
host-side cache of the reader's output by index, plumbed through the recipe
as `dataloader.cache_host`; commit c98121f22 with a unit test), the training
case is listed 64 times in the manifest so that 64 *distinct fixed*
subsamples are read once and then cycled, and training runs 320 epochs of
64 cached samples (20,480 single-sample steps) with checkpoints every 20
epochs. The evaluation still draws fresh 10,000- and 40,000-cell samples of
the case, so the readout is the fit to the *field* from 64 fixed views, and
a comparison of the 10k-sample metric with the training loss shows how much
of the floor is memorization of those views. Bars unchanged. Jobs
695431/695433/695434; code snapshot `code_ovf`, recipe copy `recipe_ovf`.

**Second amendment (2026-09-09).** The recipe's manifest resolver
deduplicates repeated entries, so the 64-fold listing produced "Train
samples: 1": each lane fit exactly one fixed 10,000-cell sample (cached), at
0.02–0.23 s per step, but for only 320 steps, and every lane on DrivAerML
and the interior finished in about three minutes with the loss still
falling. This is the literal single-sample test, so it is kept in that form
and lengthened: 20,000 single-step epochs on the one cached sample
(checkpoints every 1,000), which is one to two hours per lane. Two readouts
are then separated by construction: the training loss (fit to the fixed
sample) and the evaluation, which draws its samples of the same case with a
different sampler seed (7 against the training run's 42) at 10,000 and
40,000 cells, so it measures the fit to the *field* from one view. The
64-view variant would need a manifest resolver that keeps duplicates and is
not pursued now. Bars unchanged; the 320-step runs are archived
(`runs_ovf_attempt3/`).

**Third amendment (2026-09-09): float32 is the reporting instrument.** The
program adopted float32 inference as its reporting instrument after the
scaling study found that one ISLA checkpoint scores 0.0568 in float32 but
0.0588 or 0.0624 under two bf16 evaluation graphs, up to 31% per case
(@sec-nb-fp32-instrument). A single-sample floor is exactly the quantity such
an offset would corrupt, so every OVERFIT-1 readout is evaluated in float32
(with the bf16 evaluation alongside, for the offset table), and the bars
apply to the float32 numbers. Because training itself runs in bf16, four
float32-*training* arms were added on the HiLift case (ISLA weights on and
off, unit-drive GeoTransolver, unit-drive Transolver; run ids with the
suffix `_fp32`, array task 3, job 696023): if the bf16-trained floors sit
above their float32-trained twins by more than the seed-level 2%, the bf16
floor is numerical, not representational, and the bars are applied to the
float32-trained arms.

**Fourth amendment (2026-09-10): the schedule, not the model, set the
attempt-4 floors.** The frozen protocol's scheduler is StepLR with a step
size of 100 *epochs* and gamma 0.1, advanced once per epoch. With one sample
per epoch that is one step per epoch, so the learning rate had fallen to
1e-6 by step 300 and every lane's loss was flat from there to step 20,000
(0.036 for ISLA on DrivAerML at step 319 and at step 19,999 alike). The
evaluation confirmed that those checkpoints had not fitted even their own
training sample: relative L2 0.59 on the training sampler's draw and 0.61
on a fresh draw (float32), against 0.13 for models trained on 35 cases.
Attempt 4 is archived (`runs_ovf_attempt4/`, `ovf_evals_attempt4/`) and is
not a result. The relaunch scales the schedule to the step count
(`training.scheduler.step_size=4000`, the same one-decade-per-fifth
structure as 100 of 500 epochs) and runs both forms side by side from the
same launcher: *fixed sample* (one cached 10k-cell sample, run ids `_v1`)
and *64 views* (`cache_host_views=64`: 64 distinct subsamples of the case
read once and cycled, run ids `_v64`), ten architecture arms each plus two
float32-training arms (ISLA weights on, unit-drive Transolver) on the HiLift
case; 20,000 steps; jobs 697144–697149. The fixed-sample form measures
memorization capacity and the 64-view form the field-fit capacity; the
preregistered bars apply to the 64-view float32 readouts, with the
fixed-sample numbers reported alongside. A general note for the recipe: any
run whose epoch count is not about 500 needs the scheduler rescaled, which
the per-epoch StepLR makes easy to forget.

## 2026-09-11 — Verdict: QCOUNT — training over request sizes 2,000–20,000 reduces the interior query-count dependence by about 40% at a 3.7% accuracy cost and does not remove it {#sec-nb-qcount-verdict}

The preregistration (@sec-nb-qcount-prereg) asked whether the interior
query-token configuration's dependence on the request size is a
training-distribution artifact. Two seeds of the reference configuration
were trained with the interior request size drawn per sample uniformly
between 2,000 and 20,000 points (`DomainMeshReader.interior_n_points_range`,
snapshot `code_qcount`), otherwise the frozen protocol, and evaluated in
float32 under the guarded snapshot on 48 validation cars at 2,000, 10,000
and 20,000 requests, against the reference checkpoints at the same three
counts (deduplicated per car; zero skipped loads). Artifact:
`results/qcount_reduction_2026-09-11.json`.

**At 10,000 requests the augmented model scores 0.0567 / 0.0816 / 0.1115
(pressure, velocity, eddy viscosity) against the reference's 0.0547 /
0.0796 / 0.1116: a 3.7% pressure cost, past the 3% bar.** At 2,000 requests
it scores 0.0703 / 0.1069 / 0.1465 against the reference's 0.0753 / 0.1266 /
0.1663, so it predicts better than the reference at the count the reference
was never trained at, and its own 2,000-to-10,000 penalty is 1.24x on
pressure, 1.31x on velocity and 1.31x on eddy viscosity against the
reference's 1.38x, 1.59x and 1.49x: the dependence is reduced by about 40%
and not removed (bar 2: not supported at ≤ 1.10, and the falsifier at ≥ 1.25
missed by 0.01, so "between" by the letter and negative in substance). At
20,000 requests the augmented model improves to 0.0551 / 0.0794 / 0.1115,
so it converges upward as the reference does (bar 3 holds), and its ratio to
GeoTransolver-volume at 10,000 is 1.105 against the reference's 1.08 (bar 4
holds). Seeds agree to 0.2% at 10,000 and 2% at 2,000.

Reading, written in advance: the dependence is partly a training-distribution
artifact, which augmentation halves, and partly intrinsic to the interacting
decode, whose routing weights and query-query interactions change with the
number of requests regardless of what the training saw; query-count
consistency is therefore an architectural question after all, and the
D1-era statement that the deployment repair is augmentation rather than
architecture is retired in chapters 8 and 12. The practical rule stands:
deploy the interacting configuration at its training request count, and
state the count with every interior number. Count augmentation is recorded
as a partial mitigation with a measured price, not adopted; the reader
option stays as the instrument.

## 2026-09-11 — OVERFIT-1 verdict (surface arms): on one case ISLA's floor is 1.3–1.5x the unit-drive baselines', a wider gap than at 35 cases; the missing capacity sits on the coarse open surfaces, not in the gaps {#sec-nb-overfit-verdict}

**Setting.** OVERFIT-1 (@sec-nb-overfit-prereg) trains each architecture on a
single case for 20,000 single-sample steps, so that the floor it reaches
measures what the network can *represent* for this data with generalization
removed from the problem. The arms are ISLA with its measure weights on (the
reference configuration) and off (an ablation), and the unit-drive
GeoTransolver and Transolver, on one HiLiftAeroML wing (`geo_LHC020_AoA_12`)
and one DrivAerML car (`run_112`). Two forms ran side by side from the same
launcher: the *fixed-sample* form (one cached 10,000-cell sample of the case,
run ids `_v1`) and the *64-view* form (64 distinct 10,000-cell subsamples of
the same surface, read once and cycled, run ids `_v64`). Every readout below is
the recipe's relative L2 on the *same case* drawn with a different sampler seed
(7 against the training run's 42) at 10,000 and at 40,000 cells, in float32
(the reporting instrument, @sec-nb-fp32-instrument) with the bf16 evaluation
alongside. The preregistered bars apply to the 64-view float32 readouts at
10,000 cells. Attempts 1–4 were instrument faults (input-bound loading,
manifest deduplication, and a per-epoch StepLR that had driven the learning
rate to 1e-6 by step 300; all recorded in the amendments above) and are not
results. Attempt 5's HiLift and interior node jobs (697144–697149) reached the
4-hour wall at 12,000–14,000 steps and were resubmitted (709127–709130),
resuming from their 1,000-step checkpoints. The interior pair (ISLA query
tokens + SDF against GeoTransolver-volume) is at step 7,000–8,500 of 20,000 at
2.4 s per step and will be read out as an addendum.

**One instrument note first: the recipe's metric is a surface integral.** The
recipe's `pressure_l2` weights every sampled cell by its area (the
`target_measure` argument of the metric, fed from the mesh's cell measures),
so it is the relative L2 of the pressure *field* integrated over the surface,
not a per-point average. On the HiLift 64-view arms the per-point RMS-error
ratio Transolver/ISLA is 0.870 while the area-weighted ratio is 0.731; the
area-weighted RMS ratios reproduce the metric ratios to three digits for all
three comparisons (0.731, 0.785, 0.826). The difference is itself a finding
(below): ISLA's excess residual sits preferentially on *large* cells.

**What we saw, 64-view form (the preregistered readout).** Float32 evaluation
on a fresh 10,000-cell sample of the training case, then at 40,000 cells;
final training loss (on the cycled views) in the loss columns.

| Arm (seed 42, 20,000 steps) | HiLift p 10k | p 40k | u 10k | τ_w 10k | loss | DrivAerML p 10k | p 40k | loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA, weights on | 0.0434 | 0.0486 | 0.0716 | 0.1115 | 0.0062 | 0.1064 | 0.0857 | 3.6e-4 |
| ISLA, weights off (ablation) | 0.0358 | 0.0428 | 0.0645 | 0.0967 | 0.0036 | 0.0879 | 0.0703 | 3.3e-4 |
| GeoTransolver, unit drive | 0.0340 | 0.0358 | 0.0542 | 0.0905 | 0.0036 | 0.0766 | 0.0780 | 2.0e-4 |
| Transolver, unit drive | 0.0317 | 0.0356 | 0.0521 | 0.0904 | 0.0034 | 0.0811 | 0.0793 | 3.3e-4 |
| ISLA, weights on, float32 training | 0.0474 | 0.0425 | 0.0739 | 0.1176 | 0.0046 | — | — | — |
| Transolver, unit drive, float32 training | 0.0305 | 0.0389 | 0.0553 | 0.0886 | 0.0010 | — | — | — |

The ratios the bars were written for (pressure, 10,000 cells, float32):

| Ratio | HiLift, bf16-trained | HiLift, float32-trained | DrivAerML | Bar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA / unit-drive Transolver | **1.37** | **1.55** | **1.31** | ≥ 1.5 capacity-limited; ≤ 1.15 not |
| ISLA / unit-drive GeoTransolver | 1.27 | — | 1.39 | (reported) |
| ISLA weights off / weights on | **0.83** | — | **0.83** | ≤ 0.95 a representational cost; ≥ 0.98 a few-sample effect |
| ISLA weights off / unit-drive Transolver | 1.13 | — | 1.08 | (reported) |

**Verdict on the capacity bar: partial to capacity-limited, and never "not
capacity-limited".** With generalization removed, ISLA's floor on the wing is
1.37x the unit-drive Transolver's and 1.27x GeoTransolver's (bf16-trained
arms), and 1.55x in the float32-trained pair; on the car it is 1.31x and
1.39x. The bf16-trained arms land in the preregistered "between" band
(1.15–1.5) and the float32-trained pair crosses the capacity bar. No
comparison comes within 1.15x of the better baseline. **The single-case gap is
wider than the many-case gap**: at 35 HiLift cases the unit-drive Transolver
and GeoTransolver stand at 0.115 and 0.124 against ISLA's 0.138 (1.20x and
1.11x, @sec-nb-udrv-verdict), and at full DrivAerML data GeoTransolver leads by
about 1.09x. If ISLA's deficit were a few-sample generalization effect, fitting
one case with unlimited passes would have closed it; instead it grew. The
training losses say the same thing from the other side: on its own 64 views
ISLA (weights on) floors at 0.0062 against 0.0034–0.0036 for the other three
arms, so the gap is present on the training views themselves, before any
transfer to a fresh sampling. The deficit is therefore representational or
optimizational for this data, not a data limit.

**It is not numerical.** The float32-trained ISLA twin floors at 0.0474
against the bf16-trained 0.0434 (both float32-evaluated); float32 training
does not lower ISLA's floor, while it lowers the Transolver's training loss
3.4x (0.0034 to 0.0010) without moving its fresh-sample error (0.0317 to
0.0305). The 9% spread between the two ISLA twins, which differ only in
training precision and therefore in their optimization path, is also the best
single-seed noise gauge this test has: larger than the 2% assumed in the
prereg, but well below the 27–55% ratios above.

**Where the missing capacity is: on the open surfaces, not in the gaps.** The
facing-distance instrument of @sec-nb-hlreg-amendment splits the HiLift
surface by the distance to the nearest facing surface (near, 0.7–2% chord:
3,445 of the 9,983 evaluated cells; mid, 2–10%: 523; far, > 10%: 6,015) and
reports the per-point RMS-error ratio baseline/ISLA in each band:

| Comparison (HiLift, 64 views, float32) | near (gaps) | mid | far | all | near / rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Transolver / ISLA | 0.881 | 0.642 | 0.831 | 0.870 | 1.15 |
| GeoTransolver / ISLA | 0.884 | 0.665 | 0.776 | 0.871 | 1.20 |
| Transolver / ISLA weights off | 0.958 | 0.911 | 0.914 | 0.955 | 1.05 |

For every arm the near band carries 90–93% of the squared error (residual RMS
1.4–1.6 Pa there against 0.25–0.32 Pa far from any facing surface, on a field
whose RMS is 172–177 Pa), so the gap regions are where *everyone's* residual
lives. But ISLA's *relative* deficit is smallest there (0.88) and largest on
the mid and far open surfaces (0.64–0.83); the near/rest ratio of 1.15–1.20 is
below the 1.5 the prereg required to call the missing capacity local. The
area-weighting result points the same way: the near-gap cells are the small
ones, and weighting by area moves the Transolver/ISLA ratio from 0.87
(per point) to 0.73 (per unit area). **On this case ISLA is short of capacity
on the smooth, coarsely meshed open surfaces, where the field is easy and the
residual small, not at the slat and flap gaps.** This is the same direction as
the 35-case HLREG readout (ISLA's advantage smallest at the gaps).

**Verdict on the measure weights: a representational cost, not a few-sample
effect.** With the data fixed to one case, turning the measure weights off
lowers ISLA's floor by 17% on the wing and 17% on the car at 10,000 cells
(12% and 18% at 40,000), well past the 5% bar, and it lowers the training loss
too (0.0062 to 0.0036 on the wing). The cost that MEAS-METRIC measured under
either metric and NOW-L saw persist at 210 cases (@sec-nb-nowl-210-verdict) is
therefore paid in what the network can fit, not in how it generalizes from few
cases. Weights off is still 1.13x (wing) and 1.08x (car) behind the unit-drive
Transolver, so the weights account for roughly half of the single-case deficit
and something else accounts for the rest. Per the program's ruling, the
weights-off configuration remains an ablation; this entry proposes no change to
ISLA's reference configuration and no recipe change (a single fitted case can
locate missing capacity, it cannot license an architecture decision, which
must be argued mechanically and pass the discretization-consistency tests).

**Fixed sample against 64 views: the model must answer the same on either
sampling of the same surface, and from one view no architecture does.** In the
fixed-sample form every float32-trained arm drives its training loss to zero
(both ISLA and the Transolver memorize 10,000 points exactly), and the bf16
arms plateau at 0.010–0.013 (bf16 rounding caps the memorization of a fixed
point set). Asked the same question on a *second* sampling of the same surface,
the memorized models answer with relative L2 0.12–0.16 on the wing (ISLA 0.159,
weights off 0.120, GeoTransolver 0.137, Transolver 0.135; float32-trained
ISLA 0.147 and Transolver 0.140) and 0.29–0.36 on the car (0.323, 0.294, 0.356,
0.337). Cycling 64 views of the same surface lowers those numbers 3–4x on
both datasets with no other change. The teaching is about optimization, not
about any one architecture: a single fixed point set lets every architecture
here fit the *points* rather than the *field*, and the field is what a
resampling asks for. The two forms also bracket the many-case numbers: one
view memorized gives 0.13–0.16 on the wing, about the 35-case validation error
(0.115–0.138), and 64 views of one case give 0.03–0.05, about the 510-case
error (0.0495).

**Convergence check, 10,000 to 40,000 cells (two points, not a limit).** Every
arm was trained at exactly 10,000 cells, so the 40,000-cell reading is an
off-training-count query of the same surface. On the car the unit-drive
GeoTransolver and Transolver are insensitive between the two counts (+2% and
−2%), while both ISLA arms move 19–20% toward lower error (0.106 to 0.086 and
0.088 to 0.070); on the wing no arm is insensitive: the bf16-trained arms all
rise (ISLA +12%, weights off +20%, GeoTransolver +5%, Transolver +12%) and the
float32-trained twins move in opposite directions (ISLA −10%, Transolver
+28%), so the Transolver/ISLA ratio reads 1.37 and 1.55 at 10,000 cells and
1.37 and 1.09 at 40,000. Two counts cannot say whether any arm converges to a
single field in the fine-mesh limit; that is the BENCH sampler instrument's
question and it is not asked here. What this check does say is that the bar
readouts on the wing carry a sample-count sensitivity of the same order as the
bf16/float32 twin spread, and the bars are applied at the preregistered
10,000 cells.

**bf16 evaluation offsets** (bf16 minus float32, 10,000 cells): on the wing
ISLA 0.0% and weights off 0.0%, GeoTransolver +8%, Transolver +10%; in the
float32-trained pair ISLA +4% and Transolver +19%; on the car +2% to +6% for
every arm. The rounding offset falls on the baselines this time, in the
direction that narrows their lead under bf16, which is one more reason the
bars are read in float32.

**What it changes.** (1) ISLA's deficit to the unit-drive baselines on the
surface tasks is not a data-scarcity effect and the ladder should not be
expected to close it at higher rungs: it is present with unlimited passes over
one case and larger there than at 35 or 510 cases. (2) The missing capacity is
on the smooth open surfaces measured per unit area, not at the gaps, which
rules out "the gap physics is too hard for ISLA" and points at how ISLA
represents slowly varying pressure over large cells. (3) Half of the
single-case deficit is the measure semantics (the weights-off ablation), a
cost now shown to be representational; the other half is unexplained. (4) A
fixed single sample is a memorization test, not a capacity test, for every
architecture here; the 64-view form is the one that measures field capacity.
None of these is a recipe or architecture proposal; the mechanistic question
of *why* ISLA under-fits large-cell regions goes to the main session under the
physically-principled-change rule.

**Artifacts.** Reduction
`examples/cfd/mesh_transformer/results/overfit_single_case_2026-09-11.json`
(every arm's last loss, and the float32 and bf16 evaluations at 10,000 and
40,000 cells; interior arms filled in by the addendum); facing-distance splits
`results/overfit_hlreg_isla_vs_transolver_2026-09-11.json`,
`results/overfit_hlreg_isla_vs_geotransolver_2026-09-11.json`,
`results/overfit_hlreg_islaoff_vs_transolver_2026-09-11.json`. On the cluster:
`$T/ovf_evals/` (predictions and metrics per run, resolution and precision),
`$T/overfit/metric_recon.py` (the area-weighting reconciliation),
`$T/overfit/reduce_overfit.py`, `$T/overfit/hlreg_ovf.py`; training runs
`$T/runs/ovf_*`; archived attempts `runs_ovf_attempt1..4`. Code snapshot
`code_ovf` (worktree at 55ee54cf3, `cache_host` and `cache_host_views`
options with unit tests), recipe copy `recipe_ovf`.

**Next.** The interior addendum (bars: ν_t capacity-limited if ISLA's
single-car floor is ≥ 1.25x GeoTransolver-volume's, not if within 1.10x) when
the two lanes finish and evaluate; it decides whether the interior lead that
survived the unit-drive control (@sec-nb-udrv-verdict) is also a capacity
lead.

## 2026-09-11 — OVERFIT-1 mechanism addendum: the measure weights cut each slice's effective token count to a fifth through the sampler's heavy area tail, not by saturating on a few cells; slice states then move about twice as much between resamplings of the same surface {#sec-nb-overfit-routing-probe}

**Setting.** The OVERFIT-1 verdict (@sec-nb-overfit-verdict) found that ISLA
with its measure weights on fits a single case 17% worse than the same
network with the weights off, on both datasets, and that the deficit sits on
the coarsely meshed open surfaces once the error is measured per unit area.
This inverts the naive expectation: the measure weights put the log of each
sampled cell's area into the point-to-slice routing, so the large open-surface
cells get *more* routing mass, and the slices should track exactly the regions
that dominate the area-weighted metric. ISLA Main proposed a mechanism and a
falsifier before any further work: a handful of very large cells saturate each
slice's softmax over points, collapsing the effective number of tokens per
slice and starving the slices of the diversity needed to fit smooth variation.
The falsifier: the per-slice effective token count (the participation ratio
1 / Σ_i a_is² of the routing weights, the number of equally weighted points
that would give the same concentration) should be several-fold lower with
weights on than off, and lower on the open surfaces than at the gaps; near 1
and the hypothesis is dead.

**Derivation first.** In ISLA a slice state is z_s = Σ_i a_is h_i with
a_is = w_i e^{l_is} / Σ_j w_j e^{l_js}: a softmax over points of the routing
logits l plus log w, that is, a measure-weighted mean of the point features,
which is what makes the state a surface integral rather than a sample average.
With flat logits the routing reduces to the measure itself and the effective
token count is (Σw)² / Σw² = N / (1 + CV²), where CV is the coefficient of
variation of the cell areas in the sample. This bound depends only on the
sampler and the mesh. In the 10,000-cell uniform-over-cells samples used here
the area tail is heavy: on the HiLift wing the CV is 3.25, the largest cell is
630 times the median, 4.4% of the cells carry half the sampled area, and the
flat-routing effective count is 862 of 9,983 cells; on the DrivAerML car the
CV is 2.26, 6.8% of the cells carry half the area, and the count is 1,637 of
10,000. A surface integral estimated this way has 3.4x (wing) and 2.5x (car)
the standard error of a plain point mean of the same sample. This is the
classic importance-weight degeneracy: the quadrature is consistent (it
converges to the surface integral under any sampler as the sample grows) but
at 10,000 cells it is a high-variance estimate. Under an area-proportional
sampler the weights would be constant and the two configurations would
coincide by construction. The exponent option `measure_weight_power` scales the
tail: N_eff is 2,118 / 4,564 / 7,873 on the wing and 2,747 / 4,767 / 7,927 on
the car at exponents 0.75 / 0.5 / 0.25, with the consistency property held
exactly only at exponent 1. These numbers describe the sampler; they are not a
proposal.

**Instrument.** Two forward-pass probes on the trained 64-view checkpoints
(ISLA weights on and off, HiLift and DrivAerML; float32; 10,000 cells), run
through the recipe's `infer.py` unchanged with two monkeypatches: the ISLA
forward records the per-point measure, and every point-softmax records
per-slice statistics of its routing weights (each of the 12 slice blocks
computes two: a seed pass with feature logits only, then the pass with the
relational bias that forms the slice states; the state-forming pass is
reported). Probe 1 (one view, sampler seed 7): the effective token count per
slice, the mass on the ten largest weights, the slice's effective covered area
fraction A_eff,s / A = exp(−Σ_i a_is log(a_is / w_i)) (the area of the region
when a slice integrates uniformly over a region, one cell's area when it
collapses onto that cell), and the count split by the slice's mean log-area
quartile (large-cell against small-cell slices). Probe 2 (four views, sampler
seeds 7–10): the raw slice states z_s and anchor positions of every block, and
from them V_view (how much a slice's state moves when the surface is
resampled) relative to V_slice (how much the slices differ from each other on
one view), the effective number of distinct slice states (participation ratio
of the across-slice covariance spectrum), and the anchors' across-view jitter
relative to their across-slice spread. Scripts `$T/overfit/probe_routing.py`,
`reduce_probe.py`, `reduce_probe2.py`, `measure_tail.py`; raw outputs under
`$T/ovf_probe/` and `$T/ovf_probe2/`.

**Probe 1: the count bar is met, the saturation and localization readings are
not.** Median over the 12 state-forming passes:

| Quantity (median over layers) | HiLift on | HiLift off | DrivAerML on | DrivAerML off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Effective tokens per slice | 540 | 2,030 | 390 | 1,980 |
| Ratio on / off | **0.21** | | **0.21** | |
| Ratio on / flat-routing floor (862; 1,637) | 0.63 | | 0.24 | |
| Mass on the ten largest weights | 0.085 | 0.027 | 0.11 | 0.033 |
| Effective covered area fraction | 0.48 | 0.070 | 0.36 | 0.088 |

Per layer the count ratio runs 0.09–0.48 on the wing and 0.17–0.44 on the car,
so **the several-fold bar is met in every layer on both datasets**. But the
reduction is not saturation: ten cells never carry more than 18% of a slice's
mass (0.03–0.18 with weights on against 0.003–0.10 off), and the weights-on
count never exceeds the flat-routing floor set by the measure (0.10–1.00 of
it, reaching the floor exactly in the last wing layer). The learned logits
concentrate the routing *within* what the heavy area tail already allows; the
tail sets the ceiling. The localization prediction fails: slices routed to the
large-cell quartile are not systematically poorer in tokens than those routed
to the small-cell quartile (wing, layers 1–12, large/small: 0.54, 0.53, 0.73,
1.1, 0.53, 2.1, 3.3, 11, 3.4, 0.98, 1.2, 0.47; the car is equally mixed). The
effective covered area tells what the weights do instead: with weights on each
slice integrates over 24–93% of the surface area (0.75–0.93 in the first two
and last three layers), with weights off over 4–18%, which is about the area
fraction of the finely meshed regions, so a uniform-over-points routing is in
effect a mean over the gap regions. Yet the weights-off model, whose slice
states barely see the open surfaces, fits the open surfaces *better* per unit
area (@sec-nb-overfit-verdict): the smooth open-surface field is not
reconstructed from slice coverage of those surfaces, so "starving the smooth
regions" cannot be the mechanism.

**Probe 2: the states are noisier, about twofold, and no less diverse.**
Resampling the same surface four times and comparing slice states:

| Quantity (median over layers) | HiLift on | HiLift off | DrivAerML on | DrivAerML off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| V_view / V_slice (resampling movement relative to slice spread) | 0.052 | 0.035 | 0.065 | 0.022 |
| Ratio on / off | **1.85** | | **2.31** | |
| Effective number of distinct slice states (of 256) | 27 | 30 | 28 | 34 |
| Anchor jitter / anchor spread | 0.16 | 0.09 | 0.22 | 0.14 |

The ratio exceeds 1.5 in 8 of 12 wing layers and 11 of 12 car layers and
never falls to 1.2 (minimum 1.17 and 1.46); it reaches 3.5–4.2 in the last two
wing layers and 5.5–7.0 in the last two car layers, where the routing is
flattest and the quadrature argument applies most directly. The anchors move
1.5–1.8x more between views with the weights on. But the effective number of
distinct slice states is the same with the weights on or off (27 against 30 on
the wing, 28 against 34 on the car; both far below 256), so the weights do
*not* starve the slices of diversity, and the twofold excess is well short of
the fivefold the token-count ratio alone would predict for pure sampling
noise: the routing is not flat and the point features are not independent
draws, so most of the quadrature variance does not reach the states.

**Verdict on the hypothesis.** Supported in kind, refuted in mechanism and
short in magnitude. (1) *Confirmed*: the measure weights cut each slice's
effective token count to about a fifth. (2) *Refuted*: the cut is not a
collapse onto a handful of very large cells, and it is not concentrated on the
open surfaces; it is the heavy area tail of a uniform-over-cells sample acting
through the quadrature, bounded by N / (1 + CV²). (3) *Refuted*: slice
diversity is unchanged. (4) *Supported*: the consequence that survives is
variance. A slice state and its anchor move about twice as much when the same
surface is resampled, so the same surface point receives a different context
on every view, which is an irreducible noise floor when fitting one fixed
field from 64 views, and it is largest in relative terms where the residual is
smallest, on the open surfaces (near-gap residual 1.4–1.6 Pa against
0.25–0.32 Pa far from any facing surface). Whether a twofold excess in state
noise accounts for the whole 17% floor difference is not established here;
the direction and the localization match, the magnitude is a single measurement.

**What it changes.** The weights-off ablation's advantage on a single case has
a named cause that lives in the *sampler*, not in ISLA's integral semantics:
under uniform-over-cells sampling the consistent quadrature is the
high-variance one. The program already has an area-proportional sampler in the
BENCH instrument; under it the measure weights are constant and the two
configurations coincide exactly, so the weights-off advantage must vanish there
by construction, which is a falsifiable prediction the sampler-consistency
lanes can check without new code. Whatever remedy the main session considers,
the constraint is the one Peter set: the model must answer the same on either
sampling of the same surface, so any variance reduction must keep the
fine-mesh-limit consistency that the exponent-1 quadrature has and the
weights-off point mean does not. This entry proposes no change; the mechanistic
argument and the discretization-consistency tests belong to the main session.

**Artifacts.**
`examples/cfd/mesh_transformer/results/overfit_routing_probe_2026-09-11.json`
(probe 1, per layer, on and off, both datasets, with the measure floors) and
`results/overfit_slice_state_variance_2026-09-11.json` (probe 2, per layer:
V_view, V_slice, effective distinct states, anchor jitter and spread).

## 2026-09-11 — Verdict, MWAW: an area-weighted datapipe frame costs the repaired baselines nothing (+1.1–1.2%, "equal") and, estimated with Horvitz–Thompson weights on the drawn sample, takes their density collapse from 14–16x to 1.03–1.04x; the baselines' whole sampler dependence was the plain-mean centroid {#sec-nb-mwaw-verdict}

The MWAW lanes (@sec-nb-mwaw-prereg) retrained the measure-weighted
GeoTransolver and Transolver (unit drive, reference learning rates, two
seeds each, 500 epochs, snapshot code_mw) on the 435 DrivAerML cars with
one datapipe change: `CenterMesh` centres each case on the area-weighted
mean of the reader's uniform cut instead of the plain mean of its cells
(run ids mwaw_dr_gt_unit_lr1e3_seed{42,43}, mwaw_dr_transolver_unit_lr3e3_seed{42,43}).
Float32 evaluation on the 48 validation cars at 10,000 cells (job 711207) and
two sample-frame density probes, in which the centring is applied *after*
the 10:1 front/back draw as a biased mesher would deliver it: one with the
raw-area weighting the lanes trained with (job 711211), which under a biased
draw is still a count-biased estimate, and one with the cells' full
measures, areas times Horvitz–Thompson weights, which is the unbiased
estimate of the geometric centroid ∫x dA / ∫dA (job 711217, snapshot
code_mw_ht, the probe analogue of the repository's new
`CenterMesh(use_measure_weighting=True)`). No loader warnings in any log.
Artifact `results/mwaw_2026-09-11.json`.

| model (DrivAerML, 48 cars, 10k, float32) | in-family (42 / 43 → mean) | plain-frame twin | ratio | density 10:1, sample frame, raw-area centre (seeds → mean) | density 10:1, sample frame, HT centre (seeds → mean) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GeoTransolver, measure-weighted, area-weighted frame | 0.0502 / 0.0507 → **0.0505** | 0.0498 | 1.012x | 8.9 / 9.6 → **9.2x** | 1.042 / 1.036 → **1.04x** |
| Transolver, measure-weighted, area-weighted frame | 0.0523 / 0.0533 → **0.0528** | 0.0522 | 1.011x | 6.5 / 5.4 → **6.0x** | 1.029 / 1.030 → **1.03x** |

**Against the bars.** Accuracy: both arms are within ±3% of their
plain-frame twins (+1.2% and +1.1%, inside seed spread), the "equal" band;
the area-weighted frame does not buy accuracy, as predicted (the frame
shift on cars is 0.034 body lengths). Density: with the HT centre the
sample-frame ratio is **1.04x and 1.03x**, under the 1.5x bar and under the
1.17–1.21x floor ISLA's measure-weighted frames show; with the raw-area
centre it is 9.2x and 6.0x, which is the count bias of weighting a 10:1
biased draw by raw areas (the nuance recorded in the preregistration: the
transform's `use_area_weighting` alone is not Horvitz–Thompson under a
biased draw; `use_measure_weighting` is). The prediction held in full and
the readout is sharper than predicted: the repaired baselines' density
dependence is entirely their datapipe centroid, and with an unbiased
estimate of the geometric centroid they are as consistent under the 10:1
bias as any arm the program has measured.

**Reading.** Two defects, two repairs, both now measured on the baselines:
measure-weighted slice pooling fixes the aggregation (@sec-nb-bench-mw,
|D| under 1% with the frame held), and an HT-consistent centroid fixes the
frame (this entry). Neither touches the architecture's attention or its
learned parameters in kind; both are the two places where GeoTransolver
and Transolver read the sampling law, and both are quadrature-consistent
by construction. The 1.03x residual is smaller than ISLA's 1.2x because the
baselines' slice pooling is a single softmax over tokens whose weights
enter linearly, while ISLA's routing carries the weights through several
layers of measure-weighted attention, each with its own sampling variance.

**What this means for the ruling.** For ISLA the ruling's second clause
applies (a frame-free construction exists, so at equal accuracy it is
preferred and the HT centroid is not adopted). For the baselines no
frame-free construction exists: their choice is between two sample
statistics, the plain mean of cell centres, which reads the mesher and
collapses 12–16x, and the HT estimate of the geometric centroid, which is
the estimator of a property of the geometry and holds at 1.03x, at equal
accuracy. The preregistration's "equal → plain frame stays" was written
before this distinction was clear, and it would leave the steel-man
baseline standing on the one frame that is a mesher artifact. The
recommendation put to Peter through ISLA Main: adopt the HT-weighted
`CenterMesh` (`use_measure_weighting`) as the baselines' datapipe frame in
the fair comparison, state it beside every baseline consistency number,
and keep the plain-mean numbers as the record of the published datapipe.
Until he rules, the chapters report both frames. *Superseded 2026-09-11 by
Peter's ruling (@sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines): the released models are
not modified, so the recommendation is withdrawn; the MWAW arms stay as the
diagnostic that locates the property.*

## 2026-09-11 — MIX follow-up under refinement: the area-trained measure-weighted ISLA's swap penalty falls from 2.9x at 2,500 cells to 1.05x at 40,000, and under uniform sampling it lands at the uniform-trained model's level (+2%), not at the weights-off level {#sec-nb-mix-refinement}

The MIX verdict (@sec-nb-mix-verdict) measured mesher transfer at 10,000
cells only, where every architecture pays to swap sampling conventions,
and predicted from the consistency benchmark that the measure-weighted
ISLA's penalty would vanish with the count. The two area-trained
similarity-gauge ISLA checkpoints (mix_dr_isla_gauge_area_seed{42,43}; lr
3e-3, the rate of the uniform-trained iw_mt2_gauge reference) went through
the benchmark's three samplers at five counts (thirty lanes, job 711297,
float32 under snapshot code, no loader warnings; artifact `results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_mixarea_2026-09-11.json`). The
table sets them beside the uniform-trained gauge and the uniform-trained
constant-gauge weights-on / weights-off pair from the original benchmark.

| DrivAerML, 48 cars, float32 | 2,500 | 5,000 | 10,000 | 20,000 | 40,000 cells |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| area-trained gauge ISLA, evaluated under uniform-over-cells | 0.2243 | 0.1435 | 0.0874 | 0.0665 | 0.0591 |
| area-trained gauge ISLA, evaluated under area-proportional | 0.0780 | 0.0650 | 0.0601 | 0.0579 | 0.0564 |
| swap penalty, uniform ÷ area (its own law) | 2.88x | 2.21x | 1.46x | 1.15x | 1.05x |
| uniform-trained gauge ISLA under uniform (iw_mt2_gauge) | 0.0878 | 0.0692 | 0.0618 | 0.0591 | 0.0579 |
| area-trained ÷ uniform-trained gauge, both under uniform | 2.55x | 2.07x | 1.42x | 1.13x | 1.02x |
| uniform-trained gauge ISLA under area (iw_mt2_gauge) | 0.2389 | 0.1887 | 0.1370 | 0.0993 | 0.0683 |
| uniform-trained ÷ area-trained gauge, both under area | 3.06x | 2.90x | 2.28x | 1.72x | 1.21x |
| uniform-trained constant gauge, weights on (iw_mt2_lr1e3), under uniform | 0.0796 | 0.0625 | 0.0561 | 0.0540 | 0.0530 |
| uniform-trained constant gauge, weights off (now_mt2_lr1e3), under uniform | 0.0708 | 0.0593 | 0.0544 | 0.0527 | 0.0518 |

**Two readings.** First, the MIX prediction holds: a measure-weighted ISLA
trained on one sampling law and deployed on the other pays 2.9x at 2,500
cells, 1.45x at 10,000 (the MIX study read 1.63x at its 10,000-cell
evaluation on a different draw) and **1.05x at 40,000**, so at the
benchmark's largest count the convention swap costs the measure-consistent
model 5%, against the flat 3–7x the baselines showed at 10,000 cells;
"train on one mesher, deploy on another" is a property the measure-weighted
estimator acquires in the fine-mesh limit, as @sec-principle requires and
@sec-nb-mix-verdict predicted. The reverse swap converges the same way
(uniform-trained under area: 2.72x → 1.21x from 2,500 to 40,000 cells).
Second, the triple ISLA Main asked for
(#sec-nb-overfit-routing-probe in the program notebook): read under the
uniform sampler at 40,000 cells, the area-trained weights-on model (0.0591)
sits at the uniform-trained weights-on level (0.0579, +2%), not at the
weights-off level (0.0518, which would be 0.88x of the weights-on 0.0530 at
the constant gauge); training under the constant-weight law does not
recover the weights-off advantage, so the operative part of that advantage
on the cars is not the training-time variance of the weights. The
uniform-sampler off-advantage on the cars does shrink with count (0.89 →
0.98 from 2,500 to 40,000, @sec-nb-bench-verdict data), which is the
evaluation-time variance signature; on the wings it is flat at 12–13% and
is mesh-pattern content. Confounds stated: the weights-off arm is the
constant gauge at lr 1e-3 while both weights-on gauge arms are at 3e-3, and
the area-trained model under uniform sampling is off its training law, so
its +2% may be residual swap penalty rather than a floor; the triple is a
one-line check, not a headline.

## 2026-09-11 — FRAME-FULL, DrivAerML half: the exact full-geometry frame passes the joint bar on the cars (centre-and-scale arm 0.0544, −2.4%, density 1.13x; centre-only arm 0.0565, +1.5%, 1.20x); the HiLift half, which decides the reference, is training {#sec-nb-frame-full-drivaer}

FRAME-FULL (@sec-nb-frame-full-prereg) gives ISLA its frame from the full
surface mesh at data-preparation time: the geometric centroid ∫x dA / ∫dA
and the root-mean-square radius of every training and validation surface,
computed in float64 over every cell (8.3 × 10⁹ cells for DrivAerML,
cross-checked against an independent pyvista computation to 7 × 10⁻¹⁴)
and handed to the model as global data, so the frame has zero sampling
variance and no dependence on which cells a mesher produced. Two arms:
"center" takes only the centroid from the table and keeps the constant
reference length; "frame" takes both centroid and scale. Four DrivAerML
lanes (ff_dr_mt2_{center,frame}_seed{42,43}; unit drive, lr 1e-3, 500
epochs, snapshot code_frame, recipe copy recipe_frame with the frame
datasets, which apply no `CenterMesh`), float32 evaluation under
code_eval_frame on the 48 validation cars (job 711592) and the 10:1 density
probe with the frame taken from the table for both draws (job 711593); no
loader warnings. Artifact `results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json`.

| arm (DrivAerML, 48 cars, 10k, float32) | pressure (42 / 43 → mean) | vs constant gauge 0.0557 | density 10:1 (42 / 43 → mean) | joint bar (within 3%, ≤ 1.2x) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FRAME-FULL, centre only (constant reference length) | 0.0570 / 0.0560 → **0.0565** | +1.5% | 1.18 / 1.22 → **1.20x** | pass |
| FRAME-FULL, centre and scale | 0.0543 / 0.0545 → **0.0544** | -2.3% | 1.13 / 1.13 → **1.13x** | pass |

For the record beside them (same instrument): constant gauge 0.0557 at
12.0x; measure-centred constant length 0.0548 at 1.17x; RELFRAME
reference-length 0.0566 at 1.21x and total-measure 0.0552 at 1.235x;
similarity gauge at the reference rate 0.0543 at 1.20x.

**Reading, DrivAerML.** Both arms pass the joint bar. The centre-and-scale
arm is at parity with the most accurate ISLA configurations on the cars
(0.0544 against 0.0543 for the rate-matched gauge and 0.0548 for the
measure-centred frame, all inside seed spread) and has the lowest density
ratio any ISLA frame has shown, 1.13x with both seeds agreeing. That number
is the diagnostic the preregistration asked for: with the frame's sampling
variance removed exactly, what remains under the 10:1 draw is the
measure-weighted routing's own variance, 1.13x; the frame-estimate variance
therefore accounted for the difference to the 1.17–1.24x the estimated and
frame-free constructions show, and the rest is the routing integral. The
scale matters here as it did not elsewhere: the centre-only arm sits at
1.20x, the same floor as the measure-centred and relative frames, so on
the cars the exact scale is worth 0.07 in ratio and 2–4% in accuracy.

**What it does not decide.** The reference rule (@sec-nb-relframe-verdict)
turns on the wings: the exact geometric frame becomes the reference
candidate only if it lands within 3% of 0.1377 at 35 HiLift cases at a
density ratio ≤ 1.2x, where the frame-free construction paid 11%. The four
HiLift lanes are on their second links; until they read out the reference
stays RELFRAME with the total-measure scale by the rule, and the chapters
stay "under decision".

## 2026-09-11 — Verdict, FRAME-FULL: the exact full-geometry frame pays 14–16% at 35 HiLift cases, more than the frame-free construction's 11%; the HiLift price of leaving the plain mean is the mesher's pattern, and by the preregistered rule the reference configuration is RELFRAME with the total-measure scale {#sec-nb-frame-full-verdict}

FRAME-FULL (@sec-nb-frame-full-prereg; @sec-nb-frame-full-drivaer for the
DrivAerML half) was the diagnostic that separated the two readings of the
11% the frame-free ISLA pays at 35 HiLift cases (@sec-nb-relframe-verdict):
either positional information lost with the four dropped seed features, or
the mesh-density content of the plain-mean frame. It keeps every positional
seed and relational invariant of the constant-gauge reference and replaces
only the frame: the geometric centroid ∫x dA / ∫dA (arm "center", constant
reference length kept) or the centroid and the root-mean-square radius
(arm "frame"), both computed in float64 over every cell of the full surface
mesh (6.0 × 10¹⁰ cells for the 215 HiLift cases) and passed as global data,
so the frame has zero sampling variance and no mesher dependence. Four
HiLift lanes (ff_hl_mt2_{center,frame}_super_scarce_seed{42,43}; 35
training cases, unit drive, lr 1e-3, 500 epochs, snapshot code_frame,
recipe_frame), float32 evaluation on the 180 validation cases under
code_eval_frame (job 711878, no loader warnings). Artifact `results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json`.

| ISLA frame at 35 HiLift cases (180 val, float32) | pressure rel-L2 (42 / 43 → mean) | vs constant gauge 0.1377 | what the frame is |
|---|---|---|---|
| constant gauge (reference until today) | 0.1349 / 0.1408 / 0.1375 → **0.1377** | 1 | plain mean of the sampled cell centres: a mesher statistic, displaced 0.131 body lengths from the geometric centroid |
| similarity gauge (@sec-nb-wave4-prereg) | three seeds → 0.1482 | +7.6% | measure-weighted mean and RMS radius of the sample: HT estimates, sample-variant |
| constant length, measure-weighted centring (@sec-nb-center-lanes-verdict) | 0.1519 / 0.1521 → 0.1520 | +10.4% | HT estimate of the geometric centroid from the sample |
| RELFRAME, reference length (@sec-nb-relframe-verdict) | 0.1568 / 0.1491 → 0.1530 | +11.1% | no frame: anchor-relative positions only |
| RELFRAME, √(total measure) | 0.1567 / 0.1490 → 0.1529 | +11.0% | no frame; scale from the integrated surface measure |
| **FRAME-FULL, exact centroid** | 0.1584 / 0.1617 → **0.1600** | **+16.2%** | exact geometric centroid from the full mesh, zero variance |
| **FRAME-FULL, exact centroid and scale** | 0.1590 / 0.1552 → **0.1571** | **+14.1%** | exact centroid and RMS radius from the full mesh, zero variance |

**Against the preregistered readings.** *Recovers* was within 3% of 0.1377
at density ≤ 1.2x; *pays* was ≥ 7% worse. Both FRAME-FULL arms **pay**, by
16% and 14%, more than the frame-free construction (11%) and more
than every estimated frame (7.6–10.4%). A model that keeps all of the
constant gauge's positional features and is given the exact geometric
frame, with no variance to blame, is the least accurate ISLA on this rung.
So the 11% is not positional information lost with the seeds: putting the
seeds back with a correct frame makes it worse, not better. It is the
mesh-density content of the plain-mean frame. On the 35-case wing rung the
plain mean of the cell centres sits 0.131 body lengths from the geometric
centroid, the same displacement whether computed from a 10,000-cell sample
or from all 6 × 10¹⁰ cells, so it is a deterministic function of where the
mesher refined; on an in-distribution validation set drawn from the same
mesher that displacement is an informative input (it says where the
leading edges, flaps and slats are, because that is where the cells are),
and every frame that does not carry it pays for its absence. That is the
stated cost of the principle on this rung, and not a reason to reinstate a
sample statistic; under a different mesher the same input is what
collapses 12x (@sec-nb-bench-verdict, @sec-nb-mw-postcenter).

**The rule fires.** The decision rule written with Peter's ruling
(@sec-nb-relframe-verdict): *the reference is RELFRAME with the
total-measure scale unless FRAME-FULL passes its joint bar.* FRAME-FULL
fails it on the wings (it passes on the cars, 0.0544 at 1.13x). **ISLA's
reference configuration is therefore the relative frame with the
total-measure scale** (`frame_mode=relative`, `scale_mode=total_measure`;
runs rf_*_meas_*): no centroid, no sample scale, no per-dataset reference
length; translation invariance from anchor-relative positions alone.
Its standing numbers, float32: DrivAerML 435 cars 0.0552 (constant gauge
0.0557), density 10:1 in the sample frame 1.235x (seeds 1.20 / 1.27),
consistent under all three benchmark samplers on both datasets
(@sec-nb-relframe-hl-bench); 35 HiLift cases 0.1529 (+11% against the
constant gauge). The two RELFRAME scales are indistinguishable on every
readout (accuracy, density, samplers, both datasets), and the total-measure
scale is the one with no dataset-dependent constant, which the ruling
("one flagship, never dataset-dependent") requires. Per the WAVE-4
preregistration's decision clause, the price is stated beside every number
and the constant-gauge results are kept as the prior configuration's
record: the accuracy tables of chapters 5 and 6 were measured with the
constant gauge, which remains on the ladder rungs the relative frame has
not been trained on (fixed angle, 4 and 21 geometries, 210 and 1,260 cases,
deflection, interior, poses). Training the reference configuration on those
rungs is the follow-up ladder (RELFRAME-LADDER), the first rung the fixed
angle, where the discriminator of @sec-nb-wave4-fixed-angle also lives.

**Consequences for the frame story, in one paragraph.** Five frames were
trained at 35 HiLift cases and on DrivAerML. On the cars every consistent
frame is at parity with the plain mean (0.0543–0.0566 against 0.0557) and
the exact frame is best; on the wings every consistent frame pays 8–16% and
the plain mean is cheapest. The difference between the datasets is the
displacement of the plain mean from the geometric centroid, 0.034 body
lengths on the cars and 0.131 on the wings: the mesher's information is
worth what the mesher's pattern is worth, and the wing meshes carry far
more of it. The density floor of the consistent frames on the cars is 1.13x
with the exact frame and 1.17–1.24x with estimated or absent frames, so the
routing integral's own variance is 1.13x and the frame estimate adds up to
0.1. The code path for the exact frame (global_data `frame_center` and
`frame_scale`, `SetGlobalFieldsFromTable`) stays in the repository as the
diagnostic it was built to be.

## 2026-09-11 — Preregistered: RELFRAME-LADDER, the reference configuration on the HiLift rungs it has not been trained on, fixed angle first, with the scale-normalization discriminator {#sec-nb-relframe-ladder-prereg}

With the reference configuration decided (@sec-nb-frame-full-verdict:
relative frame, total-measure scale), every accuracy number in chapters 5
and 6 on the rungs other than 35 HiLift cases and DrivAerML 435 is the
prior configuration's record, and the WAVE-4 preregistration's clause
requires the price of the reference to be stated beside each. This ladder
trains it there. First rungs, launched now (training snapshot code_frame,
which carries the relative-frame code path, and evaluation snapshot
code_eval_frame, identity-checked to 7e-8 against code_eval on a legacy
checkpoint; recipe copy recipe_frame with the standard per-split dataset
yamls; unit drive, lr 1e-3, 500 epochs, two seeds, launcher
frame/rf_hl_aga.sbatch, lane table frame/rf_lanes.tsv rows 4–9, jobs
712017–712022, all six accepted at 0.13–0.14 s per step with
`frame_mode: relative` resolved in their configs; the recipe's
`isla_surface_reference.yaml` is the same configuration as a named model
config): the fixed angle (`single_aoa_12`, 126
geometries at 12°, 18 never seen) in **both** scales, reference length
(rf_hl_mt2_ref_single_aoa_12_seed{42,43}) and total measure
(rf_hl_mt2_meas_single_aoa_12_seed{42,43}), and the 4-training-geometry
rung (`geometry_super_scarce`) in the reference scale only
(rf_hl_mt2_meas_geometry_super_scarce_seed{42,43}). The remaining rungs (21
geometries, 210 and 1,260 cases, deflection) follow as nodes free.

**Readouts and bars.** Float32 pressure rel-L2 against the constant-gauge
prior on the same rung (fixed angle 0.0348; 4 geometries 0.2496), graded in
the WAVE-4 bands: ≤ 5% "cheap", 5–15% "the known price", > 15% "expensive
at this rung". **The discriminator** (@sec-nb-wave4-fixed-angle): the
similarity gauge paid 14.4% at the fixed angle, its largest price, and one
reading was that the gauge's scale normalization discards the absolute
size of the geometry on the rung whose whole task is geometry. The two
RELFRAME scales separate this from the frame: the reference-length arm
keeps absolute size, the total-measure arm normalizes it away, and both
carry no centroid. *If the total-measure arm pays ≥ 5% more than the
reference-length arm at the fixed angle*, scale normalization is a real
cost on geometry-only tasks and the reference configuration's scale choice
must be revisited (the ruling prefers no dataset constant, but a
demonstrated accuracy cost is what it said would justify one). *If the two
arms are within 3% of each other*, the fixed-angle price is the frame's,
the scale choice stays free, and the total-measure scale stands.
**Predictions.** Both arms pay 10–15% at the fixed angle (the same meshes
and the same 0.131 body-length mesher displacement as the 35-case rung,
where the reference paid 11%), within 3% of each other; the 4-geometry rung
pays 5–10% (the gauge paid 7.4% there). **Consistency half** for the
fixed-angle checkpoints: the BENCH samplers at five counts (lane table to
be built as bench_lanes_rf.tsv was), where the prior collapses 10.6x /
14.9x at 40,000 cells and the gauge is consistent; the reference is
predicted consistent (|D| ≤ 3% at 40,000) as it was at 35 cases.

## 2026-09-11 — Verdict, FARWAKE: far-field oversampling of the training queries makes every interior field worse (ν_t far shell 0.193 against 0.118; recipe pressure +36%); falsified as a remedy, with the query-distribution swap stated as the confound {#sec-nb-farwake-verdict}

*Setting.* ISLA's interior configuration (surface tokens plus interior
query tokens carrying the signed distance to the wall) leads
GeoTransolver-volume on interior velocity and trails it on eddy viscosity,
and the whole eddy-viscosity deficit sits in the far wake beyond 0.4 body
lengths downstream, a region holding about 2% of a uniform interior sample
(@sec-interior-task). The preregistered FARWAKE arm (@sec-nb-farwake-prereg)
asked whether that deficit is an under-sampling effect: the training loss is a
mean over the sampled queries, so the far wake receives about 2% of the
gradient signal. The arm drew a 40,000-point uniform interior pool per case,
kept points with probability proportional to a step function of the signed
distance (weights 1 below 0.05 body lengths, 3 to 0.4, 8 beyond), normalized
to an expected 10,000 kept points, and recorded the exact inclusion
probabilities so the objective's reweighting is known. Two seeds, the
reference query-token configuration otherwise frozen, 500 epochs
(`v0_isla_qtsdfval_farwake_seed42/43`, recipe copy `recipe_farwake`,
transform `SdfBiasedSubsampleInteriorPoints`). Peter approved the arm as a
cause-elimination experiment: "either we get the right answer, or we rule
out one more cause."

*Instruments.* Float32 inference under the guarded evaluation snapshot on the
standard uniform 10,000-point interior validation sample of the 48 DrivAerML
validation cars (job 712231; 48 predictions per seed, zero skipped loads),
then the wall-distance band decomposition of the saved predictions
(`transfer/far_field_shells_farwake.py`, the companion's far-field
instrument with the FARWAKE arm added) against the reference two seeds and
the unit-drive GeoTransolver-volume. Artifacts:
`results/farwake_reduction_2026-09-11.json` (recipe metrics) and
`results/farwake_far_field_shells_2026-09-11.json` (bands).

*Bars (written in advance).* Supported if the far-band (≥ 0.05 L)
eddy-viscosity error is ≤ 0.085 with the near-wall band and the recipe
pressure and velocity within 3% of the reference; falsified if ≥ 0.095;
reference about 0.101, GeoTransolver-volume 0.068.

*What we saw.* **Every band of every field is worse than the reference.**
Recipe metrics, two-seed means: pressure 0.0754 against 0.0553 (+36%),
velocity 0.0984 against 0.0804 (+22%), eddy viscosity 0.164 against 0.111
(+48%). In the far shell beyond 0.4 body lengths the eddy-viscosity error is
0.193 against the reference's 0.118 and GeoTransolver-volume's 0.071; the
region the arm was built to help is the region it hurt most. The cost is not
confined to the far field: in the near-wall band (0.05–0.1 L) eddy viscosity
is 0.080 against 0.048 (+67%) and pressure 0.156 against 0.066. The two seeds
agree (pressure 0.0773 / 0.0736, eddy viscosity 0.171 / 0.157).

| Region (share of a uniform sample) | ν_t reference | ν_t FARWAKE | ν_t GeoTransolver-volume | p reference | p FARWAKE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.05–0.1 L (2.7%) | 0.048 | 0.080 | 0.067 | 0.066 | 0.156 |
| 0.1–0.2 L (2.6%) | 0.042 | 0.083 | 0.053 | 0.106 | 0.226 |
| 0.2–0.4 L (2.5%) | 0.039 | 0.084 | 0.038 | 0.125 | 0.192 |
| ≥ 0.4 L (2.2%) | 0.118 | 0.193 | 0.071 | 0.270 | 0.316 |

*Verdict.* **Falsified as a remedy**: under the deployment query
distribution, oversampling the far wake in training does not close the
eddy-viscosity deficit and degrades every field, so the far-wake deficit is
not something a training-time sampling law fixes. The pre-written reading
applies with one qualification. The arm trains the interacting decode on
one query distribution and scores it on another, and this book has measured
that the interacting decode's prediction at a point depends on the joint
set of queries (@sec-nb-qcount-verdict: at half the training count the error
rises 24%); the surface analogue, a model trained on one sampling convention
and scored on another, pays 1.5–1.9x at 10,000 cells
(@sec-nb-mix-verdict). So the whole-field degradation is at least in part a
query-distribution swap penalty, and this arm cannot separate "the far wake
is not under-sampled" from "the swap penalty swamps any gain". What it
does settle is the deployable question: with evaluation on the uniform
sample that every interior number in this book uses, far-wake oversampling
is not a remedy. The candidate that remains for the far-wake deficit is
representational, that the downstream coordinate enters ISLA's seed only
implicitly through the freestream direction and the signed distance, and it
is not scheduled: the interior configuration's standing (ahead on velocity,
behind on pressure and eddy viscosity at matched parameters) is stated as
measured in @sec-interior-task and @sec-limits-mechanism.

*What changes.* FARWAKE node closed as STOPPED (falsified); chapter 8's
far-wake paragraph names the arm as a closed negative; the
`SdfBiasedSubsampleInteriorPoints` transform and its tests stay in the
recipe as a measured instrument. Owner: this session.

## 2026-09-11 — OVERFIT-1 interior addendum: on one car ISLA's velocity lead is a capacity lead (0.67x), its eddy-viscosity deficit is capacity-limited (1.64x), and its full-data pressure lead is not (1.25x behind) {#sec-nb-overfit-interior}

**Setting.** The interior half of OVERFIT-1 (@sec-nb-overfit-prereg) trains
the two interior architectures on a single DrivAerML car (`run_112`) for
20,000 single-sample steps: ISLA with query tokens and the signed-distance
inputs (the interior configuration that kept its lead under the unit-drive
control, @sec-nb-udrv-verdict) against GeoTransolver-volume with the unit
drive, about 365 surface cells and 10,000 interior queries per step, in the
same two forms as the surface arms (one fixed cached sample, `_v1`; 64 cycled
views of the car, `_v64`). Each lane took four 4-hour links (2.4 s per step
with the pin-memory workaround), resumed from checkpoints by the automation.
Readout as before: the recipe's relative L2 on the same car resampled with
seed 7, at 10,000 and 40,000 interior queries, float32 with bf16 alongside;
the preregistered bars apply to the 64-view float32 readout at 10,000: ISLA is
*capacity-limited on ν_t* if its floor is ≥ 1.25x GeoTransolver-volume's, not
if within 1.10x.

**What we saw.** Float32, 64-view form, pressure / velocity / eddy viscosity
on the training car, fresh sampling; the fixed-sample form below it.

| Arm (seed 42, 20,000 steps) | p 10k | u 10k | ν_t 10k | p 40k | u 40k | ν_t 40k | loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA query tokens + SDF, 64 views | 0.0801 | 0.0926 | 0.1507 | 0.0599 | 0.0826 | 0.2419 | 0.0016 |
| GeoTransolver-volume, unit drive, 64 views | 0.0642 | 0.1393 | 0.0916 | 0.0721 | 0.1464 | 0.1200 | 0.0022 |
| ratio ISLA / GeoTransolver-volume | **1.25** | **0.67** | **1.64** | 0.83 | 0.56 | 2.02 | |
| ISLA query tokens + SDF, fixed sample | 0.3405 | 0.4092 | 0.5833 | 0.2546 | 0.4247 | 0.6069 | 0.0068 |
| GeoTransolver-volume, unit drive, fixed sample | 0.3579 | 0.4356 | 0.6832 | 0.4227 | 0.5051 | 0.6921 | 0.0267 |

For reference, the full-data interior ratios ISLA / GeoTransolver-volume
(unit drive, @sec-nb-udrv-verdict) are 0.92 / 0.65 / 1.30 for p / u / ν_t.

**Verdict.** Three different answers for the three fields, and each one is
informative against the full-data numbers. (1) **Velocity: a capacity lead.**
With the data fixed to one car ISLA's velocity floor is 0.67x
GeoTransolver-volume's, the same ratio as at full data (0.65x). The
interior velocity lead is what the architecture can represent, not what it
generalizes; it does not depend on the training-set size at all. (2) **Eddy
viscosity: capacity-limited.** ISLA's ν_t floor is 1.64x GeoTransolver-volume's
on one car, over the 1.25x bar and wider than the full-data 1.30x. The ν_t
deficit that FARWAKE and the interior density work have been probing is a
representational limit of the query-token construction for this field, and
more cars will not close it. (3) **Pressure: the full-data lead is not a
capacity lead.** ISLA leads GeoTransolver-volume on interior pressure at full
data (0.92x) but trails it on one car (1.25x). The pressure lead therefore
comes from generalization across cars, which is the reading the surface test
gave for none of ISLA's surface comparisons; on the interior it holds for one
field. The single-case floors themselves (0.06–0.15 for ISLA, 0.06–0.14 for
GeoTransolver-volume) sit at the full-data error level (0.057–0.13), as on the
surface: 64 views of one car teach as much about that car as the full
training set does about a validation car.

**Fixed sample.** Neither interior arm memorizes its one sample in bf16 (loss
floors 0.0068 and 0.0267 against 3.6e-4–0 for the surface arms; the interior
sample is 365 surface cells plus 10,000 queries, and the loss covers three
fields with ν_t hardest), and both are near-useless on a resampling of the same
car (0.34–0.68 relative L2, ISLA 0.85–0.95x GeoTransolver-volume's). The
64-view form lowers those numbers 4–5x, the same optimization teaching as on
the surface: a single point set is fitted as points, the field is learned from
views.

**Convergence check, 10,000 to 40,000 queries (two points, not a limit).**
Both arms were trained at 10,000 queries. GeoTransolver-volume moves 5–31%
between the counts (p +12%, u +5%, ν_t +31%); ISLA moves −25% on pressure,
−11% on velocity and **+61% on eddy viscosity**, so the ν_t ratio reads 1.64
at 10,000 and 2.02 at 40,000. This is the query-count dependence of the
query-token construction that QCOUNT measured and reduced by about 40% without
removing it (@sec-nb-qcount-verdict); on a single fitted car it is at its most
visible, and it is largest on the field where ISLA is capacity-limited. Two
counts cannot say whether either arm converges to a single field in the
fine-mesh limit; the bars are applied at the preregistered 10,000.

**bf16 evaluation offsets** (bf16 minus float32, 10,000 queries): ISLA
+2.5% / +4% / +10% on p / u / ν_t; GeoTransolver-volume +24% / +19% / +28%.
The interior baseline carries the largest rounding offsets measured in this
program, another reason the interior bars are read in float32.

**What it changes.** The interior lead is now decomposed by field with the
data held fixed: velocity is a representational advantage of the query-token
construction, pressure an advantage in generalization across cars, and eddy
viscosity a representational deficit that also carries the query-count
dependence. Together with the surface verdict (@sec-nb-overfit-verdict): ISLA's
surface deficits and its interior ν_t deficit are capacity, its interior
velocity lead is capacity, and its interior pressure lead is generalization.
No recipe or model change is proposed here; where the ν_t capacity is missing
(far wake, near wall, or the query-count coupling) is the FARWAKE and QCOUNT
sessions' question, and any construction change must pass the
physically-principled and discretization-consistency tests. OVERFIT-1 is
complete.

**Artifacts.** `results/overfit_single_case_2026-09-11.json` now carries the
interior arms (keys `v1:v0`, `v64:v0`); evaluations under
`$T/ovf_evals/ovf_v0_*`; training runs `$T/runs/ovf_v0_*` (jobs
697148/697149 → 709128/709130 → 711244/711277 → the fourth links).
