## 2026-09-11 — RELFRAME-LADDER amendment: the 21-geometry and 210-case rungs launched, with the recurrence prediction stated before they read {#sec-nb-relframe-ladder-amend}

The 4-geometry result (@sec-nb-relframe-ladder-geo4) turned the ladder's
open question into a prediction: the plain-mean frame's mesher pattern
should be worth something to the constant gauge only where validation
geometries recur in training. The next two rungs discriminate it directly.
**21 geometries** (`geometry_scarce`, 210 training cases, 180 validation
cases from 18 never-seen geometries): same case count as the 210-case rung,
unseen geometries. **210 cases** (`scarce`, 210 training cases drawn across
geometries and angles, validation geometries recurring): same case count,
recurring geometries. Lanes rf_hl_mt2_meas_geometry_scarce_seed{42,43} and
rf_hl_mt2_meas_scarce_seed{42,43} (reference configuration: relative frame,
total-measure scale; unit drive, lr 1e-3, 500 epochs, snapshot code_frame,
recipe_frame; lane table frame/rf_lanes.tsv rows 10–13, jobs 714206–714209;
evaluation snapshot code_eval_frame, eval lane table rows 14–17). Priors
(constant gauge, float32): 21 geometries 0.1014 (seeds 0.1002 / 0.1026); 210
cases 0.0643 (three seeds 0.0617 / 0.0661 / 0.0652). Similarity gauge on the
same rungs: +2.9% and +2.0%.

**Predictions, stated before either reads.** Under the recurrence reading:
21 geometries ≤ 3% (cheap, as at 4 geometries); 210 cases 8–12% (as at 35
cases, where geometries recur). Under the alternative that the price is a
data-quantity effect (the gauge's ladder fell from 7–8% at 35–40 cases to
2–3% at 210): both rungs ≤ 3%. The two readings agree on the 21-geometry
rung and disagree on the 210-case rung, which is therefore the
discriminating cell: *≥ 8% there confirms recurrence; ≤ 3% refutes it and
puts the 35-case price down to data quantity, with the 35-case rung then
the only expensive one for the reference.* Bands as before (≤ 5% / 5–15% /
> 15%).

## 2026-09-11 — Ruling: the released GeoTransolver and Transolver are not modified; measure-weighted and HT-centred baselines are research variants that locate a property, and every transferable finding is written as a pro of ISLA {#sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines}

Peter's ruling, relayed by ISLA Main and binding on both sessions.
GeoTransolver and Transolver as released in PhysicsNeMo are stable, in use
and published; they will not be modified, and back-porting ISLA's findings
to them is engineering-infeasible (it would need a follow-on paper).
Consequences for this fork's work: (1) the measure-weighted slice pooling
(MW, @sec-nb-mw-verdict) and the HT-centred datapipe frame (MWAW,
@sec-nb-mwaw-verdict) remain in the book as *research variants, not the
released models*, whose only role is to locate a property in the fair
comparison: consistency under resampling is a property of the frame and
the aggregation, not of the attention; they are never written as
recommendations or deployable options. (2) The open question of the
baselines' datapipe frame in the fair comparison is closed as moot: the
released datapipe is the comparison, the MW and MWAW rows are the
diagnostic; the recommendation in @sec-nb-mwaw-verdict is withdrawn. (3)
Every transferable finding, measure-consistent aggregation,
frame-free or HT-consistent frames, sampler consistency in the fine-mesh
limit, is a pro of ISLA, the architecture people will adopt. (4) No further
baseline-modification lanes; the reference ladder
(@sec-nb-relframe-ladder-prereg) and the WAVE-4 remainder are unaffected.
(5) Engineering focus moves to ISLA productization: the reference
configuration, defaults, kernel speed, recipe integration. The repository's
`CenterMesh(use_measure_weighting=True)` stays a general library
improvement (default off), not a change to the released recipes.

## 2026-09-11 — Engineering: the relative frame with the total-measure scale is now ISLA's class default; legacy configs and tests pin the centered construction {#sec-nb-defaults-relative}

*Setting.* The reference configuration decided this morning
(@sec-nb-frame-full-verdict) is the relative frame with the total-measure
scale: no centroid anywhere in the forward pass, positions entering only as
differences against slice anchors, and the length unit taken from the total
quadrature measure of the sample. Until now it was reachable only through
`frame_mode="relative"` and `scale_mode="total_measure"`; the class
defaults were the centered construction with a constant reference length,
the configuration behind the constant-gauge checkpoints now labelled the
prior configuration. Peter's ruling this evening that ISLA is to be
introduced as a new architecture, rather than its findings back-ported to
the released baselines, makes the class default the thing users will get,
so it should be the reference.

*What changed.* `ISLA()` now defaults to `frame_mode="relative"` and
`scale_mode="total_measure"`; `center_mode` keeps its default of `"plain"`
and is used only under `frame_mode="centered"`. The module docstring
describes the default construction and names the options that require the
centered frame (`similarity_gauge`, `odd_head`, `seed_mode="raw"`,
`scale_conditioning`, any `center_mode`), and the constructor's error
messages tell a caller who passes one of them to set
`frame_mode="centered"` (and `scale_mode="reference_length"`). Checkpoints
store their constructor arguments, so every model saved under the earlier
defaults loads and evaluates unchanged; the guarded evaluation snapshot on
the cluster is a copy and is unaffected. In the recipe, the constant-gauge
configs (`isla_surface.yaml`, `isla_surface_frame.yaml`,
`isla_volume_support.yaml`, the last of which carries the similarity gauge
for the interior configuration) now pin `frame_mode: centered` and
`scale_mode: reference_length` explicitly, so what they train is bitwise
what they trained before, and `isla_surface_reference.yaml` states the
defaults it now shares. The legacy contract tests were written for the
centered construction; each of their constructor calls now passes an
explicit `_CENTERED` dictionary so they keep verifying that construction,
and a new test, `test_default_is_relative_total_measure`, pins the default
(one seed invariant, six relational invariants, relative frame,
total-measure scale). The five ISLA test files and the checkpoint tests
pass: 108 passed, 8 skipped (GPU-only).

*What it means for the contracts.* The reference configuration trades one
invariance for another: it is exactly invariant to a uniform geometric
rescale (positions by $k$, areas by $k^2$) and *not* to rescaling the
measure weights alone, since the total measure is its length unit; the
centered construction had the opposite pair. Chapter 2 now describes the
relative frame as the forward pass (one seed, six relational invariants,
the vector head's radial direction taken from the token's soft anchor) with
the centered construction as the documented prior, and its contract table
carries the relative-frame test and the default test.

*Open.* The interior configuration (`isla_volume_support.yaml`) still uses
the similarity gauge, a sample-statistic frame, because no relative-frame
interior lane has been trained; it is pinned to the centered frame for now
and a relative-frame interior pair is the natural next lane if the interior
configuration is to share the reference frame. Owner: this session.

## 2026-09-11 — Engineering: every ISLA constructor argument and forward input is keyword-only {#sec-nb-kwargs-only}

*Setting and request.* Peter asked that all inputs for ISLA be keyword
arguments, so that models can be hot-swapped later without positional
bookkeeping. The recipe already calls the model as `model(**forward_kwargs)`
with names resolved from the dataset configuration, and Hydra instantiates
the class from keywords; only the tests, a handful of result-generating
scripts and any direct caller used positional order.

*What changed.* `ISLA.__init__` and `ISLA.forward` now take keyword-only
arguments (a bare `*` after `self`). A positional call raises a `TypeError`
immediately. Every positional forward call in the repository was rewritten
to keywords with an ast-based tool that names arguments in the signature's
order (`points`, `normals`, `drive`, `measure_weights`, then the optional
inputs): the five ISLA test files and the checkpoint tests, the two recipe
tests that build the model, and the result-generating scripts
(`isla_sparse_routing_bench_2026-09-09.py`, `isla_perf_round2_2026-09-09.py`,
`mom2_second_moment_benchmark_2026-09-08.py`, `isla_profile_2026-09-09.py`,
`isla_vs_baselines_cost_fastkernel_2026-09-09.py`, `m3_demo.py`,
`transfer_program/studies/paired_conditions/train_arms.py`). One test that
passed a tuple of refined inputs by `*refined` now passes a dictionary. A new
test, `test_constructor_and_forward_are_keyword_only`, asserts that
positional construction and positional forward calls raise. Checkpoints are
unaffected (the loader instantiates from a stored keyword dictionary), as
are the cluster snapshots.

*Verification.* ISLA and checkpoint suites: 109 passed, 8 skipped
(GPU-only). Recipe test directory: 252 passed, 2 skipped. One recipe test
needed its Hydra override changed from `+model.scale_mode=global` to
`model.scale_mode=global`, because the constant-gauge configs now state
`scale_mode` explicitly (@sec-nb-defaults-relative). Owner: this session.

## 2026-09-11 — RELFRAME-LADDER, fixed-angle rung: the reference configuration pays 10% (0.0384 against 0.0348), less than the similarity gauge's 14%; the reference-length arm pays 26%, so scale normalization is not the fixed-angle cost, and the fixed angle stays the outlier that the recurrence reading does not explain {#sec-nb-relframe-ladder-fixed-angle}

Second rung of the reference-configuration ladder
(@sec-nb-relframe-ladder-prereg): the fixed angle (`single_aoa_12`, 126
training geometries at 12°, 18 never-seen geometries for validation), run in
both scales so that the scale-normalization reading of the gauge's 14.4%
price (@sec-nb-wave4-fixed-angle) could be tested against the frame.
Four lanes (rf_hl_mt2_{ref,meas}_single_aoa_12_seed{42,43}; relative
frame with the constant reference length ("ref") or the total-measure scale
("meas", the reference configuration); unit drive, lr 1e-3, 500 epochs,
snapshot code_frame), evaluated in float32 under code_eval_frame (job
718945, no loader warnings). Artifact `results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json` (block hilift_val). Priors on
the rung, float32: constant gauge 0.0348 (seeds 0.0342 / 0.0353),
similarity gauge 0.0398 (0.0411 / 0.0385), unit-drive GeoTransolver 0.0270,
Transolver 0.0298.

| fixed angle (18 never-seen geometries, float32) | pressure rel-L2 (42 / 43 → mean) | vs constant-gauge prior | vs similarity gauge | vs unit GeoTransolver | vs unit Transolver |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ISLA, reference (relative frame, total-measure scale)** | 0.0363 / 0.0405 → **0.0384** | **+10.3%** | 0.964x | 1.42x | 1.29x |
| ISLA, relative frame, reference-length scale (discriminator arm) | 0.0389 / 0.0486 → **0.0437** | +25.7% | 1.099x | 1.62x | 1.47x |
| ISLA, similarity gauge | 0.0411 / 0.0385 → 0.0398 | +14.4% | 1 | 1.47x | 1.33x |
| ISLA, constant gauge (prior) | 0.0342 / 0.0353 → 0.0348 | 1 | 0.874x | 1.29x | 1.17x |

**Against the bars.** The reference pays 10.3%, the "known price" band,
and is 3.5% more accurate than the similarity gauge on the rung where the
gauge paid most; the prediction of 10–15% for it held. The reference-length
arm pays 26%, the "expensive" band, with a 22% seed spread (0.0389 /
0.0486) against 11% for the total-measure arm and 3% for the constant gauge.
**The scale discriminator reads the opposite way from the hypothesis.** The
preregistered trigger was the total-measure arm paying ≥ 5% *more* than the
reference-length arm; instead it pays 12% *less*. Normalizing away the
absolute size does not cost accuracy on the geometry-only rung, it helps
(or, given the seed spread, is at worst neutral), so the gauge's 14.4% here
was not its scale normalization, and the total-measure scale stands as the
reference's without a caveat on this rung.

**What the fixed angle does to the recurrence reading.** The 4-geometry
rung suggested that the plain-mean frame's mesher pattern sells only where
validation geometries recur in training (@sec-nb-relframe-ladder-geo4).
The fixed angle is a never-seen-geometry rung, and under that reading the
reference should have been cheap here; it pays 10%, so recurrence is not
the whole account. What is specific to this rung is the fixed drive
direction: with every case at 12°, the reference configuration's seed
(n̂·d̂ and the measure) varies only with the surface normal, and everything
else a token knows about its place on the wing comes through anchor-relative
positions, whereas the constant gauge's positional seeds (|r|, r̂·d̂,
r̂·n̂ about the plain mean) tell each token directly where it sits along
the chord and span, which at a fixed angle is most of what determines its
pressure. The two candidate accounts of the 10% are therefore the same two
the 35-case rung had, with the balance possibly different here: the mesher
pattern in the plain mean (0.131 body lengths on these wings), or the
positional seeds themselves. At 35 cases FRAME-FULL separated them (exact
frame plus all seeds paid *more*, @sec-nb-frame-full-verdict); at the fixed
angle that discriminator has not been run and would need the frame table
extended to the 126 fixed-angle training cases (a CPU job of a few hours)
before a two-lane pair. It is the next ladder follow-up once the 21-geometry
and 210-case rungs, which test recurrence from the other side, have read
out. A third seed on both fixed-angle arms is also warranted by the spreads.

**Consistency half** of this rung (three samplers, five counts, both arms;
job 718951, 60 lanes) is running; the constant-gauge prior collapses 10.6x
/ 14.9x at 40,000 cells there and the gauge is consistent
(@sec-nb-wave4-fixed-angle-bench). Reference ladder so far (float32, vs the
constant-gauge prior): DrivAerML 435 cars −0.9%, 4 geometries +1.0%, fixed
angle +10.3%, 35 cases +11.0%.

## 2026-09-11 — Fixed-angle rung, consistency half of the reference: converges under both samplers (area +45% → +2.6%, bias +81% → +5.5% from 2,500 to 40,000 cells) and is the most accurate arm at every count; the bias reading at 40,000 is still in the inconclusive band where the similarity gauge has already passed {#sec-nb-relframe-ladder-fixed-angle-bench}

The fixed-angle reference checkpoints (@sec-nb-relframe-ladder-fixed-angle)
went through the consistency benchmark's three samplers at five counts,
both scales, two seeds (60 lanes, job 718951, float32 under
code_eval_frame with the bench recipe copy; no loader warnings, all lanes
rc 0; lane table bench/bench_lanes_rffa.tsv; artifact `results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_rffa_2026-09-11.json`), beside the
gauge and constant-gauge rows from @sec-nb-wave4-fixed-angle-bench and
@sec-nb-bench-verdict.

| fixed angle, 18 never-seen geometries, float32 | 2,500 | 5,000 | 10,000 | 20,000 | 40,000 cells |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| reference (relative frame, total-measure scale), uniform error | 0.0540 | 0.0461 | 0.0402 | 0.0375 | 0.0364 |
| reference (relative frame, total-measure scale), area ÷ uniform − 1 | +44.6% | +16.4% | +12.0% | +7.6% | +2.6% |
| reference (relative frame, total-measure scale), bias ÷ uniform − 1 | +80.5% | +35.8% | +24.1% | +14.4% | +5.5% |
| relative frame, reference-length scale, uniform error | 0.0572 | 0.0501 | 0.0444 | 0.0421 | 0.0414 |
| relative frame, reference-length scale, area ÷ uniform − 1 | +40.3% | +15.8% | +8.7% | +6.0% | +1.1% |
| relative frame, reference-length scale, bias ÷ uniform − 1 | +126.1% | +42.8% | +23.9% | +11.8% | +4.4% |
| similarity gauge, uniform error | 0.0577 | 0.0483 | 0.0430 | 0.0403 | 0.0389 |
| similarity gauge, area ÷ uniform − 1 | +25.7% | +12.0% | +7.3% | +4.3% | -0.1% |
| similarity gauge, bias ÷ uniform − 1 | +66.1% | +37.4% | +16.4% | +7.9% | +2.4% |
| constant gauge (prior), uniform error | 0.0465 | 0.0401 | 0.0361 | 0.0347 | 0.0338 |
| constant gauge (prior), area ÷ uniform − 1 | +989.9% | +1162.0% | +1245.1% | +1205.8% | +960.3% |
| constant gauge (prior), bias ÷ uniform − 1 | +990.4% | +1145.4% | +1291.9% | +1339.3% | +1385.4% |

**Against the bars** (|D| ≤ 3% consistent, ≥ 10% reads the distribution,
between inconclusive). The reference is consistent under the
area-proportional sampler at 40,000 cells (+2.6%) and converging under the
10:1 bias (+5.5%, from +81% at 2,500), both monotonically, with its
uniform error falling 1.48x over the same range; the reference-length arm
behaves the same way (+1.1% and +4.4%). The constant-gauge prior reads
the samplers by 960% and 1,385% at 40,000 cells with no convergence, so the
reference passes the consistency test the prior fails, as it did at 35
cases and on the cars. Two honest qualifications. First, the similarity
gauge is the more consistent arm at 40,000 cells on this rung (−0.1% and
+2.4%, both inside the bar) while the reference's bias reading is still
converging; the gauge's frame is a sample statistic that happens to track
the biased draw's own centroid, and the reference has no frame to track it
with, so what is left is the routing integral's variance under a 10:1
sample at a larger relative size on an 18-case validation set than on the
180-case sets, and 40,000 cells is not yet its fine-mesh limit here.
Second, the reference is nevertheless the most accurate configuration
under every sampler at every count (0.0364 at 40,000 uniform against the
gauge's 0.0389), so the price of its consistency shortfall at 40,000 is
smaller than the gauge's accuracy price: under the biased sampler at
40,000 the reference scores 0.0384 and the gauge 0.0399. The consistency
half of the fixed-angle rung is therefore "converging, not yet at the bar
under the bias", stated as such beside the accuracy row.

## 2026-09-12 — Verdict, UDRV-L 510 cases: unit-drive GeoTransolver 0.84x and Transolver 0.90x of the prior ISLA (168 of 180 cases each); the prediction holds at six of seven rungs {#sec-nb-udrvl-510-verdict}

*Setting.* The HiLiftAeroML ladder trains on nested subsets of 35, 210, 510
and 1,260 cases and validates on one 180-case set. The original ladder fed
GeoTransolver and Transolver the physical freestream velocity while ISLA
received a unit direction, which collapsed the baselines' global-context
projector and manufactured ISLA's small-data advantage
(@sec-part-baseline). The unit-drive reruns restore the matched input,
change nothing else, and were preregistered with one prediction: the
unit-drive baselines match or beat ISLA at every rung
(@sec-nb-udrvl-210-verdict for the bars). Five rungs had been measured;
the 510-case rung is the sixth, and the 1,260-case rung remains.

*Instruments.* Four lanes from the wave-2 table (rows 69–72):
GeoTransolver at its reference learning rate of 1e-3 and Transolver at
3e-3, seeds 42 and 43, unit direction supplied through the Hydra
forward-kwargs override, otherwise the frozen ladder protocol (10,000
tokens, 500 epochs). Float32 evaluation under the guarded snapshot on the
180 validation cases (job 724818; 183 rows per run deduplicated to 180 by
sample id; zero skipped loads), reduced with seed means and paired per-case
comparisons on seed-mean pressure against the prior-configuration ISLA of
the ladder (`lad_hl_mt2_medium_seed42/43`, constant gauge) and against the
physical-drive baselines of the original ladder.
Artifact: `results/udrvl_510_reduction_2026-09-12.json`.

*What we saw.* **Unit-drive GeoTransolver scores 0.0410 (seeds 0.0418 /
0.0402) against the prior ISLA's 0.0489 (0.0478 / 0.0499), a ratio of
0.84, and is lower on 168 of the 180 cases; unit-drive Transolver scores
0.0441 (0.0437 / 0.0444), a ratio of 0.90, also lower on 168 of 180.** Both
fall in the "baseline ahead" band of the preregistered bars (0.90 or
below with the baseline lower on at least two thirds of cases;
Transolver sits at the band's edge). The physical-drive baselines of the
original ladder scored 0.0557 and 0.0586 on the same cases, 1.14x and 1.20x
behind ISLA; the unit direction improves GeoTransolver by a median factor of
0.62 per case (lower on 167 of 180 against its physical-drive self) and
Transolver by 0.67 (170 of 180). The 510-case "advantage" of the original
ladder was therefore the input-scale artifact, as at every other rung.

*Reading.* The prediction has now held at six of the seven rungs (35, 210,
510 cases; 4 and 21 geometries; the fixed angle), with GeoTransolver ahead
by 0.76x to 0.92x and Transolver by 0.86x to 0.93x, and the 1,260-case
rerun is the last. Along the case ladder the baseline-to-ISLA ratio is
flat: GeoTransolver 0.80x at 35, 0.83x at 210, 0.84x at 510; Transolver
0.83x, 0.91x, 0.90x. The ISLA value here is the prior configuration's
record; the reference configuration (relative frame, total-measure scale)
has not been trained on this rung, and on the rungs where it has, it pays 0
to 11% relative to the prior, so the ordering would not change. The
bfloat16 evaluation of the same checkpoints (job 724819) is running for the
record and is not used here. Owner: this session.

## 2026-09-12 — RELFRAME-LADDER verdict, 21-geometry and 210-case rungs: the reference pays 5% where geometries are never seen and 11% where they recur, so the recurrence reading is confirmed on its discriminating cell; across six rungs the frame-free reference beats the similarity gauge on never-seen geometries and loses to it on recurring ones {#sec-nb-relframe-ladder-verdict}

The two rungs preregistered together in @sec-nb-relframe-ladder-amend read
out (lanes rf_hl_mt2_meas_geometry_scarce_seed{42,43} and
rf_hl_mt2_meas_scarce_seed{42,43}; reference configuration, unit drive, lr
1e-3, 500 epochs, snapshot code_frame; float32 under code_eval_frame, jobs
725855 and 727672, no loader warnings; artifact `results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json`, block
hilift_val). **21 geometries** (210 training cases, 18 never-seen validation
geometries): 0.1048 / 0.1084 → **0.1066**, +5.2% against the
constant-gauge prior 0.1014 and +2.2% against the similarity gauge's
0.1043. **210 cases** (recurring geometries): 0.0706 / 0.0726 →
**0.0716**, +11.3% against the prior 0.0643 and +9.1% against the
gauge's 0.0656.

**Against the preregistered predictions.** The discriminating cell was the
210-case rung: ≥ 8% confirms the recurrence reading, ≤ 3% refutes it in
favour of data quantity. It reads +11.3%, **recurrence confirmed**: with the
same 210 training cases, the reference pays 11% where the validation
geometries recur in training and 5% where they do not, and the 35-case rung
(recurring) paid 11% too. The 21-geometry cell was predicted ≤ 3% by both
readings and reads +5.1%, just past the cheap band; the recurrence reading
survives with the amendment that never-seen rungs are cheap but not free
when there are many training geometries at varied angles (the 4-geometry
rung, +1.0%, had too few for the pattern to matter either way). The fixed
angle (+10.3%, never seen) remains the one rung the reading does not
cover, as @sec-nb-relframe-ladder-fixed-angle stated.

**The ladder, complete on six rungs** (float32; all rate-matched at lr
1e-3 except the DrivAerML gauge row, which is rate-matched separately):

| rung | training cases | validation geometries | constant gauge (prior) | similarity gauge | **reference** (relative frame, total measure) | reference ÷ gauge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DrivAerML, 435 cars | 435 | same family | 0.0557 | 0.0543 (-2.5%) | **0.0552 (-0.9%)** | 1.017x |
| HiLift, 4 geometries | 40 | never seen | 0.2496 | 0.2680 (+7.4%) | **0.2520 (+1.0%)** | 0.940x |
| HiLift, 21 geometries | 210 | never seen | 0.1014 | 0.1043 (+2.9%) | **0.1066 (+5.2%)** | 1.022x |
| HiLift, fixed angle | 126 | never seen | 0.0348 | 0.0398 (+14.4%) | **0.0384 (+10.3%)** | 0.965x |
| HiLift, 35 cases | 35 | recurring | 0.1377 | 0.1482 (+7.6%) | **0.1529 (+11.0%)** | 1.032x |
| HiLift, 210 cases | 210 | recurring | 0.0643 | 0.0656 (+2.0%) | **0.0716 (+11.3%)** | 1.091x |

**Reading.** Two frames sit beside the plain mean now on every rung. The
similarity gauge estimates a centroid and a scale from the sample; the
reference has no frame at all. Where validation geometries recur in
training (35 and 210 cases) the gauge is 3% and 9% more accurate than the
reference; where they are never seen (4 geometries, fixed angle) the
reference is 7% and 3.5% more accurate, and at 21 geometries and on the
cars they are within 2%. That pattern says what a frame is worth: an
estimated centre and scale give every token an absolute position on *this*
wing, which is reusable information when the same wings return and a
liability that has to be unlearned when they do not. The plain mean adds
the mesher's density pattern on top, which is why it beats both on the
recurring rungs and the fixed angle and neither on the never-seen rungs.
Under @sec-principle and Peter's ruling the reference stays the reference:
the property the program is buying is generalization to geometries,
meshers and poses the training set did not contain, and on the rungs that
test new geometries the frame-free construction is the most accurate ISLA
on the ladder. The price of that choice is now stated per rung: about 11%
where validation geometries recur, 5% at 21 never-seen geometries, 10% at
the fixed angle, and nothing on the cars or at 4 geometries. **The
recurring-rung price is a pro for the frame-free construction only if the
reader's deployment is on new geometries; for a fixed fleet of shapes the
gauge's frame is worth 3–9% and the plain mean's mesher pattern more.**
Both are written into the recommendation rather than hidden.

**Follow-up launched.** The fixed angle is the unexplained rung, and it
now has the prerequisite: the full-geometry frame table for its 144 cases
(frame/frame_table_hilift_single_aoa_12.json; plain-mean displacement 0.132
body lengths, max 0.215). The FRAME-FULL pair at the fixed angle
(exact centroid and scale, all positional seeds kept;
ff_hl_mt2_frame_single_aoa_12_seed{42,43}) separates the two candidates for
its 10%: *positional seeds at a fixed drive* if it recovers to within 3% of
0.0348, *the mesher pattern* if it pays ≥ 7% as the 35-case FRAME-FULL did.
Third seeds of both fixed-angle reference arms (seed 44) are launched with
it, because the pair's spreads (11% and 22%) are the widest on the ladder.
